div.head: Sweetgum-Water Oak Bottomland Hardwood Forest
div.p: Often occurring on low ridges, this Bottomland Hardwood Forest association has the least intense hydric conditions. Plant diversity generally increases with shorter hydroperiod, so this type is also the richest in plant species of the Bottomland Hardwood Forest types.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Bottomland Hardwood Forest is a significant habitat in Louisiana, having historically occupied an estimated 6 million to 8 million acres (Smith 1993). Substantial acreage of this habitat type remains on the landscape today; however, much that remains has been hydrologically altered. and food. Giant Cane was used extensively by Native Americans for building materials and as a food source. Native Americans also managed Canebrake with fire and increased cane extent when their abandoned agricultural fields reverted to cane. This anthropogenic influence is believed to have accounted for the largest and most extensive Canebrake habitat (Noss 2013, Brantley andPlatt 2001). It is hypothesized that the extinct Passenger Pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius) also contributed to the establishment and expansion of Canebrake. Huge flocks of Passenger Pigeons disturbed forests by breaking tree limbs and creating canopy openings. These sunny openings, plus large amounts of nutrient-rich excrement expelled by the birds, created the fertile conditions suitable for Giant Cane (Noss 2013). Canebrake began to decline rapidly after European settlement and, by the early 1900s, had nearly disappeared throughout the southeastern United States. The extinction of the Passenger Pigeon, excessive grazing, altered burning regimes, agricultural land clearing, and flood control projects all contributed to the disappearance of the Canebrake ecosystem (Brantley and Platt 2001).

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Canebrake likely occurred statewide on rich alluvial soil in large and small floodplains and was probably most extensive in the Mississippi and Red river valleys. This habitat is now extirpated in Louisiana.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Identify historical occurrences of Canebrake using General Land Office land survey records and plat maps; concentrate search within the MRAP in areas that are currently captured by conservation lands. 2. Initiate an experimental habitat restoration project on at least one site on an existing conservation area known to have been a Canebrake based on historical evidence and where Giant Cane is still present.

div.head: HARDWOOD FLATWOODS FOREST
div.p: Rarity Ranks: Mesic: G1G2?/S2S3 Wet: G2G3/S2S3 Prairie Terrace Loess Forest: G2/S1 Synonyms: Willow Oak Flat, Pin Oak Flat Wet Hardwood Flatwoods Forest and Mesic Hardwood Flatwoods Forest are sometimes described as two distinct communities but are combined here. Also included in this habitat are Pleistocene Terrace Flatwoods and Prairie Terrace Loess Forest, a mesic flatwoods type restricted to East Baton Rouge Parish.

Wet Hardwood Flatwoods occur on flat, poorly drained settings on older (Pleistocene) landscapes. Mesic Hardwood Flatwoods Forest and Prairie Terrace Loess Forest, also a mesic type, occur on slightly higher and better drained sites. While species composition may overlap substantially with various types of Bottomland Hardwood Forest, Hardwood Flatwoods do not occupy floodplains. Hardwood Flatwoods are also found on sodic (alkali) soils.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Most known occurrences of Hardwood Flatwoods Forest are on the Macon Ridge in northeast Louisiana and on the Prairie Terrace in the northwest part of the state. A small amount of this habitat is captured by Bodcau WMA in Bossier Parish. The Louisiana Army Ammunition Plant in Bossier and Webster parishes supports high-quality Hardwood Flatwoods Forest (McInnis and Martin 1995). In addition to East Baton Rouge, Prairie Terrace Loess Forest may have been present in the adjacent parishes of East Feliciana and Livingston. The historical extent of all types of Hardwood Flatwoods Forest is not known. Prairie Terrace Loess Forest is estimated to have occupied 500,000 to 1 million acres historically, with 1% to 5% remaining today (Smith 1993). Ecology of Hardwood Flatwoods Forest is a major knowledge gap in Louisiana.

div.head: Threats
div.p: This habitat faces potential residential and commercial development and conversion to anthropogenic habitat types. Forestry practices, particularly site preparation methods such as bedding, negatively impact the hydrology, soil, and vegetation composition of Hardwood Flatwoods Forest. Disturbance associated with increased human interface and invasive plants and animals also threaten this habitat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions 1. Implement research on ecology, classification, and extent
div.p: of this habitat type.

div.head: Conduct better mapping of this habitat, particularly on
div.p: Pleistocene terraces. This can be done to some degree with high-resolution LiDAR. 3. Designate this habitat as a high priority for inventory. 4. Seek habitat protection opportunities through conservation easements and land acquisition.

div.head: FOREST SYSTEMS
div.p: Macon Ridge Green Ash Pond, Franklin Parish

div.head: EXTENT OF MACON RIDGE GREEN ASH POND
div.p: Hardwood Flatwoods and, possibly, other forest types on higher elevations of the Macon Ridge. On today's landscape, they are often surrounded by agricultural fields. General Land Office survey records sometimes referred to Macon Ridge Green Ash Ponds as spicewood ponds or spicewood brakes, a possible reference to the aromatic shrub Pondberry, which is federally endangered.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Macon Ridge Green Ash Pond was apparently abundant in pre-settlement times. Many ponds were lost to agriculture; faint outlines of these extirpated ponds in cultivated fields are sometimes evident on aerial imagery. However, many ponds were likely spared, because they were too wet to farm. Some of these extant ponds are now embedded in agricultural fields.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Macon Ridge Green Ash Ponds are threatened by invasive species (particularly EAB), basin alteration and disturbance, and input of agricultural chemicals from adjacent fields. Grand Isle is Louisiana's only Barrier Island that supports a forested community. This forest is restricted to interior portions of Grand Isle, where it is sufficiently buffered from the harsh shoreline environment. Trees in Barrier Island Live Oak Forests can exhibit the effects of saltwater spray and wind, having a stunted appearance and leaning away from the prevailing wind (West 1938, Brown 1930). This community is impacted by development, invasive species, vehicle traffic, clearing of understory vegetation, and habitat fragmentation. Conservation of this system is imperative to the survival of Neotropical migratory birds, which use this habitat for stopover during migration.

div.head: Importance to Neotropical Migratory Birds
div.p: Coastal Live Oak-Hackberry Forest is extremely important as stopover habitat for Neotropical migratory birds during spring and fall migration. The majority of migrants fly nonstop for more than 600 miles to cross the Gulf of America each spring. At least 82 species of migratory birds regularly use these wooded habitats to replenish energy reserves necessary to successfully complete their migration. During fall migration, Coastal Live Oak-Hackberry Forest provides important corridors and staging areas for both trans-Gulf and circum-Gulf migrants, which move along the coast through Texas and around the Gulf of America on their journey to Central and South America.
FOREST SYSTEMS

div.head: SALT DOME HARDWOOD FOREST
div.p: Rarity Rank: G1/S1 Synonyms: None

In the Mississippi Interior Salt Basin, salt domes occur where large, underground salt deposits (deposited by evaporating seas in the Jurassic Period) have risen to or near to the surface (Stern et al. 2011). Louisiana contains approximately 425 salt domes on the mainland and offshore, varying in depth from the Earth's surface (Beckman and Williamson 1990). In cases such as coastal Louisiana's "Five Islands" (Jefferson Island, Avery Island, Weeks Island, Cote Blanche Island, and Belle Isle), the salt domes have raised the surface, creating ridges that rise up from the surrounding marsh habitat. Soils covering most of the islands are very fertile and loess-derived. The hardwood forests of these islands are hilly with deep, shaded ravines, up to 60 feet deep in some places. Ravines are dominated by ferns, and, in many areas, the canopy supports lianas (woody vine species that utilize trees for support and as a means to reach the canopy), giving these forests a tropical appearance (Reese and Thieret 1966). Typically, the herbaceous layer is sparse and consists of several Caric sedges (Carex spp.) and other shade loving herbs.

div.head: FOREST SYSTEMS
div.p: with the original species complement disproportionately represented in extant occurrences. Further field inventories are needed to more fully understand and define this community. Fire, although uncommon, may play an important role in Live Oak-Pine-Magnolia Forest.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: This community is very restricted in Louisiana, known only from St. Tammany Parish along the northshore of Lake Pontchartrain.

The few extant examples of this natural community appear to have an association with fire, as many of the older trees including Live Oak exhibit significant fire scars. The historical extent and status of this natural community are largely unknown. Small tracts of this habitat are protected at Big Branch Marsh NWR, Fontainebleau State Park, and Northlake Nature Center.

div.head: Threats
div.p: This habitat occurs in a rapidly developing part of the state and is threatened by this development and disturbance associated with increased human interface. Potential increased tropical storm frequency and severity associated with climate change also threatens this habitat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Support and conduct inventory and research to identify general ecological characteristics and processes of this habitat. 2. Support invasive species control in this habitat. Baldcypress is not a typical component of this habitat elsewhere in the state. Several ferns and living peat moss (Sphagnum spp.) are often conspicuous in the understories of Acidic Bay Forest. Landscape position can vary from broad depressions or small stream bottoms in flatwoods to narrow stream valleys in hilly terrain, sometimes even occurring on upper slopes. Acidic Bay Forest was historically shaped by natural fire and is typically flanked by fire-dependent pine systems. Acidic Bay Forest receives frequent fire along its edges and only occasionally burns through; therefore, it often serves as a natural fire break. The up-slope edges of Acidic Bay Forest historically experienced fire and likely support species to which a fire-frequent edge is important. These forests naturally vary from a few acres to more than 100 acres in size (Brooks et al. 1993, Smith 1996). (Kelley andBordelon 2024, Smith et al. 1989).

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Calcareous Forest was estimated to occupy 50,000 to 100,000 acres in Louisiana in pre-settlement times, but only 25% to 50% of the original cover remains today (Smith 1993)

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Hardwood Slope Forest once occupied 100,000 to 500,000 acres historically, with an estimated 25% to 50% still remaining (Smith 1993

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: In Louisiana, Pondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest is restricted to the eastern Florida Parishes. No estimates of historical areal extent have been made.
Pondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest, Joyce WMA, Tangipahoa Parish

div.head: Threats Assessment
div.p: Pondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest is threatened by fire suppression and introduction of excessive nutrients, which alters species composition of this acidic and oligotrophic habitat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Conduct field inventories to gain a better understanding of the conservation status of and variation within this habitat. 2. Discourage introduction of partially treated municipal waste water into Pondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest; this swamp type is acidic and oligotrophic and can be degraded by nutrient input. (Beech-Magnolia Forest). This forested wetland is a critical component of the landscape, filtering surface and subsurface flows, improving water quality, and storing sediment and nutrients (Rummer 2004). Spruce Pine is a common associate in the Florida Parishes, and Baldcypress and Loblolly Pine are occasional associates statewide. Historically, this system was intermingled with Canebrake. Mild, low, surface fires largely restricted to the duff layer, would occur in this system; however, the fire intensity and frequency would not alter species composition or structure.

div.head: EXTENT OF SMALL STREAM FOREST
div.p: FOREST SYSTEMS

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Small Stream Forest is widely distributed in broad uplands.

An estimated 25% to 50% of Louisiana's original Small Stream Forest, which is estimated to have been 1 million to 2 million acres, is thought to remain intact (Smith 1993). A number of high-quality examples occur on KNF, Fort Polk-Vernon WMA, and Fort Polk North WMA.

div.head: Threats
div.p: The most impactful threat to this habitat are invasive species, gravel mining, impoundment of streams for reservoirs, as well as natural system modification.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Spruce Pine-Hardwood Flatwoods Forest is restricted to Louisiana, occupying a narrow range in Livingston, East Baton Rouge, East Feliciana, and Ascension parishes. Pre-settlement acreage is estimated at 50,000 to 100,000 acres, with 10% to 25% currently remaining (Smith 1993). Protected occurrences of this habitat occur on Tickfaw State Park and on BREC's Frenchtown Conservation Area and Palomino Park.

div.head: Threats
div.p: The predominant threat to this habitat type is conversion to commercial and residential developments due to the rapid expansion of urbanization along the Interstate 12 corridor in the Florida Parishes. Other major factors threatening this association include conversion to commercial pine plantations and hydrological alterations. Invasive species further threaten this habitat. and nutrient-poor substrates of fine sandy loams or loamy fine sands with relatively high organic matter content (Smith 1996, Plummer 1963). (Barker 1980). This habitat type is extremely sensitive to surrounding land management activities and is easily degraded or destroyed by activities that alter natural hydrologic regimes.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Eastern Hillside Seepage Bog is a habitat type that is naturally small in size. Pre-settlement extent of seepage bogs in the EGCP of Louisiana was estimated to be less than 2,000 acres with only 10% to 25% remaining in St. Tammany and Washington parishes (Smith 1993) Fire, soil conditions, and a seasonally high water table work in concert to regulate community structure in Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna; however, fire is considered the critical element in its maintenance. All of the species indigenous to pine savannas have evolved over millennia within a regime of frequent (once every one to three years) surface fires, and most depend on fire for perpetuation. Fire stimulates flowering and fruit/seed production of savanna herbs and shrubs, deters invasion by fire-intolerant woody vegetation, and exposes mineral soil for herb and Longleaf Pine seedlings to become established. In the absence of frequent burning, pine savannas quickly succeed into shrub/tree thickets, and sun-loving herbs are reduced and eventually eliminated (Smith 1996).

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna remnants are limited in size compared to the broad expanses that once existed. Historically, the eastern Florida Parishes of Louisiana were dominated by extensive stands of this habitat; barely 1% of the original estimated 100,000 to 500,000 acres of Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna remains (Smith 1993). Habitat conversion, development, and timber production were initial factors in this habitat loss. Today, there are a few thousand acres in small blocks scattered across this area. TNC protects and manages Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna on portions of their Abita Creek Flatwoods, Lake Ramsay Savannah, and Talisheek Pine Wetlands preserves. LDWF owns and manages Lake Ramsay Savannah WMA (796 acres of savanna) which is adjacent to TNC's Lake Ramsay Preserve. Big Branch NWR, Bogue Chitto NWR, and Pearl River WMA contain "pine flatwoods" with remnants of herbaceous savanna flora, and some of these sites are in the process of being restored to Longleaf Pine systems. Wetland mitigation banking has become a valuable tool for restoring Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savannas. Several mitigation banks located in close proximity to TNC preserves are protecting and restoring this habitat.

div.head: Threats
div.p: This habitat occurs in a rapidly developing part of the state and is threatened by residential and commercial development and disturbance from human interface. This habitat is firedependent and is threatened by fire exclusion and inadequate fire. Invasive species also pose a threat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Prioritize this habitat type for inventory to determine extent and condition with a focus on identifying the surrounding landscape context (e.g., residential developments, etc.) that might be affected by prescribed burning.

2. Carry out habitat assessments and botanical and zoological surveys on mitigation banks supporting this habitat; work with USACE and mitigation bank sponsors to maximize ecological value of this habitat on mitigation banks. 3. Educate landowners, adjacent residents, developers, parishes, and the general public about the crucial role of prescribed burning in the management of Longleaf Pine systems and promote the advantages of growing Longleaf Pine and associated herbaceous ground cover. 4. Work with partners to incorporate strategies for Longleaf Pine management and restoration into current restoration efforts. 5. Target this habitat for acquisition from willing sellers, protection (e.g., servitudes), and stewardship implementation. This includes pursuing tracts that are degraded but restorable with timber harvesting and prescribed fire. 6. Develop and support a Prescribed Burn Association for this region. EXTENT OF EASTERN UPLAND LONGLEAF PINE SAVANNA AND WOODLAND

div.head: EASTERN UPLAND LONGLEAF PINE SAVANNA AND WOODLAND
Threats
div.p: Most of the historical extent of this habitat has already been converted to anthropogenic forests, and much has been lost to residential and commercial development. The most pressing threats to remaining occurrences are inadequate fire and invasive species.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Educate landowners, adjacent residents, developers, and the general public about the crucial role of prescribed burning in the management of Longleaf Pine systems, the advantages of growing Longleaf Pine and associated herbaceous ground cover, and promote value-added products produced from Longleaf Pine to encourage landowners to replant Longleaf Pine instead of Loblolly Pine.
2. Continue to provide cost-share funds through various programs to reduce or eliminate landowners' costs associated with conducting prescribed burns on their property.

div.head: Work with partners to incorporate strategies beneficial to
div.p: Longleaf Pine into management and restoration efforts. 4. Target this habitat for acquisition from willing sellers, protection (e.g., servitudes), and stewardship implementation. This includes pursuing tracts that are degraded but restorable with timber harvesting and prescribed fire. 5. Develop and support a Prescribed Burn Association for this region.

div.head: SLASH PINE-PONDCYPRESS WOODLAND
div.p: Rarity Rank: G2?/S1 Synonyms: Slash Pine Flatwoods, Wet pine-Pondcypress Savanna

This wetland habitat is restricted to the wet, acidic flatwoods on the far eastern Pleistocene Prairie Terrace of Louisiana's EGCP. Slash Pine-Pondcypress Woodland is situated in wetter depressions of Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna. This community is characterized by a diverse understory, similar in species composition to those found in wet Longleaf Pine savannas, though it is more closely associated with more hydric site conditions. It features an open to semi-open canopy savanna to woodland structure with a species-rich ground layer and is a fire dependent system. Its structure and species composition can vary significantly from site to site, influenced by subtle differences in topography, soil characteristics, hydrology, and fire history (Teague et al. 1995).

Soils of the Slash Pine-Pondcypress Woodland are hydric, strongly acidic, and nutrient poor silt loams and fine sandy loams. Surface soils are typically saturated for much of the year, and shallow water may be present in the late fall, winter, and early spring, and after rains during the growing season.

Slash Pine-Pondcypress Woodland evolved with recurrent lightning-season ground fires, and regular, low intensity, surface fire appears critical in maintaining this community. Both Slash Pine and Pondcypress (Taxodium ascendens) are fire-adapted species and can survive fires once they attain a certain size; however, neither is as fire resistant as Longleaf Pine. The natural fire return interval of this community is short (two to three years) and similar to adjacent Longleaf Pine savannas, though fires in this community were likely less intense and less effective on the wetter expressions of this community type. This allowed for uneven encroachment and regeneration of Slash Pine and Pondcypress, at times, as well as precluded complete dominance of the site by Slash Pine, Pondcypress, and hardwoods.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: In the EGCP of Louisiana, Slash Pine-Pondcypress Woodland is primarily associated with flatwoods ponds, Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna, and Acidic Bay Forest. Protected examples occur on TNC's Talisheek Pine Wetlands and Abita Creek Flatwoods preserves. In Louisiana, this system is restricted to southern portions of St. Tammany Parish and possibly a portion of southern Tangipahoa Parish.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Conversion to anthropogenic habitats has affected this habitat and is expected to continue, along with fire exclusion and disturbance from human activities.

Chapter 5: Natural Communities . Some examples of this community are prairie-like with little to no canopy and dense herbaceous understories, while others appear to take on brushy woodland characteristics. Notably, Pondberry has been reported along edges of a Lowland Sand Prairie within the Coffee Prairie Natural Area in southern Arkansas and may be associated with Ouachita Sand Prairie and Woodland habitat edges in northern Louisiana.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Additional field survey work is needed in order to accurately determine the status and extent of Ouachita Sand Prairie and Woodland.
Ouachita Sand Prairie Ouachita Sand Prairie

div.head: EXTENT OF OUACHITA SAND PRAIRIE AND WOODLAND
Threats
div.p: Examples of Ouachita Sand Prairie and Woodland have been mostly found in an impaired or degraded state. In some of these areas, this may be due to failed conversions to Loblolly Pine plantations, which are now mostly covered with Chinese Tallow Tree and excessive brush. The historical role fire played in this community is yet to be determined, but fire suppression may be a threat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Prioritize surveys for Ouachita Sand Prairie and Woodland to determine history, extent, and status. 2. Create a management plan to control brush and invasive species (particularly Chinese Tallow Tree) while considering the historical role of fire in this community.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Sandstone Glades are thought to have occupied less than 2,000 acres in pre-settlement times with an estimated 50-75% remaining today (Smith 1993). Most known occurrences are on the Kisatchie District of KNF in southern Natchitoches Parish.
There are a number of Sandstone Glades on private lands in Sabine Parish.

div.head: Threats
div.p: This habitat is threatened by disturbance and the resulting soil erosion. Glades with deeper soil are fire-dependent and are degraded by woody encroachment without adequate fire.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Continue surveys to determine the current extent and condition of this habitat type and support research on the community classification of Sandstone Glade/Barren. 2. Encourage and fund the use of prescribed fire and chemical and mechanical brush control as management tools. 3. Work with timber companies to ensure they can recognize this plant community and apply appropriate management techniques and buffers when warranted. Little is known about this habitat in Louisiana.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: In Louisiana, this habitat is only known from the xeric, sandy, upland Longleaf Pine Woodland on the Sparta Formation in Bienville Parish and likely occupies less than 100 acres.

Chapter 5: Natural Communities . It occurs commonly on mid-to lower slopes on saturated, strongly acidic (pH ca. 4.5 to 5.5), and nutrient-poor substrates of fine sandy loams or loamy fine sands with relatively high organic matter content (Smith 1996). Soil series names have generally not been assigned to bogs due to the naturally limited acreage in the state (Smith 1996). Soils of this bog type are generally persistently wet from seepage and are saturated at or near the surface for most or all of the year. This bog type is variable in size being most often less than one acre, but rarely exceeding 10 acres. (Barker 1980).

The degree to which a bog remains wet throughout the year depends on the size of the watershed, the soil infiltration rate upslope, the rate of saturated flow in the soil, the topographic position of the bog, the bog's water storage capacity, and the rate of water leaving the bog from evapotranspiration and through surface and subsurface flow. In general, the greater the infiltration rate of the watershed soils and the water holding capacity of bog soils, the smaller the recharge area needed to maintain seepage throughout dry periods of the year. Therefore, bogs are extremely sensitive to surrounding land management activities and are easily degraded or destroyed by activities that alter natural hydrology of the surface or subsurface, especially actions such as timber harvesting, bedding, and fire break installations.
Western Hillside Seepage Bog, Fort Polk, Vernon Parish

div.head: SAVANNAS AND WOODLANDS
div.p: EXTENT OF WEST GULF COASTAL PLAIN MUCK BOG

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: This habitat occurs as small patches and is historically thought to have occupied less than 2,000 acres with an estimated 50% to 75% remaining today. In the WGCP, Hillside Seepage Bog is found from Calcasieu north to Natchitoches and Winn parishes.

Most known occurrences are in Vernon and Natchitoches parishes on KNF and Fort Polk-Vernon WMA, and there are possibly many more bogs within this geography (e.g., few biological inventories have occurred in Beauregard Parish).

div.p: Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna -Saline

div.head: Threats
div.p: Fire exclusion or inadequate fire and invasive species (especially Feral Hogs), and hydrology alterations are the main threats to this habitat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Continue surveys to determine the extent and condition of this habitat type. 2. Work with staff of KNF and Ft. Polk to implement appropriate management, including optimal fire timing and frequency. 3. Encourage landowners to include this community type in prescribed burning plans and discourage the placement of firebreaks or bedding in and around bogs. 4. Provide additional cost-share funds for landowners to reduce or eliminate the costs associated with conducting prescribed burns on their property. 5. Develop and support a Prescribed Burn Association throughout the range of this natural community. 6. Support control of Feral Hogs within and near this habitat type.
Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna -Acidic

div.head: WESTERN LONGLEAF PINE FLATWOODS SAVANNA
div.p: Rarity Rank: Acidic: G2G3/S2 Saline: G1/S1 Synonyms: Open Savanna, Pine Savanna, Pine Flatwoods, Grass-Sedge Bog, Pitcher-Plant Prairie, Coastal Meadow, Pine Meadow, Pine Barren, Pitcher-Plant Meadow, Pitcher-Plant Bog, Herbaceous Bog, Flatwoods Bog Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savannas are herb-dominated wetlands that are naturally sparsely stocked with Longleaf Pine. This community is most often dominated by numerous grasses and sedges in the understory and is noted for very high plant diversity, including insectivorous plants, showy orchids, lilies, and many other types of wildflowers. Club-mosses (Lycopodium spp.) and peat mosses are often conspicuous. One essential difference between Western and Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savannas is that the western expression of this system is typically associated with pimple-mounded topography, generating a complex matrix of upland and wetland plant communities. The only known extant Louisiana occurrences of American Chaffseed (Schwalbea americana), which is federally endangered, are found on pimple mounds in Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna in Allen and Beauregard parishes. Pine savannas historically dominated the Gulf Coastal Plain flatwoods regions of southeast and southwest Louisiana (Smith 1996).

Two types of Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna are recognized: Acidic (S2) and Saline (sodic/alkali; S1). Acidic Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna occurs on a variety of soils, while Saline Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna is restricted to mainly Brimstone Silt Loam and possibly other sodic or alkali soil types.

Wet savannas in the WGCP occupy the poorly drained and seasonally saturated/flooded depressional areas and low flats, whereas the non-wetland flatwoods occupy better drained, low ridges. Pine savannas experience a highly fluctuating water table, ranging from surface saturation/shallow flooding in late fall, winter, and early spring to growing season drought. Soils are hydric, very strongly acidic, nutrient poor, fine sandy loams and silt loams, and are low in organic matter. The surface soils for both western and eastern types may be underlain by slowly permeable subsoil through which air and water move slowly.

Frequent fire is a major factor controlling species occurrence and community structure. All of the species indigenous to pine savannas have evolved over millennia within a regime of frequent (once every one to three years) surface fires, and most depend on fire for perpetuation. Fire stimulates flowering and fruit/seed production of savanna herbs and shrubs, deters invasion by fire-intolerant woody vegetation, and exposes mineral soil for herb and Longleaf Pine seedlings to become established.Without frequent fire (particularly growing season burns, which more accurately mimic historical fire regimes), shrubs and trees, especially Loblolly and Slash pines, will gain dominance and eventually eliminate the herbaceous flora.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna and embedded habitats are highly threatened and much reduced from their original extent. This habitat is estimated to have occupied 1 million to 2 million acres in pre-settlement times with an estimated 1% to 5% remaining (Smith 1993).

Most extant Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna occur on private land, although one of the largest tracts occurs on the southwestern portion of KNF Vernon Unit. A combination of factors has favored their continued existence during the last 100 years, including their utilization as rangeland (involving frequent burning). Several examples are captured by the newly acquired LDWF Flatwoods Savanna WMA and conservation lands owned by TNC. When science-based criteria and standards are employed, wetland mitigation banking can be a key tool for conservation of this habitat. Recovery potential in degraded examples varies depending on the site history. In some cases, much of the diverse herbaceous ground cover has returned with the reintroduction of fire.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Threats include conversion to Slash or Loblolly pine plantations, residential and commercial development, fire exclusion or inappropriate fire regime, hydrological alterations, contamination by chemicals (herbicides, fertilizers), and physical damage from timber harvesting and planting activities (Smith 1996), severe weather events, and climate change. Invasive species also threaten this habitat.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Most of the historical acreage of this habitat now supports anthropogenic forests. Due to rarity and limited opportunity, additional habitat conversion is expected to be infrequent but to have severe consequences where it does occur. This habitat is mainly threatened by inadequate fire. Climate change, with its projected increase in severe weather, threatens this habitat.
Several sources of human disturbance also degrade this habitat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Continue surveys to determine the extent and condition of this habitat. 2. Educate landowners, adjacent residents, developers, and the general public about the crucial role of prescribed burning in the management of Longleaf Pine. 3. Continue to promote advantages of growing Longleaf Pine and associated herbaceous ground cover in cooperation with the Longleaf Alliance and incorporate their strategies for restoration into new and ongoing restoration efforts. 4. Promote value-added products produced from Longleaf Pine to encourage landowners to replant Longleaf Pine instead of off-site pine species. 5. Support and provide cost-share opportunities to offset costs to landowners for management activities such as prescribed burning, brush control, and invasive species control in this habitat. 6. Target this habitat for acquisition, protection (e.g., conservation servitudes), and stewardship implementation. This includes pursuing tracts that are degraded but restorable with timber harvesting and prescribed fire. Trees, often appearing stunted, may be present in deeper, more frequently flooded and, therefore, less fire-exposed, areas of ponds. The hydrologic regime of these ponds is characterized by a seasonally fluctuating water level -dry in summer and fall and flooded to various depths in winter and early spring. This water level fluctuation causes distinct vegetation zones with species occurring according to their relative tolerance or competitive adaptations to flooding and saturated soil conditions. The Flatwoods Pond natural communities were historically maintained by frequent lightning-generated fires that swept the Longleaf Pine flatwoods savannas every few years. Such fires burned into the ponds during the late spring/summer dry season, killing back encroaching shrubs and trees and rejuvenating the herbaceous ground cover. These communities provide important breeding habitat for many amphibians, including several SGCN. Smith (1993) estimated that Flatwoods Pond habitat occupied 2,000 to 10,000 acres historically. Bridges (1988) surveyed the WGCP of Louisiana extensively for this community and estimated that less than 100 Flatwoods Ponds remain and determined that less than 20 were still of high-quality. Based on recent surveys by LDWF staff, it is estimated that less than 80 Flatwoods Ponds remain in Louisiana and that approximately 12 to 15 remain in a high-quality state. It is not clear if Smith's estimate is for all Flatwoods Pond habitat or simply those in the WGCP. However, these features are significantly more prolific in the WGCP than the EGCP. Examples of high quality Flatwoods Ponds can be observed at the newly acquired LDWF Flatwoods Savanna WMA in Allen Parish.

div.head: SHORTLEAF PINE/OAK-HICKORY WOODLAND
div.p: Rarity Rank: G2G3/S1 Synonyms: Shortleaf Pine-Oak Woodland, Oak-Hickory Forest

The Shortleaf Pine/Oak-Hickory Woodland community occurs on dry hills, principally in north-central and northwestern Louisiana as well as in the Florida Parishes. In the UWGCP, this was the most prevalent habitat on the landscape (i.e. it was the matrix community). Small pockets of this community type also occur in the Longleaf Pine region of the WGCP. The overstory is composed of a combination of Shortleaf Pine (Pinus echinata) and various dry-sited hardwood species, predominantly oaks and hickories.

The herbaceous component of this community is just as much, if not more, important than the canopy component. The ground cover was historically grassy and similar to that of Longleaf Pine systems. However, the ground cover in Shortleaf Pine/ Oak-Hickory Woodland was likely variable and possessed some shaded areas with associated shade-loving plants, in contrast to large continuous stands of sun-loving plants found in Longleaf Pine grasslands. Some expressions of this community have a calcareous component and, thus, are similar to calcareous woodland and forest types. Fire is an important process in this community, and historical fire frequency is thought to have been 5 to 15 years (Martin and Smith 1993) or more frequently but with very low intensities and restricted to the duff layer, especially for Shortleaf Pine/Oak-Hickory Woodland embedded within other pyrogenic communities.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: There was an estimated 4 million to 6 million acres of Shortleaf Pine/Oak-Hickory Woodland in Louisiana (Smith 1993) and, of this original extent, less than 5% is thought to remain today. Most

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Xeric Sandhill Woodlands are more frequent west of the Mississippi River. A few examples of this habitat are known from stream terraces (e.g., along Pushepatappa Creek). Pre-settlement extent of Xeric Sandhill Woodland habitat west of the Mississippi River is estimated to have been 50,000 to 100,000 acres, with 10-25% remaining today (Smith 1993)

div.head: Threats
div.p: The main threats to this habitat are destruction by residential and commercial development and conversion of land for energy production and anthropogenic forests, as well as disturbance from several sources including mineral extraction and other human activities. Inadequate fire is also a threat to occurrences that are situated in a position on the landscape where fire was historically important in shaping the habitat. Brackish Marsh is usually found between Salt Marsh and Intermediate Marsh, although it may occasionally lie adjacent to the Gulf of America. This community is irregularly tidally flooded and is dominated by salt-tolerant graminoids. Small pools or ponds may be scattered throughout. Plant diversity and soil organic matter content are higher in Brackish Marsh than in Salt Marsh. Brackish Marsh is typically dominated by Marshhay Cord Grass (Spartina patens). Two other major autotrophic groups in Brackish Marsh are epiphytic algae and benthic algae. Vertebrate species population levels are generally higher in Brackish Marsh compared to Salt Marsh. Brackish Marsh is of very high value to estuarine larval forms of marine organisms such as shrimp, crabs, and Menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus). Brackish Marsh salinity averages about 8 ppt; however, this community may transition to other marsh types by shifts in salinity. Intrusion of salt water from the Gulf via numerous waterways exerts a major influence in the configuration of the various marsh types.

div.head: Research Needs and
div.p: High Marsh is a unique form of coastal marsh that occurs on slightly higher elevation sites and is thus flooded infrequently, typically only during extreme tides, spring tides, and storm surge events. management of these sites is largely aimed at preserving and improving wintering waterfowl habitat. This involves the use of water control structures to regulate water levels and salinity input, water and sediment diversions to abate marsh deterioration, and prescribed burning to improve habitat and food quality for wildlife.

div.head: Threats
div.p: The main threats to this habitat include sediment supply reduction due to development, levees, canal dredging, subsidence, SLR, incompatible fire and livestock management practices, and the effects of potential increases in storm frequency and intensity associated with climate change.

div.head: EXTENT OF COASTAL MANGROVE-MARSH AND SHRUBLAND
div.p: several important ecological functions: the extensive root systems stabilize the shoreline and reduce erosion; the cover and food they provide create an excellent nursery area for fish and shellfish; the community improves surrounding water quality by filtering nutrients and suspended sediments; and many colonial waterbirds use mangroves for nesting.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Coastal Mangrove-Marsh and Shrubland in Louisiana is found along the fringes of the Deltaic Plain coastal marshes, most commonly flanking large bays and on the leeward side of barrier islands. Estimations of areal coverage by this habitat have varied widely. The limitations of past and present aerial photography technology and difficulties associated with ground-truthing can make estimating acreage problematic. Research Needs and Conservation Actions 1. Promote the continued planting of mangrove as a soil stabilizer in habitat restoration projects. 2. Support partner efforts for shoreline stabilization and habitat restoration. 3. Work with partners to support coastal restoration projects, specifically targeting habitat and habitat features important for SGCN.

div.head: FRESHWATER FLOATING MARSH
div.p: Rarity Rank: GNR/S2 Synonyms: Flotant, Peat Marsh, Prairie Tremblant

Freshwater Floating Marsh is an emergent marsh that, along with peat (decomposing organic matter), composes a freefloating mat that rises and falls with water levels. The flotant described herein has a 2-3 ft. thick mat that typically supports the weight of a person. The grass Maidencane (Hymenachne hemitoma) is the dominant plant in this community and is apparently the best species for forming buoyant floating mats due to its prolific root production. Evidence suggests that this Freshwater Floating Marsh developed from detachment of a rooted marsh following formation of a peat zone (Swarzenski et al. 1991, Sasser et al. 1995, Sasser et al. 1996). Buoyancy of the floating mat is affected by the capacity of the vegetation to float (internal air spaces, vegetative characteristics), capacity of the substrate to retain metabolic gases, and low bulk density of the substrate (Swarzenski et al. 1991, Sasser et al. 1995, Sasser et al. 1996). The Maidencane-dominated Freshwater Floating Marsh is buoyant year-round, whereas thick-mat Freshwater Floating Marsh dominated by Bulltongue (Sagittaria lancifolia) is only seasonally buoyant (Swarzenski et al. 1991). Freshwater Floating Marsh of the type described here is typically rainfall, rather than floodwater-driven (Swarzenski et al. 2005), and the pH is usually acidic (C. Swarzenski, personal communication).

Peat mosses (Sphagnum spp.) are often conspicuous. This habitat supports a number of plants that otherwise occur in acidic seepage wetlands in interior Louisiana, including several showy orchids. As with interior prairies and pine grasslands, Freshwater Floating Marsh is readily colonized by the shrub Wax-myrtle. Fire is required to prevent conversion of emergent herbaceous marsh to shrub thicket.

The Maidencane Freshwater Floating Marsh is restricted to freshwater environments. State transitions can occur with environmental changes such as increases in salinity, sediment input, and nutrient input. With increasing salinity, the plant community may transition to a Bulltongue-dominated community (Sasser et al. 1996, Swarzenski et al. 1991). Key to the sustainability of the Freshwater Floating Marsh is a thick healthy mat. Nutrients and sulfate introduced by seawater can weaken the floating mat by accelerating decomposition of the peat. More than half of the Freshwater Floating Marshes in the Terrebonne

Basin have converted to thin, unstable mats and open water over the past 50 years (Visser et al. 1996). Concurrently, the source of fresh water in the Terrebonne Basin has shifted from rain water to river water (Swarzenski et al. 2008). Eutrophication by introduction of Mississippi River water via diversions may destabilize intact floating marshes (Swarzenski et al. 2008). Salinity pulses, if increasing in persistence and duration, could also destabilize thick mat Freshwater Floating Marsh.

Colonization of stands of free-floating plants by emergent marsh vegetation can happen. For example, free-floating invasives such as Water Hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) and Common and Giant Salvinia (Salvinia minima and S. molesta, respectively) can recruit emergent aquatic and wetland plants, eventually forming a well-developed floating mat (Penfound and Earle 1948). Such floating mats are outside of the concept of the Freshwater Floating Marsh discussed here, despite the broad and general application of the term "flotant."

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: The majority of floating marsh in Louisiana is associated with the Deltaic Plain. However, a unique form of freshwater floating marsh was described by O'Neal (1949) from the eastern portion of the Chenier Plain. Floating marshes of all types are estimated to occupy 375,000 acres (Evers et al. 1996, Sasser et al. 1996) Chapter 5: Natural Communities

div.head: Threats
div.p: Freshwater Floating Marsh is threatened by input of nutrients and salinity, which is hastened by human activities associated with placement of canals and diversions as well as other habitat alteration to the marsh landscape. Inadequate fire is also an issue for some occurrences, which allows shrub dominance. Because this marsh type is highly buoyant, it has some resilience to subsidence; however, increases in salinity associated with subsidence of surrounding rooted marshes poses a serious threat to this habitat. Aerial overspray from herbicide applications or excessive herbicide use may have prolonged negative impacts and cause floating mash collapse.

div.head: NON-FORESTED GRASSLANDS AND OPEN TERRAIN
div.p: Freshwater Marsh, southeast Louisiana

div.head: FRESHWATER MARSH
div.p: Rarity Rank: G3G4/S2 Synonyms: Fresh Marsh, Paille Fine (pronounced "pie feen") Marsh

Freshwater Marsh is normally located adjacent to Intermediate Marsh along the northern most extent of the coastal marshes, although it may occur beside coastal bays where freshwater enters (e.g., Atchafalaya Bay). Small pools or ponds may be scattered. The floristic composition of these sites is quite heterogeneous and variable from site to site. Frequency and duration of flooding, which are intimately related to microtopography, seem to be the primary factors governing plant species distributions. Substrate, current flow, salinity, competition, and allelopathy are also important in determining species distribution patterns. Freshwater Marsh has the greatest plant diversity and highest soil organic matter content of any marsh type. Chabreck (1972) As with the other marsh types, Freshwater Marsh acts as an important nursery area for the young of many marine species such as Atlantic Croaker (Micropogonias undulates), Spotted Seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus), Black Drum (Pogonias cromis), and flounder (Paralichthys spp.). This community may change to a more saline marsh type due to saltwater intrusion or may become open water due to subsidence.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Coastal marshes are highly dynamic systems; thus, the acreage of each marsh type has varied greatly across time. Presettlement, Louisiana coastal marshes covered approximately 4.5 million acres (Smith 1993). Based on surveys conducted in 2021, the remaining total coastal marsh extent in Louisiana is 3.62 million acres (Nyman et al. 2022), which is approximately 80% of the estimate pre-settlement extent. Statewide coastal marsh surveys conducted in 2021, estimated that approximately 992,000 acres are Freshwater Marsh (Nyman et al. 2022).

Freshwater Marsh has undergone the largest reduction in acreage of any of the marsh types over the past 30 years, due mainly to saltwater intrusion; canal dredging; and commercial, industrial and residential development. The largest contiguous tracts of Freshwater Marsh occur in Terrebonne, St. Mary, Vermilion, Cameron, Lafourche, and St. Charles parishes (Hartley et al. 2000). In the Chenier Plain of southwestern Louisiana, federal lands containing Freshwater Marsh include Sabine, Cameron Prairie, and Lacassine NWRs. White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area captures a substantial amount of Freshwater Marsh on state land. In the Deltaic Plain of southeastern Louisiana, LDWF lands with Freshwater Marsh include the Atchafalaya Delta, Salvador, Timken, Pass-a-Loutre, and Pearl River WMAs, and to a lesser extent, Joyce and Maurepas Swamp WMAs. Federal lands with Freshwater Marsh in the Deltaic Plain include Delta, Bayou Sauvage, Big Branch Marsh, and Mandalay NWRs.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Threats to this habitat include sediment and freshwater supply reduction due to levees, canal dredging, subsidence, SLR, salinity input, and invasive species (especially Feral Hogs and Nutria). Increased storm frequency and intensity associated with climate change would subject Freshwater Marsh to a greater disturbance and potentially result in higher incidences of saltwater intrusion in concert with SLR.

div.head: INTERMEDIATE MARSH
div.p: Rarity Rank: G4?/S3 Synonyms: Oligohaline Marsh Intermediate Marsh is fresh most of the time but is occasionally affected by saltwater inputs associated with tropical storm surges. This marsh type typically lies between Brackish Marsh and Freshwater Marsh and in estuaries, although it infrequently may be adjacent to the Gulf of America. Intermediate Marsh has an irregular tidal regime and is oligohaline (salinity of 3-10 ppt). Small pools or ponds may be scattered throughout the marsh. Plant diversity and soil organic matter content is higher than in Brackish Marsh. This marsh is characterized by a diversity of species, many of which are found in Freshwater Marsh and some of which are found in Brackish Marsh. Chabreck (1972) Intermediate Marsh, St. Tammany Parish

div.head: SALT MARSH
div.p: Rarity Rank: G5/S4 Synonyms: Smooth Cord Grass Marsh, Saltgrass Marsh, Saline Marsh Typically, Salt Marsh is the marsh area closest to the beach rim of the Gulf of America and, in general, varies from 1 to 15 miles in width. This marsh is a regularly tidally flooded, flat, polyhaline Small pools or ponds may be scattered. Salt Marsh has the lowest plant diversity and soil organic matter content of any marsh type. This community is strongly dominated by Smooth Cord Grass (Spartina alterniflora). Two other major groups of autotrophs found in Salt Marsh are microscopic algae located on the surface of the vascular plants and benthic algae (usually diatoms) living on or in marsh sediment. Soil and water conditions regulate plant growth, and salinity appears to be the primary factor determining species composition. The mean salinity of Salt Marsh is about 16 ppt. The area of Salt Marsh is increasing, apparently due to saltwater intrusion resulting in shifts in marsh salinity levels. Salt Marsh provides nursery areas for larval forms of many species such as shrimp, crabs, Red Drum, Spotted Seatrout, and Menhaden, and greatly enhances the production of such marine organisms due to the enormous primary productivity of the Salt Marsh vegetation. Factors that promote the growth of Salt Marsh plants include: (1) a long growing season, (2) abundant rainfall, (3) presence of soil nutrients, (4) low tide differential, and (5) tidally transported nutrients. Factors negatively impacting Salt Marsh include prolonged periods of inundation, subsidence, and erosion.

div.head: EXTENT OF SALT MARSH
div.p: Salt Marsh also functions as a nitrogen and phosphorus sink (at least seasonally), thereby improving the quality of water that passes through it. In addition, Salt Marsh can alleviate the effects of storms and flooding farther inland by acting as a buffer and providing storage for large amounts of water. Although Salt Marsh is known for low species diversity overall, a few species are wholly dependent on this habitat. For example, Seaside Sparrow (Ammospiza maritima) is endemic to Salt Marsh, one of only five such Salt Marsh-obligate vertebrate species on Earth (Greenberg et al. 2006).

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Coastal marshes are highly dynamic systems; thus, the acreage of each marsh type has varied greatly across time. Presettlement, Louisiana coastal marshes covered approximately 4.5 million acres (Smith 1993). Based on surveys conducted in 2021, the remaining total coastal marsh extent in Louisiana is 3.62 million acres (Nyman et al. 2022), which is approximately 80% of the estimate pre-settlement extent. Statewide coastal marsh surveys conducted in 2021, estimated that 805,650 acres are Salt Marsh (Nyman et al. 2022). Salt Marsh is most extensive on the Deltaic Plain of southeastern Louisiana. The area of Salt Marsh is currently increasing, likely due to saltwater intrusion resulting in shifts in marsh salinity levels.

div.head: VEGETATED PIONEER EMERGING DELTA
div.p: Rarity Rank: G3G4/S3 Synonyms: Delta Flats, Emergent Islands Vegetated Pioneer Emerging Delta is a dynamic community forming primarily within the actively building delta region at the mouth of the Atchafalaya and Mississippi rivers. Substrates contain a greater percentage of sand and less moisture than do marsh soils. The pioneer ridge vegetation is similar to the Sandbars and delta of the Mississippi River, whereas the pioneer marsh vegetation is similar to that of Freshwater Marsh. This community can be floristically diverse, containing many species also found on Sandbars. Rapid invasion by the invasive Torpedo Grass (Panicum repens) reduces plant species richness, particularly on higher sandy deposits. The pioneer community is successional in nature and changes rapidly with time. The new delta community's ecological functions are similar in nature to marsh and mudflat systems.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: According to Smith (1993), there was an estimated 2,000 to 10,000 acres of Vegetated Pioneer Emerging Delta in presettlement times; an estimated 75% to 100% of this amount is present today. Two areas of the Louisiana coast support this habitat: the actively forming Atchafalaya Delta and the current mouth of the Mississippi River. In the case of the former area, newly accreted delta land is incorporated into Atchafalaya Delta WMA. Pass-A-Loutre WMA, near the mouth of the Mississippi River, contains natural and constructed crevasses which promote the expansion of this habitat type.

div.head: Threats
div.p: The greatest threat to this habitat is invasive plant and animal species, primarily Feral Hogs and Nutria, which denude newly created delta habitat via rooting and wallowing behavior and direct herbivory, respectively.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Since deltaic processes have been altered due to the leveeing of the Mississippi River, no new barrier islands are expected to form. Major efforts are underway to rebuild and preserve remaining islands. These efforts include using breakwaters to buffer wave action and retain sediment, pumping sand onto beaches and dunes, creating back barrier marsh platforms, and the use of sand fencing and vegetative planting to anchor sand and stabilize the substrate.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Barrier Islands are threatened by habitat destruction and disturbance by humans, trash and marine debris accumulation, subsidence, SLR, hydrologic alterations, inadequate sand supply, and increased frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones. Calcareous Prairie is typically a small, naturally treeless area occurring on calcareous substrata in the uplands of central, western, and northwestern Louisiana. Prairie communities can range in size from less than one acre to 100 or more acres and occur in a mosaic with Calcareous Forests (Smith et al. 1989).

div.head: SANDBAR: OBLIGATE OR NEAR-OBLIGATE SGCN
div.p: Calcareous Prairie has been identified in association with four geological formations:

div.head: COASTAL PRAIRIE
div.p: Rarity Rank: G2Q/S1 Synonyms: Great Southwest Prairie, Eastern Coastal Prairie, Gulf Cordgrass Prairie, Cajun Prairie

Coastal Prairie is an extension of the tall-grass prairie of the eastern Great Plains and is characterized by a diverse flora consisting of tall grasses and forbs. A combination of historical dry climate intervals, clay-pan soils (which accentuate the effects of drought), and frequent fire are thought to account for the presence of tall-grass prairie in humid Louisiana. Studies of remnant prairies suggest there are three prairie types, based on moisture: wet (marsh-fringing) prairie, wet-mesic prairie, and dry-mesic prairie. Small, circular, soil mounds known as pimple mounds can be found in Coastal Prairie. These mounds were formed by eolian deposition during historical harsh droughts (Siefert et al. 2009) and, possibly, fluvial deposition during periods with higher than normal precipitation (Wilcox et al. 2011). Pimple mounds and embedded marshes and ponds (e.g., Prairie Pothole) add to the habitat diversity of the Coastal Prairie landscape.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Coastal Prairie historically occupied about 2.22 million acres in southwest Louisiana (Grace et al. 2000). About 0.02% (4,000 to 5,000 acres) of the original Coastal Prairie remains today (Early et al. 2024). The marsh-fringing prairie type is represented by several remnants and totals about 1,015 acres. White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area supports the largest and best examples of this wet prairie type, while small highly degraded examples are captured by Sabine NWR and Cameron Prairie NWR. Wet-mesic prairie occupies approximately 3,015 acres.

All of these remnants are on private lands in Calcasieu and Cameron parishes. LDWF is currently working with owners of most of these sites to implement stewardship. The dry-mesic prairie type, which historically accounted for most of the prairie acreage, is now known only along railroads and within pimplemounded areas imbedded in wet-mesic sites. Less than 300 acres of dry-mesic prairie likely remain. All the railroad remnants are in various states of degradation due to woody encroachment, soil disturbance, and prolonged fire suppression.

div.head: MISSISSIPPI TERRACE PRAIRIE
div.p: Rarity Ranks: G2/SX Synonyms: Macon Ridge Prairie Mississippi Terrace Prairie was a tall-grass prairie type of northeastern Louisiana found on Pleistocene terraces within the MRAP floodplain. This prairie may have been similar to the Grand Prairie of eastern Arkansas. Frequent fire and soil type would have prevented invasion of woody species. Topographic maps indicate some historical occurrences of Mississippi Terrace Prairie in northeastern Louisiana such as the Boeuf Prairie in Franklin Parish. This habitat is now considered extirpated in Louisiana.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Mississippi Terrace Prairie historically occupied less than 2,000 acres in the MRAP ecoregion in northeast Louisiana (Smith 1993). This community was converted primarily to agriculture, but some areas were also converted for housing development.
No known examples remain today. However, several small remnants of a calcareous or other unknown prairie type occur in the region, which appear to be similar to Mississippi Terrace Prairie.
Chapter 5: Natural Communities

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Conduct field surveys within and near areas that historically supported Mississippi Terrace Prairie for grasslands which retain some prairie plants, such as pastures and neglected agricultural land ("go-back" lands). 2. Promote management (e.g., prescribed fire) on prairie-like grasslands in areas where this habitat occurred historically. Upland Sodic/Alkali Barren soils have high levels of exchangeable sodium and sometimes magnesium in the subsoil and near the surface horizons, which create extreme conditions for plant growth. Such conditions include relatively high alkalinity, very poor movement of water and air in the soil, resistance to wetting that can induce droughty conditions, resistance to drying once saturated, and a sodic horizon in the subsoil which acts much like a dense claypan that is resistant to root penetration. The principal soils associated with Sodic/Alkali Barren natural communities are Bonn, Brimstone, and Lafe soil series (Reid et al. 2010). However, Guyton soils or soil map units containing the Guyton soils series are the primary mapped soil units at some Sodic/Alkali Barrens (Reid et al. 2010) et al. 2009et al. , Reid et al. 2010)). Wet Sodic/Alkali Barren occurs on lower landscape positions than upland prairie and is seasonally flooded. The flora of wet Sodic/Alkali Barren is entirely different from that of upland prairie and includes several plants that also occur in coastal saline habitats. Wet expressions of this system also feature large barren patches and are in need of more detailed floristic edaphic studies.

div.head: PRAIRIE POTHOLE
div.p: Chapter 5: Natural Communities

div.head: SODIC/ALKALI BARREN (FORMERLY SALINE PRAIRIE)
div.p: Rarity Rank: G1G2/S1 Synonyms: Alkali Flat, Barrens, Salt Barren, Slick, Saline Prairie Sodic/Alkali Barren is a small-scale grassland, often occurring within various natural community types. Sodic/Alkali Barren habitat ranges from less than one acre to about 30 acres in size. There are two types of Sodic/Alkali Barren classified by hydrology and landscape position: dry-mesic (upland) and wet. Dry-mesic Sodic/Alkali Barren occurs on fluvial terraces adjacent to active small stream floodplains, and its soils formed in Pleistocene alluvium. Wet Sodic/Alkali Barren occurs in stream valleys subject to regular flooding. Wet expressions of this community sometimes transition upslope into dry-mesic Sodic/ Alkali Barren. Some areas of these systems contain exposed or sparsely vegetated soil known as "slicks," which support "cryptogamic lips" dominated by algae, mosses, lichens, and very small flowering plants (Pittman 1988, Reid et

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Sodic/Alkali Barren was estimated to have occupied less than 2,000 acres historically (Smith 1993). It is unclear whether this estimate includes both upland and wet variants. An effort was made from 2006 to 2008 to locate Sodic/Alkali Barrens in northwestern Louisiana. This work was very successful, revealing about 10 new records and expanding the range of the Sodic/Alkali Barren to include three additional parishes (Reid et al. 2010). Sodic/Alkali Barren is likely extirpated in East Baton Rouge and Livingston parishes; however, small remnants in these parishes may persist in utility corridors that intersect sodic/alkali soils.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Sodic/Alkali Barren is threatened by disturbance associated with mineral extraction and roads and service corridors as well as afforestation attempts. Several recently rediscovered Sodic/ Alkali Barrens are under threat of commercial and residential development as they are not protected. Feral Hogs pose a serious threat to Sodic/Alkali Barren communities.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Continue surveys to monitor the current extent and condition of this habitat type.

div.head: Conduct detailed studies of flora and edaphic conditions of
div.p: Wet Sodic/Alkali Barren habitat types. 3. Conduct surveys to determine invertebrate assemblages of Sodic/Alkali Barren. 4. Provide assistance with Feral Hog control in this habitat to landowners.

div.head: Target occurrences of Sodic/Alkali Barren in northwest
div.p: Louisiana for permanent protection via servitudes or land acquisition. 6. Work with land managers, hunting clubs, extension agents, and others to discourage the placement of food plots within or near this habitat type.

div.head: INLAND AND MARINE INLAND AND MARINE
COASTAL FRESHWATER SUBMERGED AQUATIC VEGETATION
div.p: Rarity Ranks: G4/S3S4 Synonyms: none

Well-developed Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation (SAV) beds often occur in lentic water bodies within the coastal plain. Typically, this natural community consists primarily of freshwater but may include pulses or short durations of higher salinities ranging from 0 to 5 ppt salinity. Species found within the Coastal Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation natural community can overlap those found in other SAV types such as Interior Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation and Estuarine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation communities.

Floating-leaved aquatics such as water-lilies (Nymphaea spp.) are often conspicuous in Coastal Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation. This habitat occurs throughout coastal Freshwater Marsh and the interface of Baldcypress-Tupelo Swamp Forest. This SAV type develops in natural and man-made water bodies.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Exemplary occurrences of this habitat can be found in Lacassine Pool on Lacassine NWR, White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area, and Salvador WMA. Other public lands that support this community include Pass-a-Loutre, Atchafalaya Delta, and Lake Boeuf WMAs and Delta NWR. The historical extent is unknown, and current acreage has not been estimated.

div.head: INTERIOR FRESHWATER SUBMERGED AQUATIC VEGETATION
div.p: Rarity Ranks: G4/S5 Synonyms: none

Interior Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation is highly variable and can occupy swamps, lakes (e.g., oxbows), reservoirs (especially upper ends), sluggish bayous, Beaver ponds, and small farm ponds. Water turbidity, temperature, substrate, wave action, nutrient loads, and light penetration are key factors in determining the composition of the flora and fauna of SAV beds. The benefits of SAV include oxygenation of water, habitat structure for all forms of aquatic life (e.g., shade for fish), and a basis for aquatic food webs that benefits all wildlife. The magnitude of benefits may vary based on the quantity and quality of habitat

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: This habitat occurs statewide in a variety of water bodies. Areal extent, degree of development, and plant species richness vary widely.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Interior Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation is threatened by residential and commercial development; contamination by agricultural, municipal, and industrial effluents; eutrophication; trash dumping; aging infrastructure; and invasive species such as Water Hyacinth, Giant Salvinia, and Hydrilla. Climate change poses an additional threat, especially if there are reductions in precipitation.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Continue surveys to document and describe exemplary occurrences of this SAV type. 2. Produce literature presenting information on the identification of aquatic plants and explaining the benefits of SAV.

div.head: Produce and distribute a poster series highlighting Interior
div.p: Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation habitat and associated native and exotic aquatic plants. 4. Continue to invest in cleaning stations at boat ramps to limit the spread of invasive aquatic plants. 5. Work with partners to minimize human impacts and develop preventative measure to avoid or minimize impacts from nutrient loading, sedimentation, and other pollution affecting this natural community type.

div.head: LAKES AND RESERVOIRS
div.p: Lakes are larger and usually deeper than ponds, but no strict size or depth criteria exist for designating a particular water body as a lake. Natural lakes in Louisiana include oxbows and other floodplain lakes occupying abandoned river channels.

Oxbow lakes form when a river meander is cut off and left as a free-standing water body; as a result, oxbows are typically U-shaped. Other natural lakes occur in coastal Barataria, Calcasieu, Mermentau, and Terrebonne basins. Natural lakes provide valuable fish and wildlife habitat.

Reservoirs are man-made lakes created by impounding streams and can be relatively small or up to thousands of acres (e.g., Toledo Bend). The Red River Raft lakes (Lake Bistineau, Caddo Lake, and Cross Lake) were formed by damming of the Red River by the "Great Raft," a massive log jam that persisted for centuries. Following clearing of the Great Raft in the 19th century, water levels in these lakes fluctuated greatly until control structures were installed to maintain these lakes as reservoirs. Although reservoirs can provide habitat that is utilized by native species, including some SGCN, it is always desirable to remove impoundments and restore natural hydrology and habitat connectivity.
Interior Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation, Sabine Parish

div.head: INLAND AND MARINE
div.p: Oxbow Lake associated with Tensas River, Concordia Parish

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: River Delta Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation beds are associated with the Mississippi and Atchafalaya river deltas. This community can be found on Atchafalaya Delta and Pass-a-Loutre WMAs as well as Delta NWR.

div.head: Threats
div.p: River Delta Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation is threatened by disturbance associated with mineral extraction, canals, utility corridors, and damage from outboard motors. Invasive species and the possible increase in frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones associated with climate change may impact this habitat. Increased salinity due to altered hydrology, marsh loss, and SLR also threaten this community.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Conduct studies to determine the areal extent of this SAV type and address basic ecological questions regarding its development and maintenance. 2. Reduce human disturbance of this habitat type on public and private lands and waterways.

div.head: RIVERS, STREAMS, CREEKS, AND BAYOUS
div.p: Rarity Rank: GNR/SNR Synonyms: None River, stream, and creek are interchangeable terms for flowing water, with no technical definition (USGS 2018). In general, rivers are typically considered the largest of the three, with streams intermediate in size and creeks the smallest. These water bodies are formed when water moves from an area of higher elevation to an area of lower elevation due to gravity. Water comes from direct precipitation but also as runoff from the surrounding land surface. Land surfaces that drain water into rivers, streams, and creeks are known as basins; for more information on the basins in Louisiana, see pages 167-181.

Bayous are slow-moving, typically shallow, water bodies, found in flat areas where water pools. They can consist of fresh, brackish, or salt water and often have abundant vegetation. Some bayous, like Bayou Bartholomew, have high biological diversity and are critical habitat for mussel SGCN.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Louisiana contains over 120,000 miles of rivers, streams, creeks, and bayous throughout the state (XU 2004). The Mississippi River, the second longest river in the United States at approximately 2,300 miles long, is a major transporation artery that empties into the Gulf of America (NPS 2025). Bayou Bartholomew, the longest bayou in the world, flows for approximately 364 miles through Arkansas and Louisiana, before converging with the Ouachita River (LDEQ 2025).

div.head: Threats
div.p: Rivers are threatened by residential and commercial development; commerce and transportation; contamination by agricultural, municipal, and industrial effluents; loss of riparian habitat; instream and gravel mining; loss of instream and lateral connectivity; flow alteration; and invasive species such as bigheaded carps (Xenocyprididae) and Giant Salvinia. Streams, creeks, and bayous face many of the same challenges as rivers but on a more localized scale.

div.head: Aerial view of Cane Bayou
div.p: Pearl River

Research Needs and Conservation Actions 1. Investigate the impacts of impediments to aquatic organism passage and mitigate impacts with fish ladders, bypasses, conservation locking, and barrier removal, where appropriate. 2. Utilize green infrastructure, BMPs, and habitat restoration to minimize pollution and sedimentation inputs. 3. Restore natural flows and connections to floodplains to encourage resilient and healthy ecosystems. 4. Partner with LDEQ to promote practices such as requiring updated sewage systems in communities around lakes. 5. Inventory, prioritize, and mitigate barriers to aquatic organism passage at road/stream crossings. 6. Measure flood reduction effectiveness and ecological impacts of post-storm debris removal on aquatic ecosystems and work with policymakers, agencies, and stakeholders to minimize unnecessary ecological impacts. 7. Restore riparian zones and floodplain habitat to improve water quality and ecosystem resilience. 8. Conduct fish, mussel, crayfish, and macroinvertebrate SGCN studies in streams, creeks, and bayous to better understand population status and life history needs.

div.head: ESTUARINE SUBMERGED AQUATIC VEGETATION
div.p: Rarity Rank: G4?/S1 Synonyms: none

The Estuarine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation brackish water community consists of submerged, rooted vascular plants growing in shallow, protected waters with low turbidity. Water temperature, salinity (5 to 10 ppt), substrate, wave action, nutrient loads, and light penetration are key factors in determining the composition of the flora and fauna of SAV beds.

The substrate is often predominantly sand, but other substrates such as other minerals or Soft Mud Bottom can occur. In lower salinity regimes, these bottoms may be vegetated by water milfoils (Myriophyllum spp.), Widgeon-Grass (Ruppia maritima), Southern Naiad (Najas guadalupensis), and other species. The presence of SAV provides additional structure, shelter, and food to the animals dependent upon these habitats. Estuarine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation is more likely to be abundant in smaller, sheltered areas of Soft Mud Bottom and less likely to be present or abundant in areas where wave action or other factors causing turbulence and turbidity are persistent. Small scattered beds occur in relative abundance in brackish water ponds throughout coastal Louisiana. More extensive beds are found in the Lake Pontchartrain and Barataria basins. Although a small component of the larger estuarine ecosystem, these beds play an important ecological role. The beds support a diverse invertebrate and epiphytic population and serve as nursery grounds and shelter for many species of fishes and shellfish. In addition, these beds are extremely productive and release detritus and nutrients to surrounding waters. These beds lack widespread distribution due to the general turbidity of most of the estuaries in Louisiana.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: Historical extent of this SAV type is unknown (Smith 1993). This SAV occurs in waters subject to occasional salinity pulses like those in Lake Pontchartrain and several lakes in the Barataria Basin such as Lake Salvador.
Estuarine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation

div.head: EXTENT OF ESTUARINE SUBMERGED AQUATIC VEGETATION
Threats
div.p: Estuarine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation faces threats from various sources of human disturbance, including damage from outboard motors. Activities that increase the turbidity in the waters surrounding SAV beds threaten the viability of this community. Alteration to salinity levels due to marsh loss, tropical cyclones, and SLR also threaten this habitat.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Continue surveys to determine the extent and condition of this habitat type; revisit and evaluate existing occurrences in the Wildlife Diversity Program database. 2. Recommend a maximum vessel speed, vessel draft, and engine draft when boating in particularly sensitive areas such as shallow SAV beds and provide education about methods for boaters to reduce negative, unintentional impacts. 3. Protect this SAV type from damage resulting from boat traffic and development of oil and gas infrastructure. 4. Generate greater public awareness of the importance of SAV. Chapter 5: Natural Communities bottoms. Wave action, currents, temperature, salinity, substrate characteristics, and light penetration affected by turbidity determine species assemblage. Violent storms may drastically disrupt or alter community structure. Although this grass bed is a relatively small part of the ecosystem in coastal Louisiana, it is believed they play an extremely important role. The actual ecological value of this benthic grass community is poorly understood and may be underestimated. This is an extremely productive community often as productive as Salt Marsh. It provides food for a number of animals and acts as a nursery area and refuge for the young of many fishes and invertebrates. It can support a diverse epiphytic biota, including algae, fungi, bacteria, protozoans, bryozoans, and hydrozoans, thus creating a unique environment that allows for the existence of indigenous grass bed species. It supplies detrital material and nutrients to the water, adds oxygen via photosynthesis, and stabilizes bottom sediments by increasing deposition of suspended particulate matter.

div.head: Extent and Status
div.p: This habitat is restricted to the Chandeleur Islands, where it is extensive in the clear shallows on the leeward side of the islands.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Long-term survival of the Marine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation natural community depends on having adequate protection from the Chandeleur Islands, which have degraded in recent decades. Impacts to seagrass beds by tropical cyclones, SLR, and outboard motors threaten this community.

div.head: Research Needs and Conservation Actions
div.p: 1. Determine areal extent of, and map Marine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation at Chandeleur Islands. 2. Conduct inventory and monitoring to determine changes in condition and extent over time and to identify emerging threats.

div.head: Work with CPRA and other agencies to implement
div.p: measures to nourish the Chandeleur Islands, such as augmenting sand supply.

div.head: MARINE SUBSTRATE HABITATS
div.p: Rarity Rank: SNA Synonyms: None

The following marine habitats are all submerged, primarily nonvegetated habitats and are described based on characteristics such as seafloor composition and the presence of seagrass beds. Although listed as "marine" habitats, the following substrates, except State Territorial Open Water, can be found adjacent to all marsh types and across all salinity regimes. Fishery managers in the Gulf of America suspect that estuarine hard bottoms support more diverse, complex communities than adjacent soft bottoms, prompting an increase in low profile artificial reefs.

div.head: Threats
div.p: Shell and Shell Hash Bottom habitats are affected by variability in temperature and salinity levels that are a result of climate change, coastal restoration projects, and management practices that disrupt natural hydrology.
