A small 'x' indicates that COA encompasses highly-ranked ecological opportunity for the action and, thus, could be considered a secondary focus of the COA.

div.head: CONSERVATION OPPORTUNITY AREAS AND CONSERVATION LANDS
AMITE-TICKFAW
div.p: The Amite-Tickfaw COA was delineated to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions in the Pine Forests and Woodlands ecosystem and the Floodplain Forests and Woody Wetlands ecosystem as well as restoration of linear connectivity (Table 7.2). Compared to the rest of the state, this area has somewhat lower terrestrial resilience to changes in climate. Further, as of 2021, 7.1% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 24.8% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is higher than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060). (LEFT) Wilson's Plover (Anarhynchus wilsonia). (RIGHT) American Bumblebee (Bombus pensylvanicus).

div.head: BOGUE CHITTO-PEARL
div.p: The Bogue Chitto-Pearl COA was delineated to capture priority areas in the Pine Forests and Woodlands ecosystem and the Floodplain Forests and Woody Wetlands ecosystem for (1) protection and restoration, (2) linear connectivity, and (3) restoration of connectivity to the floodplain (Table 7.3). Compared to the rest of the state, this area has somewhat lower terrestrial resilience to changes in climate. Further, as of 2021, 12.8% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 34.8% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is higher than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060).

div.head: BIOME ECOSYSTEM GROUP NATURAL COMMUNITY S-RANK
CALCASIEU PRAIRIE
div.p: The Calcasieu Prairie COA was delineated in 2015 to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions of grassland ecosystems (Table 7.4). This update included those actions and recognized that opportunities exist to restore lateral and linear connectivity of streams and rivers. Compared to the rest of the state, this area has somewhat lower terrestrial resilience to changes in climate, but higher coastal resilience to sea level rise. Further, as of 2021, 4.1% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 51.5% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is higher than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060).

div.head: BIOME ECOSYSTEM GROUP NATURAL COMMUNITY S-RANK
CHENIER
div.p: The Chenier COA was delineated in 2015 to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions in chenier ecosystems (Table 7.6). This update also identified opportunities to restore the lateral and linear connectivity of streams and rivers. As of 2021, 4.7% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 9.7% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is higher than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060).

div.head: LITTLE RIVER
div.p: The Little River COA was primarily delineated to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions in the Floodplain Forests and Woody Wetlands ecosystem as well as restoration of linear and lateral connectivity (Table 7.7). This analysis also identified some action opportunities for pine forest and grasslands. Compared to the rest of the state, this area has higher terrestrial resilience to changes in climate. Further, as of 2021, 5.9% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 2% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is lower than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060).

div.head: BIOME ECOSYSTEM GROUP NATURAL COMMUNITY S-RANK
OUACHITA-BARTHOLOMEW
div.p: The Ouachita-Bartholomew COA was primarily delineated to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions in the Floodplain Forests and Woody Wetlands ecosystem as well as restoration of linear connectivity (Table 7.8). This analysis also identified some action opportunities for pine forest, grasslands, and lateral connectivity. Compared to the rest of the state, this area has similar terrestrial resilience to changes in climate. Further, as of 2021, 7.5% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 8.9% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is slightly higher than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060).

div.head: BIOME ECOSYSTEM GROUP NATURAL COMMUNITY S-RANK
SALINE BAYOU
div.p: The Saline Bayou COA was primarily delineated to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions in the Floodplain Forests and Woody Wetlands ecosystem as well as protection of existing lateral connectivity (Table 7.10). This analysis also identified some action opportunities for pine forest, grassland, and linear connectivity. Compared to the rest of the state, this area has slightly higher terrestrial resilience to changes in climate. Further, as of 2021, 5.3% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with a very low probability for additional urbanization by 2060.

div.head: BARATARIA-TERREBONNE
div.p: The Barataria-Terrebonne COA was delineated in 2015 to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions of seagrass and barrier island ecosystems (Table 7.11). This COA was included in the 2025 set without further analysis. However, the 2023 Blueprint Report (see supplemental materials) identified that only 17% of seagrass and barrier island ecosystems in this part of the state scored in fair to good or better coastal condition. Further, the assessment found about 50% of the area to be important for sea turtles and 41% of the acreage to be important for marine mammals, ranking both above the 70th percentile. However, NOAA sea level rise inundation data indicates nearly all the island acres evaluated would be affected by a 2.7' sea level rise by 2060.

div.head: BIOME ECOSYSTEM GROUP NATURAL COMMUNITY S-RANK
SABINE PRAIRIE
div.p: The Sabine Prairie COA was delineated in 2015 to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions of grassland ecosystems (Table 7.9). This update included those actions and also recognized that opportunities exist to restore lateral and linear connectivity of streams and rivers. Further, as of 2021, 4% of the acres in this COA has been identified as urban with an additional 64% considered to have at least a moderate probability for urbanization by 2060, which is much higher than the state as a whole (statewide urban increase of 7.5% by 2060).

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Louisiana is home to a multitude of unique ecosystems with habitats that support a rich diversity of species, some of which can be found nowhere else in the world. Many of the species that Louisiana has identified as Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) depend on these ecosystems to exist. It is important to recognize potential threats to these ecological communities to better manage and conserve habitat to preserve these key species.

Much of Louisiana has been altered from its original state by human expansion and development resulting in the reduction and impairment of suitable habitat for SGCN. State Wildlife Action Plans are required to identify threats that may adversely affect SGCN and the habitats that support them. This chapter focuses on 12 threat categories with applicable subcomponents, which are mostly based on the Conservation Measures Partnership's Direct Threats Classification, 2.0 (CMP 2016). In many instances, the definitions associated with each threat have been pulled directly from the original source document. The exception is Data Gaps, which LDWF included as an additional threat to those officially listed in the threats classification document.

div.head: RESIDENTIAL AND COMMERCIAL DEVELOPMENT
div.p: Threats posed by human settlements and other nonagricultural land uses with a substantial footprint can be further broken down into three subcategories: residential, commercial, and associated development. Despite much of the landscape remaining relatively sparsely populated, development is a primary threat to SGCN.

div.head: HOUSING AND URBAN AREAS
div.p: According to the 2020 U.S. Census Bureau, Louisiana is the 33rd largest state by area but the 25th most densely populated state, with over 4.6 million residents occupying roughly 52,419 square miles or 33.5 million acres, of which 9,168 square miles or 5.9 million acres is water.

Intensive development destroys natural habitats and can alter local hydrology and facilitates the introduction of invasive species (whether intentional or inadvertent) and cause considerable disruption to the environment. Urbanization, road construction, and forest fragmentation can also increase impacts to the environment by hindering the dispersal and migration of forest plants and animals.

Cities and towns, including non-housing development associated with housing, occupy an increasingly large area of former wildlife habitat. Louisiana's overall recent population growth has not been dramatic, with an overall increase of 2.7% from the 2010 to the 2020 census (Figure 8.1). Chapter 8: Threats

Generally, human expansion focuses development around areas of higher populations (i.e. urban sprawl). The amount of land conversion associated with urban growth varies across the state but is correlated with these population centers.

div.head: COMMERCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL AREAS
div.p: In addition to housing and population expansion, it is important to consider other aspects of development that can have a large impact to habitat through land fragmentation and conversion.

Commercial development consumes large amounts of space, providing retail opportunities, distribution centers, business centers, and entertainment opportunities that attract supporting economies and often results in population growth. These areas change the surrounding landscape and can drastically alter local ecology.

h Action Strategy: Work with the legislature to develop tax incentives for landowners to encourage conservation of priority natural communities. h Action Strategy: Provide educational information on natural communities and the importance of SGCN to landowners and managers through participation in outreach events, presentations, workshops, and online resources. h Action Strategy: Use citizen science programs to monitor natural communities and the impacts of commercial developments.

div.head: AGRICULTURE AND AQUACULTURE
div.p: Agricultural and aquacultural threats can be subdivided into multiple categories, each with its own unique set of challenges that can affect the surrounding landscape and natural communities.

div.head: ANNUAL AND PERENNIAL NON-TIMBER CROPS
div.p: Non-timber crops are cultivated in farms, plantations, orchards, vineyards, and mixed agroforestry systems for purposes such as food, fodder, fiber, fuel, and other uses. Agricultural production and development serve as vital economic engines, significantly influencing communities, local and national food supplies, and individual livelihoods. The USDA\NASS 2024 State Agriculture Overview for Louisiana identifies soybeans, rice, and corn as the three leading annual crop commodities, with harvested areas measuring 1,060,000 acres for soybeans, 459,000 acres for rice, and 443,000 acres for corn. However, these activities can also negatively affect habitats, species ecology, and habitat continuity.

h Action Strategy: Encourage the use of farming practices and plant varieties that provide ecosystem services and minimize the impacts to native wildlife. h Action Strategy: Promote the establishment of native plant buffer strips along agricultural field edges and waterways to capture excess nutrients, reduce surface water runnoff, and provide wildlife corridors. approximately 8 million acres of that land was in private, nonindustrial ownership (LDAF 2025). Tracts planted as monocultures such as most pine plantations provide little tangible habitat and resources for wildlife. However, proper management of these areas can, in some cases, provide limited benefits.

div.head: WOOD AND PULP PLANTATIONS
div.p: h Action Strategy: Encourage silvicultural practices that promote natural processes and ecosystem dynamics.

div.head: LIVESTOCK FARMING AND RANCHING
div.p: Livestock operations, if not managed responsibly, can have unintended consequences on the landscape. Activities related to cattle ranches, dairies, hog farms, and poultry operations can contribute to increased nutrient runoff and erosion, both of which are known to degrade water quality and damage habitats.

h Action Strategy: Work with landowners to prevent over grazing of sensitive habitat and to minimize livestock access to flowing waters. h Action Strategy: Work with landowners to conduct operations aimed at minimizing runoff of animal waste through responsible drain design and buffers.

div.head: MARINE AND FRESHWATER AQUACULTURE
div.p: Aquaculture in Louisiana is a multimillion dollar industry with over 800 operations contributing to the state's agricultural economy (USDA 2024). Water quality, operational controls, and site containment strategies are key in supporting these types of operations and minimizing their potential ecological impacts.

h Action Strategy: Discourage the use of non-native species in aquaculture operations. h Action Strategy: Implement and promote the use of BMPs and SMZs in appropriate habitat and promote the creation of Hazard Analysis Control Point (HACP) plans for potential aquaculture releases.

div.head: ENERGY PRODUCTION AND MINING
div.p: Threats from production of non-biological resources can be direct and indirect. This section discusses the potential issues surrounding energy production and mineral extraction.

div.head: OIL AND GAS DRILLING
div.p: The exploration, development, and production of petroleum and other hydrocarbons in the form of oil and gas wells can negatively affect SGCN and their habitats. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Louisiana currently ranks 6th in the country for energy production. Louisiana accounts for approximately 10% of the nation's natural gas production (Figure 8.2) and is among the top 10 states for crude oil reserves and production (Figure 8.3). Construction of access roads to these sites impacts species and further contributes to habitat fragmentation (Figure 8.4). In addition, catastrophic oil releases at well sites can cause acute and chronic impacts to wildlife and their habitats.
h Action Strategy: Implement and promote the use of BMPs during exploration, production, and de-commissioning of energy production infrastructure.

LOUISIANA'S OIL WELLS LOUISIANA'S NATURAL GAS WELLS (LEFT) Breton Island after an oil spill. (BELOW LEFT) A coastal marsh after an oil spill. (BELOW RIGHT) A Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) at Queen Bess Island covered in oil after an oil spill.
h Action Strategy: Provide information to oil, gas, and seismic companies and encourage resource survey and mining techniques that avoid or minimize impacts to SGCN and their habitats.

div.head: MINING AND QUARRYING
div.p: The exploration, development, and production of minerals and rocks in the form of mines, quarries, and sand and gravel pits can negatively affect SGCN and their habitats. These activities can include those that not only alter habitat but can also result in terraforming that converts the entire area from its natural state. These operations can result in additional land fracturing, chemical seepage, and sediment loss, which can further degrade habitat over time.
h Action Strategy: Encourage protection of natural sediments of sand and gravel bars by working with the LDWF Scenic Rivers Program and partners.

div.head: RENEWABLE ENERGY
div.p: The exploration, development, and production of renewable energy through solar and wind farms can pose risks to SGCN and their habitats. Often such projects require large footprints, destroying habitat and creating barriers to migration corridors, thus displacing or isolating wildlife populations. Birds and bats face direct mortality from collisions with wind turbines, and Louisiana's location within the Mississippi Flyway and the trans-Gulf migration corridor may heighten the collision risks for migratory birds. In addition to collisions, wind energy development may displace birds from otherwise high quality habitat, leading to functional habitat loss. It is essential to take precautions during all project phases to minimize or mitigate negative impacts. Careful consideration of the timing, location, and scale of these projects can help minimize their environmental effects.

In addition, large-scale solar farms covering extensive contiguous areas can permanently displace species like the Gopher Tortoise. If these projects are not properly designed and maintained, they may also lead to further issues related to erosion, habitat fragmentation, and establishment of invasive species.

div.head: TRANSPORTATION AND SERVICE CORRIDORS
div.p: Threats from long, narrow transportation and service corridors include habitat destruction and fragmentation and wildlife mortality from vehicular strikes.

div.head: ROADS AND RAILROADS
div.p: Surface transport on roadways and dedicated tracks includes highways, secondary roads, logging roads, bridges and causeways, and railroads. Fencing associated with roads is included with this threat. Additional roadways and improvements to heavily trafficked areas can provide additional access and opportunities for local human populations. However, these travel corridors can be barriers to local wildlife if not properly sited and constructed and can promote further establishment of invasive plant species. Although pollution from roadways is a concern for local biodiversity, it is addressed in the Pollution section of this chapter.
h Action Strategy: Work with partners to promote the use of bridges and culverts designed for wildlife and fish passage such as the installation of oversized culverts below grade.
In addition, minimize impacts of road, bridge, and culvert construction and replacement on stream quality.

div.head: UTILITY AND SERVICE LINES
div.p: Transport of energy and resources includes electrical and phone wires, aqueducts, and oil and gas pipelines. Fragmentation of habitat occurs when new rights-of-way (ROW) are cleared.
Transmission lines and pipelines can often act as corridors for invasive plant species, and chemical releases from pipelines can cause acute and chronic impacts to wildlife and their habitats.

In addition, overhead power lines can act as barriers for bats and birds, increasing the likelihood of collisions. Although much of the infrastructure is already in place, proper management practices for these areas and additional consideration to minimize impact to SGCN during the planning phase of future projects can aid in minimizing and mitigating some of the unintended impacts.

div.head: SHIPPING LANES
div.p: In order to maintain shipping lanes for transport in freshwater and coastal waterways, dredging of stream bottoms is necessary. However, dredging degrades habitat for many fish and mollusk SGCN. Wakes from cargo ships and barges damage shorelines, which can further degrade habitat and cause a variety of issues affecting sedimentation and water quality. In addition, commercial and recreational boats may strike and critically injure or kill wildlife.

h Action Strategy: Encourage and maximize the beneficial use of dredge material. h Action Strategy: Promote no wake zones in areas critical for wildlife. h Action Strategy: Post signage in work areas and at boat launches of water bodies where manatee may occur to reduce strike risk.

div.head: FLIGHT PATHS
div.p: Air transport may result in noise disturbance and bird strikes.

Most bird-aircraft strikes take place at or near airports, generally occurring during take-off or landing. This potential threat is not unique to Louisiana, and these strikes account for a relatively small amount of bird deaths per year (USFWS 2024). This can, however, compromise air travel safety; therefore, bird movements should be considered by airports and air crew.
h Action Strategy: Work with partners to incorporate language into airport hazard mitigation plans that benefits wildlife.

Threats associated with the consumptive use of "wild" biological resources encompass both intentional and unintentional consequences of harvesting. These impacts can affect both target and nontarget species as well as their habitats. This includes the persecution and control of specific species as well as nontargets that may be injured as bycatch.

div.head: HUNTING AND COLLECTING TERRESTRIAL ANIMALS
div.p: This subcategory includes the killing or trapping of terrestrial wild animals for commercial or recreational use, subsistence, research, cultural purposes, or for predator control/persecution reasons. It also includes accidental mortality of nontarget species.

The Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission is tasked with the control and oversight of all regulations of terrestrial wildlife in the state. It receives and reviews biological, socioeconomic, and other technical data as well as management recommendations from LDWF staff. Combining these data with public input, the Commission votes on actions for long term management and sustainability of the resource. These regulations include, but are not limited to, hunting seasons and harvest limits.
h Action Strategy: Ensure management plans include considerations for SGCN.

div.head: LOGGING AND WOOD HARVESTING
div.p: Forest harvesting activities are typically associated with the removal of trees for timber, wood pulp, fiber, or energy.

div.head: FISHING AND HARVESTING AQUATIC RESOURCES
div.p: Like with terrestrial wildlife, the Louisiana Wildlife and Fisheries Commission is tasked with the control and oversight of all aquatic wildlife in the state. These regulations include, but are not limited to, fishing seasons, creel limits, and the collection and sale of amphibians and reptiles.

The harvest of aquatic wild animals for commercial or recreational use, subsistence, research, cultural purposes, or for control/persecution reasons may include accidental mortality and trawling bycatch. Abandoned traps and fishing gear allowed to remain in place while not in use (e.g., derelict crab traps) can result in the continued catch and kill of species and pose a strike hazard to watercraft.

h Action Strategy: Remove passive fishing gear that are not in use, including derelict crab traps, in order to minimize mortality of wildlife and fish species. h Action Strategy: Promote harvest of invasive species (e.g., Silver Carp [Hypophthalmichthys molitrix]) in place of native species for bait and other purposes.

div.head: HUMAN INTRUSION AND DISTURBANCE
div.p: Human activities related to various non-consumptive uses can modify and disturb habitats. While these threats typically do not result in permanent habitat destruction, the potential effects from human disturbance can be significant to many SGCN and their habitats, with certain species being especially vulnerable. Non-consumptive use refers to activities where the resource remains intact and can be enjoyed by multiple user groups.

div.head: RECREATIONAL ACTIVITIES
div.p: People spending time in nature or traveling in vehicles outside of established transportation corridors for recreational purposes may affect SGCN. This category includes off-road vehicles, motorboats, personal watercraft, mountain bikes, hikers, birders, pets in recreation areas, and temporary campsites, among others. This section does not include permanent recreation facilities or permanent transport corridors, which have been previously covered in this chapter.

div.head: BIOLOGICAL RESOURCE USE
div.p: LDWF manages over 1.6 million acres of land and waterways designated as wildlife management areas, refuges, and conservation areas. These spaces are vital for numerous species that rely on diverse habitats. However, these lands are not just protecting Louisiana's natural resources, they are also offering various outdoor recreational opportunities to the public.

Camping sites, if not properly kept, can result in habitat disturbance that can disrupt and harm vulnerable species. The accumulation of human rubbish in an area, when not properly disposed of, can be an attractant to nuisance species, which may also prey on at-risk species in the area. Pets, particularly dogs, can also harass local wildlife, leading to unnecessary mortality.

The use of all-terrain vehicles is a popular pastime, but without proper knowledge and care, these activities can result in negative impacts to sensitive habitats such as wetlands, sandbars, beaches, and more. These activities can not only disrupt or destroy wildlife nesting areas, they can cause direct mortality of adults and active nests. Off-roading can also result in large ruts that can destabilize stream banks, leading to additional habitat degradation.

To ensure the long-term sustainability of these areas, Louisiana is dedicated to collaborating with conservation partners and the public. This includes helping to identify sensitive regions and their habitats, raising awareness, and minimizing the negative effects that recreational activities may have on these environments.

h Action Strategy: Work with partners to minimize the impacts of recreational activities, including ORV use, in sensitive areas. h Action Strategy: Promote conservation compatible land use. h Action Strategy: Use signs, stewards, and symbolic fencing to protect nesting and other sensitive areas.

h Action Strategy: Support outreach and education aimed at minimizing human impacts to SGCN and priority habitats. h Action Strategy: Educate the public on the impacts of domestic and feral animals (e.g., dogs, cats, and hogs). h Action Strategy: Promote legislation to prevent the intentional release of helium-filled balloons.

div.head: MILITARY ACTIVITIES
div.p: Military exercises and training activities have the potential to impact SGCN and their habitats. Beyond the facilities and bases, the military also conducts training exercises that covers a large physical footprint across the state.

An important means of collaboration between Louisiana and the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) is through Integrated Natural Resource Management Plans (INRMPs). INRMPs serve as management plans for the highly diverse habitats for which the DoD is responsible.

These plans are installation-specific and designed to balance conservation and military activities to satisfy environmental legal requirements without compromising the capability of installation lands to support the military's mission. INRMPs are mandatory for all installations, including state-owned National Guard installations, that have significant natural resources.

INRMPs must be prepared in cooperation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and appropriate state fish and wildlife agencies and are intended to reflect the mutual agreement of the agencies concerning the conservation, protection, and management of fish and wildlife resources.
h Action Strategy: Continue to work with military installations to minimize the impacts of activities, training exercises, and ranges.

div.head: NATURAL SYSTEM MODIFICATIONS
div.p: This category is defined as "threats from actions that convert or degrade habitat in service of 'managing' natural or seminatural systems, often to improve human welfare" (CMP 2016). Modifications are frequently implemented in an attempt to address or mitigate effects of disturbances and natural processes. However, these management efforts have the potential to adversely impact or eliminate natural processes essential to ecological communities if not planned carefully.

div.head: FIRE AND FIRE SUPPRESSION
div.p: In the southeastern United States, low level fires play a crucial role in maintaining various ecosystems. Fire-dependent communities such as pine savannas, woodlands, and prairies have evolved with frequent low intensity fires and provide critical habitat for many SGCN.

Various factors such as habitat fragmentation and fire suppression can lead to a reduction of fire on these landscapes. If left without fire, these systems will begin to transition into a ruderal or contemporary forest community. This shift will reduce ground level forest fuels and create a positive feedback loop that further suppresses fire (Loudermilk et al. 2011) while also reducing fire resiliency.

Fire caused by lightning strike is a natural and necessary part of fire-dependent ecosystems. However, on the contemporary, fragmented landscape, allowing fuels to accumulate while awaiting this ignition source can result in larger, high-intensity fires (wildfires). These larger fires have greater potential to cause damage to property and loss of life than more frequent low-intensity fires in the same area. The regular use of fire is an efficient management tool that can reduce competition and fuel levels to maintain the overall health of these systems and minimize the risk of catastrophic wildfires.

Chapter 8: Threats h Action Strategy: Support use of prescribed fire to maintain appropriate habitat. h Action Strategy: Reintroduce fire to fire-dependent remnant prairie, marsh, and savanna habitats. h Action Strategy: Establish and promote Prescribed Burn
Associations in all parishes throughout the state that have fire-dependent ecosystems.

div.head: DAMS AND WATER MANAGEMENT/USE
div.p: Altering water flow patterns beyond their natural range of variation, whether intentionally or unintentionally, can have substantial impacts.

Human activities have significantly disrupted the natural hydrology of Louisiana. Actions such as dam construction and operation; sediment management; alterations to saltwater regimes, saltwater diversion levee, dike, and weir construction; groundwater extraction; channelization; and the creation of artificial lakes have drastically changed natural water flow in the state. These changes frequently reduce the quality and quantity of habitats available to SGCN. Hydrological obstructions, for example, can also lead to increased saltwater intrusion during times of drought by restricting natural flows. Increased saltwater can damage important habitat and affect drinking water. The alteration of flow patterns from human activities should be managed, where possible.

The timing, frequency, magnitude and duration of flows and connectivity are vital components of aquatic systems and provide critical habitat needed for species to survive. In addition, a well-connected network of water allows species to access additional areas, promoting a healthy and resilient ecosystem with migration opportunities.

h Action Strategy: Work with partners to review materials (e.g., as fill or bank stabilization) permitted as beneficial use in streams. h Action Strategy: Promote aquatic species passage by establishment and conservation of connectivity through the removal of aquatic barriers and discourage creation of new aquatic barriers.
h Action Strategy: Promote instream flows at levels that will support populations of SGCN. h Action Strategy: Minimize and mitigate the impacts and occurrence of saltwater intrusion.

div.head: OTHER ECOSYSTEM MODIFICATIONS
div.p: Other actions that convert or degrade habitat in service of "managing" natural systems to improve human welfare include land reclamation projects, abandonment of managed lands, mowing, bush-hogging, beach construction, the removal of snags from streams, and the addition of riprap on shorelines.

h Action Strategy: Retain emergent and submerged woody debris (subsidize if warranted) and provide education and outreach regarding the importance of this habitat component. h Action Strategy: Create or restore bird nesting islands when and where feasible and explore potential partnerships and funding mechanisms to support such construction. h Action Strategy: Promote the use of BMPs for mowing. h Action Strategy: Retain overhanging vegetation in waterways to provide thermal refugia and to minimize adverse temperature fluctuations.

div.head: REMOVING/REDUCING HUMAN MAINTENANCE
div.p: This threat includes the absence or reduction of current or historical maintenance regimes (e.g., supplemental feeding, mowing, and controlled burns) for important key ecological attributes. These regimes are typically maintained by protected area staff, farmers and ranchers, indigenous peoples, private landowners, and other resource managers.

h Action Strategy: Support use of prescribed fire to maintain appropriate habitat. h Action Strategy: Promote conservation grazing in historical prairie and savanna regions. h Action Strategy: Reconnect hydrology and reintroduce natural flow regimes to reduce invasive species and promote native flora and fauna. h Action Strategy: Promote planting of resilient native flora with local genetics.
LEFT: LDWF biologists conduct a prescribed burn during a prescribed burn workshop. RIGHT: Prescribed fire on a Coastal Prairie.

div.head: INVASIVE AND PROBLEMATIC SPECIES, PATHOGENS, AND GENES
div.p: This threat includes non-native and problematic native plants, animals, pathogens and microbes, and genetic materials that have (or are predicted to have) harmful effects on biodiversity following their introduction, spread, or increase in abundance or virulence. This section gives a brief overview on the potential ecological impacts that these elements may pose and suggests some potential mitigation strategies. Additional information on invasive species can be found in Chapter 6.

div.head: INVASIVE NON-NATIVE/ALIEN PLANTS AND ANIMALS
div.p: Harmful plants, animals, pathogens, and other microbes introduced and spread by human activities into areas in which they were not originally found can negatively impact native habitat and species.

The subtropical environment of Louisiana provides suitable habitat for species from many parts of the world. Non-native organisms present a major threat to SGCN. Once introduced, they can rapidly multiply and spread, exploiting habitat and food resources vital for native species. Impacts to habitat can be particularly noticeable in plant communities; where non-native species take over, plant communities can be reshaped, leading to a decline in native diversity and the degradation of habitat quality over time. Invasive terrestrial animals also destroy sensitive habitats as well as agricultural lands. According to the LSU AgCenter, Feral Hogs cause an estimated economic loss of $91.1 million annually in Louisiana (Salassi et al. 2022).

Numerous invasive and non-native aquatic plants and animals have been documented in Louisiana waters. Aquatic invasions, though occasionally less detectable than those on land, are no less impactful to habitat and wildlife. In addition to posing a threat to SGCN, they can also impact recreational activities by replacing or reducing populations of local sport fish or by clogging waterways with unabated, vegetative growth.
h Action Strategy: Promote compliance with lists of banned, invasive, and potentially invasive species of plants and animals.

div.head: PROBLEMATIC NATIVE PLANTS AND ANIMALS
div.p: Native plants and animals, when their populations become "out of balance," usually through human influence, can become problematic species. Examples include overabundant deer populations, excessive vegetation due to the loss of foraging species, improper stocking rates, and more.
h Action Strategy: Promote BMPs and control measures for problematic native species.

div.head: INTRODUCED GENETIC MATERIAL
div.p: Human-altered organisms or genes include pesticide-resistant crops, genetically modified insects for biocontrol, genetically modified fishes, and genetically modified trees and crops. Modified introduced species have the potential to hybridize with local populations and pass their genetic material to local communities.

Genetically engineered crops may also pose a risk to nontarget species. In addition, consistent pesticide application on crops that are herbicide resistant may facilitate the development of resistant weeds and plants, which could lead to a cycle of increased pesticide use.
Chapter 8: Threats ¹ The following paragraph was provided by Dr. Ellen Hayes, SEAFWA Regional Wildlife Health Coordinator.

h Action Strategy: Use integrated pest management for the control of invasive and problematic native plants and animals. h Action Strategy: Maintain unique genetic trajectories and genetic diversity of local native populations.

div.head: PATHOGENS AND MICROBES
div.p: Harmful native and non-native agents including bacteria, viruses, prions, fungi, and other microorganisms can cause illness to a host. These agents can be detrimental to SGCN by affecting the species directly or indirectly and can spread rapidly if left unchecked.

Wildlife health¹ is a complex, dynamic topic that can be difficult to define and measure. It is more than just the presence or absence of disease caused by pathogens or contaminants; rather, it can be defined by a population's ability to withstand challenges, which may include climate change, habitat loss, or the introduction of a disease-causing agent. Thus, health is the result of interacting biological, social, and environmental determinants (Stephen 2014). Diseases can have significant impacts on wildlife populations. The development of disease depends on factors related to the host organism, its environment, and the disease-causing agent. Pathogens (e.g., bacteria, viruses, parasites, and prions) and contaminants are normally present in wildlife populations, with disease typically occurring at low levels, but becoming more prevalent when hosts are stressed. An emerging disease is defined as "one that has recently been discovered; has recently increased in incidence, geography, or host range; or is newly evolved" (Rachowicz et al. 2005). Two hypotheses can apply to an emerging disease: the novel pathogen hypothesis states that the disease has recently spread into new geographic areas, whereas the endemic pathogen hypothesis suggests that it has been present in the environment but recently has affected new hosts or increased in its ability to cause disease (Rachowicz et al. 2005). For example, in North America, chytridiomycosis, caused by the fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, and whitenose syndrome, caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans, have emerged following pathogen introduction and have had devastating impacts on amphibian and bat populations, respectively. Disease can have direct impacts, such as mortality, or can have indirect impacts, such as reproductive failure; both types of impacts can lead to population declines.

As some species disappear from the landscape, others can proliferate, causing an imbalance in predator-prey relationships or overuse of resources. Sometimes these diseases are zoonotic and threaten human health as well. According to the World Health Organization, 70% to 80% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic in origin. Wildlife health is a critical component of One Heath, which is the intersection of human health, animal health, and environmental health. Therefore, discussions of wildlife health must consider connections with humans, domestic animals, and ecosystems. Such connections may include game species as a food source for humans, pathogens that can be transmitted between wildlife and humans or domestic animals, and the habitats needed to support wildlife populations. In addition, healthy ecosystems provide a variety of ecosystem services for humans, including agricultural production and recreation.

h Action Strategy: Monitor disease levels for emerging pathogens. h Action Strategy: Promote BMPs for feeding stations to reduce pathogen transmission. h Action Strategy: Work with partners to address emerging diseases through surveillance and research. h Action Strategy: Promote communication and collaboration among partners to address emerging fish and wildlife health issues more effectively. h Action Strategy: Promote BMPs and protocols for disinfection of field equipment and gear to reduce pathogen transmission.

div.head: POLLUTION
div.p: Introduction of exotic and excess materials or energy from point and nonpoint sources can have dramatic effects on local species, habitats, and the environment. Damage is generally manifested by reduced air, soil, and water quality, which can directly affect plant, wildlife, fish, and human populations.

Waste and effluents originating from urban populations, municipalities, households, and industry can significantly degrade environmental conditions, affecting SGCN and their habitats. Pollutants can dramatically change aquatic systems by altering water chemistry and can damage important terrestrial systems through contamination of soil and water. It is important to consider these potential effects and the actions required to minimize these impacts.

div.head: HOUSEHOLD SEWAGE AND URBAN WASTE WATER
div.p: This threat includes water-borne sewage and nonpoint runoff of nutrients, sediments, and toxic chemicals (including pharmaceutical contaminants) from housing and urban areas. This threat also includes discharge from municipal waste treatment, leaking septic systems, untreated sewage, outhouses, oil and sediment from roads as well as fertilizers and pesticides from lawns and golf courses.

h Action Strategy: Protect aquatic species from anthropogenic threats including release of treated and untreated waste water, nonpoint surface runoff, and water withdrawals for public and industrial water supplies. Balloons on a beach.

div.head: INDUSTRIAL AND MILITARY EFFLUENTS
div.p: This threat includes water-borne pollution from industrial and military sources such as mining, energy production, and resource extraction industries. These contaminants are typically in the form of nutrients, sediments, and toxic chemicals resulting from illegal dumping of chemicals, mine tailings (waste material created from mining activities), leakage from fuel tanks, oil spills from pipelines, and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in river sediments. Pollution can cause negative impacts even when the source is not located near the affected aquatic system. Some pollutants may only impact these systems once bioaccumulation occurs in the food chain.

The Clean Water Act requires the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) to protect waters of the state as it relates to aquatic life, ecological condition, and human health concerns. LDEQ assesses watersheds within the state on a fouryear rotation, releasing an updated integrated report every two years. This report details support or non-support for designated uses in each subsegment based on water quality. Figure 8.5 displays data based on the results of the 2020 integrated report for assessed waters' ability to support fish and wildlife propagation.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) 303(d) 2024 list status, Louisiana has a disproportionately high number of freshwater streams that are categorized as impaired in terms of supporting fish and wildlife propagation. Out of 9,712 miles of streams and rivers assessed, 6,375 (66%) miles were found to have some degree of impairment for this designated use. The primary causes for this impairment include low oxygen, mercury, murky water (also known as turbidity), salts, and pesticides.

The EPA's evaluation of lakes and reservoirs in Louisiana indicated that of 581,446 acres assessed, 517,018 acres (89%) were deemed as impaired for fish and wildlife propagation, with the same top five causes contributing to this impaired status as streams and rivers.

In their wetland assessment, which evaluated 941,389 acres, the EPA found that only 75,219 acres (8%) were considered in good condition (i.e. they fully supported fish and wildlife propagation). The primary reasons for impairments are listed as low oxygen, mercury, murky water, and salts.

div.head: GEOLOGICAL EVENTS
div.p: This IUCN category was not addressed when considering threats and action strategies, because landslide and seismic activity is negligible in Louisiana, and there is no volcanic activity.
Lastly, the EPA's assessment of coastal waters within Louisiana found that 3,353 square miles (56%) of the 6,015 square miles were in good condition to support fish and wildlife propagation.
The leading causes of impairment in these coastal areas include mercury, low oxygen, pesticides, PCBs, and dioxins.
h Action Strategy: Minimize the occurrence and impacts of oil spills and other chemical releases.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL AND FORESTRY EFFLUENTS
div.p: This threat includes water-borne pollutants from agricultural, silvicultural, and aquacultural systems that include nutrients, toxic chemicals, and sediments. The effects of these contaminants can be seen on and off the sites where they were applied, generated, or stored. Improper handling or application often results in increased discharge of fertilizer and pesticide through runoff, and soil erosion also contributes to off-site pollution.
h Action Strategy: Encourage the proper application of pesticides. h Action Strategy: Encourage the use of sediment barriers and reduce soil erosion.

div.head: GARBAGE AND SOLID WASTE
div.p: Rubbish and other solid materials can entangle or otherwise harm wildlife. This material includes municipal waste, litter from cars and boats, construction and demolition debris, and waste that can trap wildlife such as open bottles, discarded fishing lines, and six-pack rings.

Wildlife entanglement is not the only threat associated with these items. The accumulation of harmful chemicals that can naturally leach out of these items poses an additional risk to ecological systems.

h Action Strategy: Ensure alternative garbage and solid waste use policies consider negative impacts to ecosystems. h Action Strategy: Promote recycling of used fishing line. h Action Strategy: Investigate and minimize the impacts of microplastics.

div.head: AIRBORNE POLLUTANTS
div.p: Atmospheric pollutants from point and nonpoint sources include acid rain, smog from vehicle emissions, excess smoke, excess nitrogen deposition, radioactive fallout, wind-dispersed pollutants from farm fields, and airborne particulate matter that can cause significant damage to organisms and their environments. These types of pollutants do not often stay in the atmosphere and, after a time, will condense and precipitate or deposit into other systems causing additional impacts over a larger area.
h Action Strategy: Promote use of no-till farming practices and other BMPs to reduce airborne particulates and pollutants.

div.head: EXCESS ENERGY
div.p: Inputs of heat, sound, and light that may disrupt wildlife or ecosystems include noise from highways or aircraft, heated water from power plants, floodlights and other outdoor lighting, and atmospheric radiation resulting from ozone gaps. Manatees have been lured to heated water discharge from power or chemical plants; such conditions may cause these individuals to attempt to overwinter, causing mortality of this threatened species. Attraction to lights can greatly impact insect behavior, possibly affecting reproductive events. Lighting also disorients migratory animals and may increase likelihood of collisions with buildings and communication towers. In addition, improperly sited lights near beaches can cause hatchling sea turtles to travel inland instead of to the water.
h Action Strategy: Promote education and outreach to reduce the impacts of light pollution. h Action Strategy: Promote wildlife-friendly lighting to reduce collision risk.

div.head: RESILIENT COASTAL SITES CLIMATE CHANGE
div.p: Changes in climate patterns and weather events that occur outside of the natural range of variation can be devastating to vulnerable species or habitats. Severe weather events may be increasing in frequency and intensity and expanding outside their historical range due to human influences. It is critical to take actions that minimize and mitigate the effects of these threats. See Chapter 10: Louisiana: A Regional Perspective for a more in depth consideration of this topic.

div.head: ECOSYSTEM ENCROACHMENT
div.p: The impacts of displaced ecosystems encroaching upon the habitats of other species can have far-reaching consequences.

The migration of an ecosystem is regarded as a form of stress to the ecosystem and its component species. This movement also creates additional pressure on neighboring systems and the species that inhabit them. Consequently, this may pose a threat to those adjacent systems, and mitigation should be considered.

Resilient sites offer diversity in microhabitat and niche types to support biodiversity while remaining connected to other sites to facilitate migration opportunities. Typically, these sites feature minimal barriers to migration and limited habitat fragmentation, which further enhances species diversity and overall ecosystem function. Coastal areas of Louisiana are particularly vulnerable to sea level rise, which can disproportionately affect lowland coastal systems and their ability to adapt and provide ecosystem services. Figure 8.7 depicts a map of coastal resiliency for southern Louisiana using the Southeast Conservation Blueprint's Resilient Coastal Sites indicator. This indicator originates from TNC's Resilient Coastal Sites project and depicts the capacity for coastal habitats to migrate to adjacent lowlands and sustain biodiversity and natural services under increasing inundation from sea level rise. It is based on the characteristics of current tidal complexes, their predicted migration space, and surrounding buffer areas. These characteristics include marsh complex size, shared edge with migration space, sediment balance, water quality, natural land cover, landform diversity, and more.

div.head: FRESHWATER RESILIENCE AND CONNECTIVITY
div.p: h Action Strategy: Establish and protect habitat corridors to provide critical habitat for SGCN to mitigate impacts from climactic shifts. h Action Strategy: Acquire property to increase and support critical habitat to mitigate future impacts from climate change. h Action Strategy: Promote restoration of natural barriers to minimize storm impacts including restoration of barrier islands, mainland beaches, and coastal marshes. h Action Strategy: Protect upslope environments to provide critical habitat for SGCN to mitigate impacts from sea level rise.

div.head: CHANGES IN GEOCHEMICAL REGIMES
div.p: The overall shift in the chemical composition in a geologic environment can be brought on by multiple causes which can be natural or human-induced and can have differing effects on habitats and systems depending on the severity of the shift.

Changes in geochemical conditions can result in changes to atmospheric CO², sedimentation, nutrient and metal content, and fluctuations in pH. These changes may have broad-scale effects to sensitive species or degraded ecosystems that may already be at increased risk and may not be able to cope with these shifts. In addition, subsidence (i.e. sinking of the land) can act in combination with sea level rise, decreasing available land in low lying areas.

h Action Strategy: Restore hydrology of the major rivers to allow sediment recharge into coastal environments. h Action Strategy: Promote restoration of natural barriers to minimize subsidence including restoration of barrier islands, mainland beaches, and coastal marshes.

div.head: CHANGES IN TEMPERATURE REGIMES
div.p: Widespread variation in normal temperatures (i.e. based on historical observations) can impact species and habitats across regions. These are typically observed as heatwaves, cold spells, and changes in oceanic temperature. Deviations from established temperature norms can result in atypical weather conditions. These fluctuations can impact an area's ability to support ecosystem functions, thereby influencing species distributions and overall biodiversity.

div.head: CHANGES IN PRECIPITATION AND HYDROLOGICAL REGIMES
div.p: According to projections from the South-Central and Southeast Climate Adaptation Centers, annual precipitation levels are anticipated to remain stable. However, there will likely be changes in the timing and intensity of major rainfall events. An increase in the severity of major rainfall events is expected to heighten flood risks, particularly in low lying areas, which can adversely affect aquatic systems and pose threats to human life and property.

In parallel to major precipitation events that may increase in intensity, the length of time between rainfall events is also projected to increase, potentially leading to drought-like conditions. Longer periods without precipitation will disrupt normal hydrological and terrestrial systems and persistent dry conditions will result in decreased plant productivity and increased wildfire risk.

Diminished rainfall and hydrological flow will likely reduce water availability. These conditions may lead to small permanent streams becoming ephemeral, which will reduce availability of sustained habitat. In addition, saltwater intrusion from the Gulf of America may be exacerbated, potentially causing further harm to freshwater systems. Mitigative steps to reduce the impact of these scenarios would benefit system resiliency and increase habitat adaptability.

h Action Strategy: Reestablish natural hydrology to stabilize sensitive ecosystems and minimize impacts of saltwater intrusion. h Action Strategy: Increase use of prescribed burns to minimize wildfire risks. h Action Strategy: Encourage the use of nature-based solutions and other environmentally beneficial approaches in floodwater mitigation projects. h Action Strategy: Encourage the use of green infrastructure to build resiliency in urban environments.

div.head: SEVERE AND EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS
div.p: Extreme weather events in Louisiana are generally seen in the form of tornadoes, hurricanes, and tropical storms. These extreme weather events can be very destructive, having the potential to produce high winds, storm surge, and heavy rainfall over a short period of time. Even though these events occur naturally in Louisiana, they are predicted to increase in frequency and intensity, weakening viable ecosystems or devastating already vulnerable systems such as low lying areas in the coastal zone (e.g., beaches, barrier and coastal islands, and marshes). In addition, extreme weather has been documented to cause high mortality events.

h Action Strategy: Monitor fish kills, wildlife impacts, and habitat impacts due to extreme weather events. h Action Strategy: Promote genetic diversity and local ecotypes to promote population resiliency to extreme weather events. h Action Strategy: Promote use of living shorelines and other natural shorelines to protect against the impacts of tropical cyclones.

div.head: DATA GAPS
div.p: Understanding SGCN, their habitats, and their interactions to external stimuli is an evolving process. Currently, there are limited occurrence and distribution data for many species. In addition, limited information is available on the response of species to changing environments and to the impacts of these changes.

Data can be procured from a variety of sources including public, private, commercial, and academic sources. Engaging and collaborating with all willing partners is crucial for enhancing our knowledge and incorporating landscape scale conservation efforts in the state. With vetting by professional biologists, crowdsourced information from community science platforms like iNaturalist has immense potential to inform occurrence and distribution data gaps and should be encouraged and utilized. These efforts could also significantly contribute to conservation management systems designed to protect important species and their habitats.

Addressing these information gaps can be achieved through research, analysis, and monitoring and provides the opportunity to obtain new insights and develop tools that will aid in deepening our understanding of these dynamics.

h Action Strategy: Engage the public in documenting and reporting species and habitat occurrences through citizen science initiatives. h Action Strategy: Work with partners to acquire new or emerging data and tools to aid in monitoring and management efforts.

div.head: Chapter 9: Monitoring
div.p: Monitoring is one of the Eight Required Elements of a State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP). Within each SWAP, a state must describe how it will monitor Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and their habitats, identify how it will gauge the effectiveness of conservation actions, and provide an outline of adaptive management strategies that may be incorporated as conditions change and as new information and technologies emerge. Monitoring is critical to ensure that the goals of the SWAP are met, to demonstrate the success of the SWAP and the State Wildlife Grants (SWG) Program, and to provide vital information to inform management efforts to conserve SGCN and their habitats.

Monitoring provides crucial data for documenting the status of habitats and species and evaluating the efficacy of conservation actions. Consistent, repeated monitoring provides the necessary data for adaptive management, which refines management actions based on the evolving needs of the target resource and its progress towards conservation goals (Ringold et al. 1996).
Monitoring can also provide the foresight necessary to identify emerging threats so that proactive intervention can take place (Beever 2006).
Monitoring programs should be developed based on quantifiable indicators that can assess the implementation of management actions towards desired conservation goals (Dalton et al. 2023).
To be most effective, monitoring programs should also address how ecological processes may impact the conservation target.

Techniques for monitoring vary considerably across and within all taxa groups, but all methods should be reliable, standardized, and repeatable so results can be compared over time and across regions. Species monitoring typically involves the collection of population metrics including species richness, abundance, and health (Dalton et al. 2023)

div.head: MONITORING SPECIES OF GREATEST CONSERVATION NEED AND NATURAL COMMUNITIES
DATABASE NEEDS
div.p: Sound biological data are the building blocks of all conservation planning efforts. Data can inform when and where conservation actions are most warranted and, with proper study design, can suggest successful management strategies. These data can also be used to review plans for construction activities and development projects, enabling staff to provide recommendations to minimize or eliminate threats to SGCN and natural communities.
Maximizing the utility of data relies on standardized protocols utilizing robust techniques, but it also requires that data be accessible, ideally stored within a secure, centralized database.

Given the exceptionally complicated and voluminous information collected by field biologists during projects, including SWG projects¹, such a database -one that captures raw data, ¹ For a list of Louisiana's SWG projects, visit: www.wlf.louisiana.gov/page/completed-and-ongoing-louisiana-swg-projects ² Only "tracked" species of SGCN are entered into Biotics 5; those SGCN that are not tracked are typically watch list species.

div.head: MOLLUSKS AND CRUSTACEANS
div.p: Although far from complete, researchers have expended considerable effort in recent years on aquatic mollusk and crustacean inventories in order to better understand their distribution and status. As regulatory agencies identify significant areas for SGCN conservation, it is important that these populations are subject to regular monitoring, both for detection of declines and validation of conservation actions that have been implemented.

In recent years, environmental DNA (eDNA) projects have assisted with aquatic mollusk and crustacean inventories in Louisiana. This technique involves searching for DNA discarded by the targeted species in water samples collected from various locations within a water body. This can be especially useful for confirming the presence of rare or cryptic species and guiding focused survey efforts.

div.head: MOLLUSKS
div.p: Detailed information on study design and standard methods for sampling freshwater mussels can be found in Strayer and Smith (2003), and many of these can be used for marine mollusks as well.
Below are examples of recommended sampling techniques that researchers have successfully used in Louisiana.

div.head: Time-Constrained Tactile Search
div.p: This is a type of qualitative survey and generally accepted to be the most efficient method for detecting rare species. For this technique, a surveyor moves their hands across and through substrate for a specified amount of time, collecting any mussels located during the process (Dunn 2000). The surveyor may employ a snorkel or SCUBA to access deeper water. The total amount of time spent in a given area is typically 1 to 1.5 personhours (Dinkins et al. 2022, Pezold et al. 2002, Brown and Banks 2001, Brown et al. 2010); however, these time intervals are likely too short to detect the majority of rare species present (Garig 2023, Metcalfe-Smith et al. 2000).

div.head: Transect Tactile Search
div.p: This is a type of quantitative survey that is useful for covering large areas systematically. Transects are run from bank to bank, perpendicular to flow. Surveyors tactilely search a specified area along the transect, usually one meter wide, at a rate usually 0.5 min/m² for homogeneous substrates and 0.75 min/m² for heterogeneous substrates (USFWS and TPWD 2023).
(ABOVE AND BELOW) Visual Search: LDWF biologists survey for Louisiana Pearlshell using a transparent-bottomed bucket.
Traps: Traps used for capturing crayfish.

div.head: Sediment Collection and Sieving
div.p: Although time consuming, this methodology is recommended when accurate mussel densities or juvenile data are required. Surveyors excavate randomly distributed quadrats, usually 0.25 m², to a depth of 10 -15 cm and strain collected material through a wire mesh. Researchers often couple this technique with tactile searches in order to obtain a more complete picture of the mussel community (Dinkins et al. 2022, Dunn 2000).

div.head: CRUSTACEANS
div.p: Techniques for sampling crustaceans vary widely with habitat type and targeted species. Researchers have used various trap designs, electroshocking, seines, dip nets, and burrow excavations to study the distribution of these organisms, primarily crayfish, in Louisiana.
The following information provides additional details on these techniques.

div.head: Traps
div.p: Minnow traps, pillow traps, and pyramid traps can be effective for sampling crayfishes in Louisiana, especially in habitats where other techniques are not feasible. Multi-day trap-soak times are generally required to achieve sufficient capture rates. Traps tend to disproportionately capture large males (Dorn et al. 2005), arguably a benefit, as large males are sometimes required for species identification. Researchers can add various baits to traps to lure crayfishes; however, information on the efficacy of this is mostly limited to commercial species and baiting may not affect capture rates of non-commercial species.

div.head: Backpack Electrofishing
div.p: This technique is an effective means of sampling for crayfishes, especially when researchers desire high capture rates, but is limited to relatively clear, shallow water with sufficient conductivity. A crew of two to three individuals is preferred; one crew member is needed to wear the backpack and move the anode across areas likely to contain crayfishes, and one or two crew members are needed as dip net operators to capture stunned crayfishes. However, it is possible for a single individual to conduct surveys using this technique (Budnick et al. 2018). Surveyors should receive safety and technique training for this gear type, which is available free of cost from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) (www. fws.gov/course/principles-and-techniques-electrofishing-online).
Chapter 9: Monitoring

div.head: Seine
div.p: This tool consists of a net extended between two poles that users pull through water while keeping the lower edge of the net in contact with the substrate. For crayfish sampling, a net length of 10 feet or less is recommended and works best in areas devoid of underwater obstructions. In streams with a swift current, users can hold seines stationary while surveyors upstream operate a backpack electrofishing unit. In addition, surveyors can disturb the substrate or vegetation using their feet, flushing hidden individuals into the seine net downstream.

div.head: D-frame Net
div.p: A robust version of a dip net with at least one flat side, this tool is used for skimming streambed substrates to capture crayfishes. Net bags are typically canvas with mesh in the bottom and are often attached to the frame via hog rings. This configuration is especially useful for sampling streams, because crayfishes in these habitats are often located among roots and under rocks and woody debris. In addition, these nets are effective for sampling ephemeral pools and ditches.

When compared to backpack electrofishing, this cost effective and widely used technique typically results in fewer individual crayfishes captured per unit of time but yields similar species richness estimates (Budnick et al. 2018).

div.head: Burrow Excavation
div.p: This is one of a limited number of options researchers have to sample crayfishes that spend most of the year in burrows (i.e. primary burrowers). Using a shovel or hand trowel, surveyors excavate a burrow featuring a recently constructed chimney. Inserting a piece of flexible tubing down the burrow beforehand will help surveyors determine the burrow path during excavation. Surveyors should search any side tunnels encountered, as the target crayfish may be in one of them.
Further details on crustacean sampling techniques can be found in Walls (2009) and Zale et al. (2012).

div.head: NON-CRUSTACEAN ARTHROPODS
div.p: The techniques for sampling non-crustacean arthropods (e.g., insects, arachnids, etc.) are as diverse as the groups themselves, and, as such, the techniques utilized are dependent upon the target organism(s). In fact, as insects may undergo complete metamorphosis, survey techniques can also vary by life stage, adding further complexity to monitoring. Active techniques include visual encounter surveys, aerial netting, sweep netting, aquatic netting, collection by beat sheets, and more. Passive techniques can include pan traps, pitfall traps, flight intercept traps, emergence traps, and others. Depending on the target species, the effectiveness of traps can be improved by adding baits, pheromones, or light sources to lure individuals to the traps. Those species less likely to be trapped (e.g., cryptic, soil-dwelling invertebrates) can often be procured using a Berlese-Tullgren funnel.

Regardless of sampling technique employed, monitoring requires repeated surveys in order to gauge changes in abundance, richness, etc. Standardization of these techniques is key to making appropriate comparisons across studies. Montgomery and colleagues (2021) present an excellent synopsis of several insect sampling methods, the suggested metadata to be collected with each, and what methods are most appropriate for several taxa. Ferro and Summerlin (2019) provide language to define collection methodology. Coordination of insect data collection and analysis, as well as identification and amelioration of threats to insects, are goals of the Status of Insects: An International Research Coordination Network (https://statusofinsects.github.io/).

Despite forward progress in standardization, significant challenges remain, and standardization is still lacking for most survey techniques and taxa. Although surveyors may readily learn proper setting and collection of traps and active sampling and collection methods, identification of most arthropods, especially to family, genus, or species, is time consuming and requires special expertise, and often, specialized equipment. In fact, for these reasons, researchers often do not identify many arthropods to species level during projects. Because of the scarcity of these data, even baseline information on arthropod distribution is lacking, which often hamstrings conservation efforts of SGCN in Louisiana. To address this knowledge gap, LDWF collects data on arthropod SGCN both through in-house efforts as well as partnering with experts. Surveys of imperiled species are vital to determine the distribution and abundance of these species so that management or conservation actions can be successfully implemented. Due to their high fecundity and short generation times, arthropods often respond rapidly to habitat manipulation and may be early indicators of habitat management effectiveness.
Examples of recommended sampling techniques for noncrustacean arthropods include:

div.head: Aspirators
div.p: Aspirators are invaluable tools used to capture terrestrial arthropods, most often using a vacuum created by the user's own lungs. Aspirators are usually made with a vial, a rubber stopper with two short pieces of metal tubing embedded in it, one short length of rubber tubing, and a piece of very fine mesh.

The mesh attaches to one end of a piece of metal tube on the vial side of the rubber stopper (i.e. inside of the vial); the rubber tubing attaches to the opposite end (i.e. outside of the vial) of the metal tube that has the mesh attached. The other metal tube, the collection tube, is often gently bent (<90°) outside the vial to assist in reach. When users inhale (ideally, only into the mouth) through the rubber tubing, the arthropod is quickly sucked into the vial via the collection tube and prevented from entering the user's mouth via the mesh. A small, plastic, in-line gasoline filter attached to the rubber tubing adds protection (Singh et al. 2024). Size of target arthropods is limited by the diameter of the collection tube.

div.head: Aerial Nets
div.p: Aerial nets are used specifically for capturing flying insects like mayflies, dragonflies, flies, bees, wasps, butterflies, and moths. An aerial net typically consists of a soft, fragile mesh bag attached to a wire loop affixed to a long handle.

div.head: Sweep Nets
div.p: Sweep nets are used for capturing terrestrial arthropods typically found on live or dead vegetation. Unlike aerial nets, sweep nets are more robust with short, strong handles and with hoops adorned with very fine mesh bags reinforced with strong fabric or with full canvas bags. Sweep nets can be swept through vegetation to dislodge and capture virtually all sizes of insects, most of which can then be quickly collected via aspirator. Sweep net effort "can be 'quantified' by maintaining a constant area swept per sweep and a consistent number of sweeps per sample" (Singh et al. 2024).

div.head: Aquatic Nets
div.p: Aquatic nets, like sweep nets, are robust and made to sustain the rigors of use, in this case, striking underwater hazards like submerged debris. Aquatic nets have sturdy handles and hoops with at least one flat side (e.g., D-shaped) meant to skim streambed substrates (e.g., submerged leaf litter) to capture aquatic or semi-aquatic arthropods. Net bags are typically canvas with mesh in the bottom and are often attached to the hoops via hog rings.

div.head: Hess Samplers
div.p: Hess samplers can be used to actively collect aquatic invertebrates in shallow, lotic waters. A Hess sampler is made from an open, upright, metal cylinder with a mesh screen on one side (upstream) to allow water flow and a collection net on the opposite side (downstream). Once the cylinder is positioned upright on the substrate, the user agitates the substrate to dislodge invertebrates, which water flow carries into the collection net. Having a fixed sampling area, Hess samplers can be used for quantitative studies. See Gibbs and colleagues for a comparison of Hess samplers with other methods (Gibbs et al. 2023).

div.head: Beat Sheets
div.p: Beat sheets are similar to sweep nets in that they are efficient for collecting terrestrial arthropods from live or dead vegetation.

A beat sheet is typically a canvas sheet reinforced with two crisscrossed dowel rods with their ends inserted into pockets in the four corners of the sheet (i.e. similar to a homemade kite). When the beat sheet is held by the dowels, the canvas sags into a very shallow "net." With the beat sheet held under vegetation, the user then vigorously strikes the vegetation with a stick; insects are dislodged and fall into the beat sheet where they are collected, usually via aspirator.

div.head: Visual Encounter Surveys (VES)
div.p: The use of VES in arthropod monitoring is limited to especially showy groups of day-flying insects like dragonflies and butterflies that can be readily identified in the field using binoculars. One rare example of nighttime VES includes the use of longwave ultraviolet (UV) flashlights for the detection of scorpions; the WDP documented almost 500 Southern Unstriped Scorpions along transects through Southern Mesophytic Hardwood Forest in just five nights using UV flashlights. VES may be combined with other techniques such as aerial netting to assist in species identification (Montgomery et al. 2021).
Light Traps: Researcher setting up a black light trap to capture non-crustacean arthropods (LEFT), and an example of a light trap used to trap insects (RIGHT).

div.head: Pan Traps
div.p: Pan traps can be created using brightly colored, plastic plates or shallow bowls filled with soapy water. Pan traps target small bees and wasps, which are attracted by the bright colors and become trapped in the soapy water. Like other techniques, recording the number of active traps and the amount of time the traps are active is vital for comparison studies. This type of trap should be checked at least once per day (Singh et al. 2024).

div.head: Pitfall Traps
div.p: Pitfall traps are often made by nesting two containers of similar size and shape in a hole in the ground with the lip of the inner container flush with the ground surface. (2016) propose pitfall trap standardization methods.

div.head: Flight-Intercept Traps
div.p: Flight-intercept traps block the flight-path of insects, forcing insects to either fly over the barrier, typically a vertical wall of very fine mesh, to escape or drop into a liquid-filled collection tray beneath the barrier. Collection trays, often trough-shaped, are partly filled with killing/preserving agents, the type of which will determine how often traps must be checked. Plastic tarps are frequently hung over the tops of these traps to prevent inundation of collection trays by rain (Singh et al. 2024).

div.head: Malaise Traps
div.p: Malaise traps are also used for capturing insects in flight, particularly those species that fly upward when confronted with an obstacle. The open, tent-shaped Malaise trap uses a vertical wall of very fine mesh to funnel flying insects into a collection container at the top (ceiling) of the tent. These traps, which are modified flight-intercept traps, can also be combined with the traditional flight-intercept trap design by adding collection trays beneath (Montgomery et al. 2021).

div.head: Light Traps
div.p: Light traps capitalize on the positive phototactic (i.e. being attracted to light) behavior of many insects. Trap designs are extremely variable from a light suspended in front of a white bed sheet to specialized traps for aquatic insects. Passive light traps typically include a collection container affixed below a funnel and/or radiating vanes situated below a light source (Montgomery et al. 2021). Light sources also vary with lightemitting diodes (LED) and Mercury vapor, UV, black light, and metal halide bulbs as options (Ferro and Summerlin 2019).

div.head: Emergence Traps
div.p: Emergence traps are used to capture insects as they transition from immature stages to adults. These traps are often openbottomed, tent-shaped structures composed of fine mesh or other material and can be floated atop water for aquatic insect capture or placed over soil for terrestrial species. Modified versions may be built in-situ around vegetation and tree trunks (Grootaert et al. 2010). Most types also include a collection container situated at the top of the trap.

div.head: Hester-Dendy Samplers
div.p: Hester-Dendy samplers are aquatic samplers composed of several stacked plates with stacked washers to vary the spacing between plates. These samplers may be deployed at different depths including lying on the streambed. Typically, samplers are suspended in the water column by floats and anchors for a few to several weeks to allow colonization by aquatic invertebrates.

div.head: INLAND FISHES
div.p: Although freshwater fish SGCN research and monitoring in Louisiana have made great strides in recent years, there are still data gaps in occurrence, distribution, abundance, habitat preference, habitat availability, movement patterns, and life history. In addition to focused research projects, regular monitoring is necessary, as aquatic habitats face many disturbances and threats, with significant impacts from changes in hydrology, land use, connectivity, and climate patterns (see the Inland Fish Threats section). Hypoxia, amplified by heat, drought, and storms, is prevalent in south Louisiana, and monitoring the impacts to and recovery of fish populations is required for effective management. Up-to-date freshwater fish SGCN data are necessary for targeted conservation and restoration efforts, determining impacts of proposed infrastructure projects, aiding in Species Status Assessments for federally petitioned species, and other applications. In addition to fish data, water quality and other physical data of waters across the state must be monitored to inform the health of aquatic systems.
Patterns in threats to aquatic habitats and fish SGCN can be found across the state; however, there are differences in magnitude and scale in different types of water bodies.

Research is especially needed in large river systems to determine impacts of impoundments, navigation, and flood control projects. Headwater streams are sensitive habitats, and monitoring the effectiveness of conservation actions and impacts of flood control projects is needed. Coastal basins face unique threats from saltwater intrusion and diversions, and monitoring changes in species composition over time is critical in these dynamic environments. Researching the impacts of fish passage barriers across all habitats, with the aid of the Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership's online support tools, is necessary to reconnect habitats and populations for more resilient aquatic communities.
LDWF conducts regular sport fish and water quality monitoring across the state, and SGCN data are recorded as they are caught, either during community sampling or as bycatch. Inland

Upon retrieval, users collect the entire sampler to ensure minimal loss of invertebrates. Later, the trap is rinsed into a collection container to isolate invertebrates from the sampler.
