The Florida Department of Environmental Protection produced the Methods of Hester-Dendy Multiplate Sampler Deployment (2006), which provides helpful suggestions on sampler design and deployment.

div.head: Burlese-Tullgren Funnels
div.p: Burlese-Tullgren funnels provide an efficient method for extracting small arthropods from soil/leaf litter samples. Each sample should be stored in the field in separate breathable bags. The sample can be sieved to remove coarse debris such as leaves, sticks, and rocks during field collection or later. The sample is then placed on a screen at the bottom of a funnel which leads to a collection container filled with alcohol. A heat-producing light source placed above the funnel creates a temperature and desiccation gradient in the sample, which drives soil invertebrates from the sample into the collection container. Junod and colleagues (2023) offer an interesting alternative pitfall design that may outperform Burlese-Tullgren funnels in some instances.

div.head: Acoustic Monitoring
div.p: Acoustic monitoring has a limited use in arthropod surveys. Grasshoppers, crickets, and cicadas, which have loud speciesspecific mating calls, are the most appropriate arthropod targets for acoustic monitoring (Montgomery et al. 2021). Use of autonomous recording units for data collection can minimize field time for personnel, but identification of species from recordings is extremely time-consuming. Increased efficacy may be obtained through machine learning but requires reference audio for training (Montgomery et al. 2021).

div.head: Metabarcoding
div.p: Metabarcoding of eDNA shows significant promise in biodiversity monitoring of insects and other arthropods (Ruppert et al. 2019, Van Klink et al. 2022, Leandro et al. 2024, van Klink et al. 2024).

Environmental DNA can be collected from samples of water, air, soil, vegetation, and several other substrates (Thomsen and Sigsgaard 2019, Uchida et al. 2020, Campbell et al. 2022, Roger et al. 2022). Once extracted, the resulting DNA is "amplified, sequenced, and categorized based on its sequence" (Ruppert et al. 2019). Such analyses can yield identifications of taxa based on libraries of known DNA barcodes; species representation in these libraries varies widely among taxa and remains a challenge in metabarcoding studies (Leandro et al. 2024). In addition, metabarcoding, although useful for determining species presence, is not especially helpful for determining species abundance, nor can it provide sex ratios or body condition (Ruppert et al. 2019). Nevertheless, metabarcoding remains a valuable tool for arthropod monitoring, particularly for "detecting the first occurrences of invasive species, the continued presence of native species thought to be extinct or otherwise threatened, and other elusive species occurring in low densities that would be difficult to detect by traditional means" (Ruppert et al. 2019). Metabarcoding is one type of eDNA method that can be used for non-crustacean arthropods. Other methods are available and may be used depending on research questions and data needs. When using eDNA techniques, users should consider the various factors that can degrade eDNA, cause contamination, or affect abundance in the environment such as ultraviolet radiation, temperature, turbidity, microbial activity, eDNA shed rate, and water chemistries (Eichmiller et al. 2016, Jo et al. 2020, Seymour et al. 2018).
Chapter 9: Monitoring Hoop Nets: LDWF staff use lead nets to survey for inland fishes.

Fisheries districts are encouraged to pursue independent research projects, which may focus on SGCN; however, research needs for freshwater fish SGCN are vast and can only be addressed with the combined efforts of state and federal agencies, universities, river authorities, and other research institutions. In addition to collaborating with the these entities, LDWF will continue to participate in partnerships such as the Mississippi Interstate Cooperative Resource Association, the Lower Mississippi River Conservation Committee, the Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership, and the Louisiana Watershed Initiative to better research and monitor freshwater fish SGCN.
Staff members are also involved with the American Fisheries Society at all levels, which aids in collaboration and awareness of the leading edge of fisheries science.

Fisheries science is ever-improving, but has a suite of welldeveloped field methods for sampling and monitoring with origins going back to the Paleolithic Era, originally in the pursuit of food. Modern materials and technologies have expanded and improved on many of these techniques, but many gear types have changed relatively little in hundreds or thousands of years.

Because of the diversity of aquatic habitats and fish morphology and habits, many techniques require modifications to best catch target species such as using a backpack electrofisher combined with a riffle kick to capture fish in a seine set downstream or adding wings and leads to a hoop net.

Recent improvements in many techniques developed in the twentieth century have greatly expanded opportunities in freshwater fish research. Electrofishing has become more precise, with improved abilities to set power and digitally track various aspects of a sampling run. Fish movement monitoring has made great strides from radio telemetry to acoustic telemetry, which allows for greater geographic coverage, detection, precision, and data sharing. With digital data storage and sharing, fisheries data from museums, agencies, and universities from across the world can be easily accessed from a personal computer.

Genetic studies are now largely performed by analyzing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), leading to much higher resolution genetic detail than was previously available. In addition to advances in genetic techniques used on individual fish and populations, genetic metabarcoding techniques can aid in determining stomach contents and species presence in a water sample using eDNA. Genetic metabarcoding techniques are strong tools, but are not foolproof, and should be used in conjunction with, or to guide, more traditional fisheries sampling techniques.

Most fisheries methods are versatile and can be used for a wide variety of target species and habitats. Knowledge of species' habits, habitats, gear options, intended uses, and inherent biases are necessary for effective fish sampling. Detailed fisheries sampling methods can be found in Zale and colleagues (2012) and Bonar and colleagues (2024). A few methods commonly used in Louisiana are listed below.

div.head: Seine Nets
div.p: Seine nets have a number of applications, based on target species, habitat features, size of net, and technique, and are intended to be used in wadeable waters. They are an active gear type and generally range in size from 10 to 50 feet long, with various mesh sizes, with or without a "bag," and come untreated or treated with net coating. Seine nets are typically pulled with the current but can be set downstream of riffles to perform a "riffle kick" or used as a block net while fish are flushed from holes or cut-banks. A seine net is one of the oldest and most versatile pieces of fishing equipment.

div.head: Gill Nets
div.p: Gill nets are passive gear used to entangle fish from a set position. Modern gill nets are usually made of nylon monofilament, which comes in various strengths and can be twisted with multiple strands for added strength. Nylon multifilament (similar to twine) nets, also known as "gar nets," provide the most strength but are not suitable for most species. Gill nets can be set for an extended period (e.g., overnight), checked periodically (e.g., every two hours), or run as strike nets that are picked up quickly after herding fish into them with a boat. Trammel nets are gill nets with extra layers of webbing, adding increased opportunity for entanglement. Gill nets come in a variety of lengths, depths, webbing sizes, and float and weight configurations. The proper gill nets should be selected based on habitat, target species, and sampling methods.

div.head: Hoop Nets
div.p: Hoop nets are a passive gear type consisting of a series of hoops, often made of fiberglass or steel, wrapped in a synthetic or metal net with a throat or series of throats at one end. They are fished horizontally pointing downstream, facing open water in lentic environments, or can be fished vertically in calm waters. Hoop nets can be fished with or without bait. This gear type is typically used to target catfish, but it is effective on a number of other types of benthic fishes, including suckers. There are also small hoop nets to target minnows and other small fish. Hoop nets can be modified with leads and walls to make lead nets and fyke nets, which can increase effectiveness.
Chapter 9: Monitoring

div.head: Electrofishing
div.p: Electrofishing is an active technique that usually targets small to medium sized fish, typically using direct current (DC), with a current flowing between a cathode (metal boat or "rat tail" on a backpack) and an anode (prod pole with metal ring or booms) to stun fish for capture. Modern electrofishing equipment offers multiple settings options to maximize effectiveness in different water conductivities on different types of fish. Most electrofishing in Louisiana is conducted from a boat-mounted or backpack unit, but other methods of electrofishing include shore shocking, tow barges, and prepositioned grids. Safety and technique training for this gear type is recommended and available free of cost from the USFWS (www. fws.gov/course/principles-and-techniques-electrofishing-online).

div.head: Hook and Line
div.p: Hook and line sampling can be active or passive and is an acceptable method in certain circumstances. Hook and line sampling can take place in the form of rod and reel, set line, trotline, or yo-yo. Successful hook and line sampling requires a fish to find and attempt to consume bait. This method can be less effective than nets, traps, and electricity, but in certain circumstances, like catching sturgeon in deep flowing water, it may be the best option.

div.head: Traps
div.p: There are also a number of traps designed for different species such as eel pots, minnow traps, and bream traps that can be used in a number of applications.

div.head: Trawling
div.p: Trawling is an active netting method conducted from a boat. Trawls are only recommended in large inland waters where the possibility of snagging on submerged debris is minimal (e.g., in the Mississippi River). This can be an effective method of catching fish in fresh waters that are difficult to sample with the above methods.

div.head: Collection of Habitat Data
div.p: Habitat data are critical to fisheries research and monitoring. Water quality, physical habitat, flow, and other habitat data are vital for understanding biotic conditions and should accompany biological research and monitoring. There are numerous approaches to taking habitat data including in-person readings, continuous monitoring gauges and probes, satellite data, and land use data that may be appropriate depending on the focus of the research.

div.head: MARINE FISHES
div.p: The status of marine SGCN is closely related to habitat threats in the coastal ecosystem, especially marsh loss and degradation, and, therefore, these species may be some of the first to exhibit population declines. Habitat threats are at a critical level in the coastal zone. In response, LDWF Office of Fisheries prioritizes these habitat and has a habitat focused approach rather than a species focused approach. Data collected through this process provides indices of community structure within and across habitats and can show trends in population abundances by habitat type.

Fixed-location stations, stratified by habitat type, are established in each Coastal Study Area (CSA), and fishing gear appropriate to that station is used to collect physical, chemical, and biological data, as appropriate. Sampling gear is deployed and data are collected and recorded according to standard protocols.

The basic framework for marine/estuarine monitoring in Louisiana was established in 1968 with the Gulf-wide Cooperative Gulf of Mexico Estuarine Inventory (GMEI) and Study (Perret 1971, Perret et al. 1971). The GMEI was further

Chapter 9: Monitoring refined with the implementation of the watershed-based CSA management system for penaeid shrimp (White and Boudreaux 1977), which was adapted for finfish monitoring in 1985. The general system for data collection established in 1968 has been used continuously since that time. Full details on the sampling protocol used and the updated inventory are available in the Louisiana Estuarine, Coastal, and Offshore Marine Species Inventory (Fischer et al. 2023). Projects rely on sampling with standardized gear over a range of habitats to characterize biological and environmental conditions. The focus of the GMEI and CSA projects is primarily to document and monitor the importance of Louisiana's estuaries as contributors to Gulf of America recreational and commercial fisheries. As a result, these projects have established long-term data sets for the various habitats and fish and invertebrate species in Louisiana's coastal habitats.

Many marine and estuarine species are understudied, and longterm trends in their abundance are seldom known. It will be necessary to identify methods to monitor and verify the status of cryptic species by documenting presence, habitat use, and life history characteristics. This type of monitoring must be in addition to and linked to standard monitoring used for more well-known species to validate trends of cryptic species.

Many conservation efforts are underway to protect, enhance, or modify coastal wetlands. These efforts will also affect the aquatic habitats and fauna associated with these coastal habitats, sometimes in ways that are not predicted or fully understood. Special purpose assessment and monitoring projects must be developed and maintained to assess the impact of these conservation efforts on both the terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems impacted.

Areas may be identified for habitat conservation or restoration through a variety of assessment procedures. Selection criteria may include species diversity (current or potential), unique nature of the habitat in the state or region, and areas recognized by previous national or state prioritization processes.

div.head: AMPHIBIANS AND REPTILES
div.p: Various survey methodologies exist for studying amphibian and reptile populations. It is important to select the sampling design and techniques that are best suited for the target species and can address the desired question, while considering cost, equipment needs, seasonal activity, weather patterns, habitat characteristics, and other variables (Graeter 2013a). Regardless of the design, surveys should be standardized throughout the project duration and should be repeated as feasible.

Repeated surveys can aid in determining species' life history characteristics and can help address the variability in detections caused by seasonality, time of day, and weather conditions. By utilizing survey constraints and standardization guidelines, survey results can be compared both within and among projects utilizing a similar design (Graeter 2013a).
The methods listed below are recommended, standard practices for monitoring amphibian and reptile populations.

div.head: Time-Constrained Designs
div.p: Time-constrained designs standardize the duration of a survey, typically in the form of surveying for a predetermined amount of time (Todd 2013a). Survey effort can be calculated by multiplying the predetermined amount of time by the number of surveyors. The number of species or the number of individuals per species can then be divided by the calculated survey effort; this will provide the number of species and/or relative abundance per person-hours. The survey effort should only include search time; any time taken to process individuals (e.g., photographing and measuring specimens) should be excluded from calculations. Time-constrained designs, however, may limit the thoroughness in which an area is surveyed; it can require a significant amount of time to adequately survey an area, and there is a potential for observer bias when using certain sampling methods. It is also important to note that in order to effectively compare survey results, the same techniques must be utilized in all subsequent surveys (Todd 2013a).

div.head: Area-Constrained Designs
div.p: Area-constrained designs standardize the size of the survey area; surveys conclude when the entire area has been surveyed completely (Todd 2013b). The predetermined size of the survey area is primarily dependent on the habitat and the focal species. Survey areas can be designed to fit a desired time commitment but should be standardized throughout a particular project and between habitat types. The area-constrained design allows for estimations of species' densities and relative abundances per unit area as well as species' presence or absence. Similar to time-constrained designs, abiotic factors can greatly influence the results of area-constrained designs, and survey replication is required to provide the most valuable data. In addition, surveys should be conducted at multiple locations of the same habitat type within the project area. This helps ensure that survey results are representative of that habitat type. The area-constrained design also has limitations in that the survey areas must be searched thoroughly and with equal effort across multiple surveys (Todd 2013b).

div.head: Transect Designs
div.p: Transect designs, which can be viewed as a type of areaconstraint, standardize a specific survey path (Fedewa 2013).

Transects can be conducted via straight lines or adapted, as necessary, to follow suitable habitat of target species (e.g., river shoreline). Surveyors are restricted to a specified path and are expected to search a standardized buffer zone that extends from the centerline of the transect path. This design can determine species' relative presence/absence, abundance, and densities across habitat types. Transect designs are particularly useful in assessing differences between habitat types (e.g., comparing upland to bottomland habitats) and determining the parameters that influence species' occupancy (Fedewa 2013).

div.head: ACTIVE SAMPLING TECHNIQUES
div.p: Active sampling involves actively searching for target species and may be aided by tools that increase detection success.

div.head: Visual Encounter Survey
div.p: Visual Encounter Surveys (VES) involve visually searching for species via randomized-walk, quadrat, or transect methods and can be time-constrained and/or area-constrained (Glaudas 2013a). Efficacy varies depending on the target species and its associated habitat type. Species that regularly elude capture by passive techniques may be detected more readily with VES; however, for species that utilize dense vegetation or areas that make detection more difficult, other techniques may be needed to adequately assess their status. VES are used to determine species richness and abundance, but comparisons between VES can be challenging, which make survey replication and collection of abiotic information critical.

div.head: Environmental DNA Surveys
div.p: Environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling is a time-efficient method to gather presence data on rare, threatened, and endangered species, specifically species that are difficult to detect with traditional techniques. These surveys are also useful in the early detection of invasive and non-native species and facilitation of invasive species management (NISC 2022). This sampling tool has been used primarily for aquatic species, including herpetofauna, to examine biodiversity in aquatic habitats (Takahashi et al. 2023). In recent years, this technique has been applied to species inhabiting terrestrial habitats, particularly for rare upland snakes (Katz et al. 2020). Sampling should occur during the active season for target species due to the seasonal fluctuations in eDNA release (Huang et al. 2022).

div.head: Dip-Netting
div.p: Dip-nets can be used during VES to enhance a surveyor's ability to catch species in aquatic habitats (Todd 2013c). This tool may be used opportunistically or as part of a structured survey of habitats. (Tesche and Hodges 2015). To improve detection and capture success of some species, surveyors may conduct dipnetting at night, with a spotlight. When sampling similar sites, researchers should keep a tally of the number of net sweeps so that effort can be compared to other areas sampled in a similar manner (Lagler 1943).

div.head: Basking Surveys and Basking Traps
div.p: Basking surveys are conducted using optical equipment to scan the environment for turtles that regularly use basking structures (Lindeman 1996, Buhlmann 2013). Spotting scopes provide a greater viewing distance than binoculars, allowing for identification with less risk of flushing basking turtles back into the water. Basking surveys can be conducted on foot or by canoe or other suitable watercraft. This technique is particularly useful to assess species presence in water bodies where it may not be feasible to employ other survey techniques due to water flow, water depth, limited site accessibility, or life history traits incompatible with other techniques. Data on turtle species, number of turtles, age class (adult, juvenile), and sex can be recorded. If turtles have been previously marked using a highly visible method (e.g., waterproof spray paint), density estimates can also be calculated.

Basking traps are useful in areas where the water column is too deep for other trapping methods and for basking turtles that cannot be captured by baited traps. These traps are opentopped and constructed of mesh material (e.g., crayfish trap wire) in the shape of a small, medium, or large basket to fit various sizes of basking logs. Traps can be attached to basking logs with nails and twine or fitted with floats along the top portion of the basket and then attached to basking logs. Traps are then placed just under the water surface and adjacent to or underneath known or potential basking structures. Surveyors return to the site after a few minutes of settling time to prompt basking turtles to retreat into the traps; surveyors can then collect trapped turtles (Buhlmann 2013).

Presence of basking sites is necessary to perform either survey technique; however, it is important to note that although a lack of basking sites may be detrimental for some species, it is not an indicator of the absence of those species (Lindeman 1999).

div.head: Detection Dogs
div.p: Detection dogs have assisted with wildlife research and management for centuries; there is renewed interest in the use of these dogs, especially for cryptic amphibians and reptiles.

Limitations to this technique include length of time to train, lifespan of the dog, personality of the dog, ability to secure an appropriate number of scent samples for training, lack of standardized protocols, and lack of understanding regarding degradation of scent in the wild. Despite the difficulties of training detection dogs, this technique can be vastly superior to some more traditional techniques. Kapfer and colleagues (2012) detected more individuals of Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina carolina) in nine hours with detection dogs than hundreds of hours of VES. Although there may be uncertainty concerning the detection of subterranean species, trained dogs have been shown to detect Eastern Indigo Snake (Drymarchon couperi) deep within Gopher Tortoise burrows in Georgia and Florida (Stevenson et al. 2010). Cablk and Heaton (2006) found that trained dogs were effective at detecting Desert Tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) and were also able to detect much smaller tortoises compared to human observers in similar studies. This technique shows great promise at detecting difficult-to-trap species and age classes. Mark-resight surveys have been used to estimate abundance and population size of basking freshwater turtles. Captured turtles are marked via a non-toxic, tree-marking spray paint on the 2nd and 3rd vertebral scutes of the carapace and released at the point of capture (Selman 2024). Basking resight surveys are conducted within two weeks of marking turtles (Selman 2024). Surveyors must capture an adequate number of turtles to use this survey method. Both mark-recapture and markresight surveys may be repeated to gather population data and assess trends in population size and demographics.

div.head: Radio Tracking
div.p: Radio tracking can provide data on movement patterns and survival over a longer timeframe than typical survey-based projects (Mullican 1988). For turtles, transmitters may be attached to the carapace via marine epoxy or bolted to the edge of the carapace. Harnesses can be used to attach transmitters to frogs, toads, and lizards. Some transmitters may be surgically implanted in other herpetofaunal species such as snakes.

Using a receiver and antenna, the location of the transmitter, and thus the individual, can be determined. The closer the receiver is to the transmitter, the louder the "chirp" detected by the receiver. Certain implanted transmitter types can record body temperature of individuals, with the temperature of the transmitter reflected by the frequency of "chirps" (White andGarrott 1990, Carter et al. 1999).
When using tracking techniques, the potential impact of the attached tracking device on the individual should be considered.

If the attachment weighs too much or greatly increases visibility, the device may impede normal movement or behavior, both of Automated Recording Units: An automated recording unit (ARU) used to record calling frogs.

which can increase the likelihood of predation and bias data collected. In addition, it is also possible for an attachment to become entangled with environmental objects or impact the ability of individuals to reproduce (Graeter 2013b).

div.head: Road Cruising Surveys
div.p: Road cruising involves surveying in a transect design where target species are known or presumed to occur (Andrews 2013). Detected individuals are often reported as Alive on Road (AOR) or Dead on Road (DOR; Smith and Dodd 2003). Habitat type, time of year, weather conditions, and other variables influence the species detected during these surveys (Andrews 2013). Therefore, it is beneficial to review available natural history information for the target species and baseline site data prior to conducting a road cruising survey (Tsaliagos 2013). These surveys are most effective at detecting target species during peak activity times such as breeding season. Number of observers present and distance traveled should be recorded to determine effort and compare survey results with other similar surveys. This technique has several limitations (Case 1978).
Larger roads can present more of an obstacle to species and may reduce the likelihood that crossing attempts will be made.

In addition, traffic and road presence can alter the behavior of target species by attracting them for thermoregulation or deterring them because of noise (Boarman andSazaki 1996, Langen et al. 2015). This technique is not adequate for population sampling; therefore, it is best suited for determining species presence (Andrews 2013).

div.head: Aerial Surveys
div.p: Aerial surveys that utilize Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) such as drones to document basking and nesting sites in or near aquatic habitats is a relatively novel technique. This method is most applicable in areas that are visually open such as grasslands, sandbars, and Longleaf Pine savannas (Glaudas 2013b). Transects are the most appropriate survey design for this technique with flight altitude, speed, and width of area sampled (including field of view of camera) remaining constant to allow for comparability (Caughley 1974). UAS should remain in view of the observers at all times. Observer bias may have a large impact on detection probability, and although this technique is inadequate at estimating population size, it can assist in determining the need for further sampling using more standard techniques (Caughley 1974, Glaudas 2013b).
In addition, the use of UAS is heavily regulated by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Those wishing to use this technique should review current FAA regulations.

Fixed-wing aerial surveys are useful for locating evidence of nesting sea turtles, particularly for remote beaches and barrier islands that are inaccessible by foot or land vehicle (Schroeder and Murphy 1999). This survey method can be standardized to evaluate trends in nesting activity, which would provide insight for management and coastal restoration activities (Lamont et al. 2023). A seaplane flies the length of the survey area at a low altitude to allow surveyors to detect sea turtle crawls as well as capture photographs to subsequently confirm species identification and nesting activity (e.g., presence of body pits).

If feasible, the seaplane lands nearshore to allow surveyor(s) to gather measurements for each crawl and body pit as well as distance to high tide line and vegetation (Lamont et al. 2023). Sea turtles typically nest during nighttime hours, therefore, surveys are conducted during early morning while crawls are still intact and less likely affected by weather events.

div.head: PASSIVE SAMPLING TECHNIQUES
div.p: Monitoring methods such as the active techniques above are effective means of evaluating population status but require considerable effort to implement. With passive technology, it is feasible to gather quality data that will inform the status and trends of various SGCN in Louisiana while reducing the demand on staff. Passive sampling involves techniques that trap or passively detect amphibians and reptiles. Some techniques collect and store data that can be processed at a time more convenient for the researcher. Passive sampling techniques can be easily standardized, minimizing potential bias, and are ideal for long-term monitoring. Results can yield species' relative abundance and, when paired with mark-recapture studies, can inform population demographics (Willson 2013). Steps should be taken to minimize negative impacts to bycatch, or nontarget animals.

div.head: Automated Recording Units
div.p: Automated Recording Units (ARUs) are commonly used to determine the presence and distribution of vocal taxa such as frogs. ARUs are installed within or on the periphery of wetlands to capture the calls of breeding amphibians. Surveys are conducted during the breeding season when individuals can be identified by their unique vocalizations. Data are analyzed by manually listening to audio files to identify species or via bioacoustics software. This software uses machine learning to assist in identification of species by their unique vocalizations.
Chapter 9: Monitoring Aquatic Funnel Traps: Hoop nets used to survey for aquatic turtles.

div.head: PVC Pipe Surveys
div.p: A polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipe can be placed vertically in the ground or attached to standing structures (e.g., trees) to act as artificial refugia for frogs and lizards. Researchers can later remove and process individuals that seek refuge within the pipes. This inexpensive and easily implemented technique is useful for determining the presence and distribution of target species in a particular area. Capture probability between individuals using the artificial refugia (PVC) compared to natural refugia should be considered for studies evaluating abundance (Glorioso and Waddle 2014).

div.head: Artificial Cover
div.p: Artificial cover may be used to detect species' presence/ absence. Cover objects include, but are not limited to, plywood, carpet sections, and sheet metal placed in systematic arrays to increase species detection (Mills et al. 2013). During sampling, surveyors can quickly lift one side of the object to look for species underneath before escape. Artificial cover objects can be used in conjunction with VES.

div.head: Drift Fences
div.p: The use of drift fences, which act as barriers to the movement of species, is not a stand-alone technique; instead, drift fences are used to improve the capture or detection success of other passive techniques. Species attempting to circumnavigate the fence are directed into a trap such as a pitfall or funnel trap. Researchers can later remove and process individuals from the traps. When using PIT tag readers or camera traps, the individuals are directed into a detection field (Enge 1997) where data are passively collected to be reviewed and analyzed at a later date. There are numerous ways to arrange traps along drift fences. Often, fences are arranged in a "Y" or "+" shape with traps at the central point, fence ends, or along the fence. Placement will largely be determined by trap type, trap availability, and target species. Aquatic drift fences can have weights along the bottom of the fence and floats along the top to create a barrier in the entire water column; however, this may not be feasible in deeper water bodies. Aquatic barriers are typically made of woven, nylon mesh or similar material, but more options are available for terrestrial barriers such as silt-fencing, hardware cloth, and aluminum flashing (Metts and Graeter 2013). Transparent materials, particularly when used as terrestrial fences, should be avoided. These transparent fences may cause species to repeatedly attempt to penetrate the barrier, risking injury (Douglas et al. 1994, Willson 2013). Due to the climbing and digging abilities of some species, terrestrial fences should be buried deeply enough and extend high enough to deter target species from easily circumnavigating these fences (Jackson et al. 2015).

div.head: Aquatic Funnel Traps
div.p: Aquatic funnel traps have a conical or flat opening that leads into the body of the trap. Inside the trap, the funnel is positioned to reduce escape; usually the funnel is raised from the floor of the trap or extends away from the edges of the trap towards the center. Many additional modifications exist to reduce escape (e.g., flaps and additional funnels). Aquatic funnel traps include, but are not limited to, hoop-nets, crab traps, minnow traps, collapsible nylon traps, pyramid traps, and crayfish traps. When using aquatic traps, a portion of the trap must be exposed above water so that captured individuals are able to surface for air. The potential for drowning makes regular trap checks imperative (Willson 2013). Replicate surveys should use traps of similar size and mesh and use the same bait for data comparison.

div.head: Terrestrial Traps and Pitfalls
div.p: Numerous designs for terrestrial traps exist. Many designs employ funnels that lead into a holding area that is usually in the shape of a box consisting of wire mesh (e.g., hardware cloth) and wood (e.g., plywood). When paired with drift fences, this technique is excellent at detecting many snake and lizard species. Treadle traps are useful for surveying species like Gopher Tortoise, mainly utilized at tortoise burrow entrances to catch the resident tortoise (Enge et al. 2012). A hinged door acts as the entry point, and when the weight of the tortoise is placed on a treadle in the back portion of the trap, the door closes. The basic design of a pitfall trap involves burying a container to its rim in the substrate, often at the ends of drift fences (Metts and Graeter 2013). As animals attempt to circumnavigate the fence, they fall into the container and are captured for processing. The size of the container can be adjusted to target specific species and age classes. Care should be taken when utilizing any of the aforementioned traps, as individuals can be subjected to dangerous temperatures, predation, inundation, and other hazardous conditions. Researchers can provide a source of water and a form of shelter (e.g., shade cloth on traps) to reduce stress.

In the case of pitfalls, containers can have perforated bottoms to allow draining or be closed off during periods of inundation. In addition, all traps should be checked at appropriate intervals to prevent mortality (Burke 1989, Enge 2001).

div.head: Camera Traps
div.p: Camera traps can reduce time-consuming field work but still gather quality data that can inform the presence and distribution of SGCN in Louisiana (Adams et al. 2017). Currently, three types of cameras are available for monitoring wildlife: time-lapse, active infrared, and passive infrared. Time-lapse cameras take photos at specified time intervals. An active infrared camera emits an infrared beam, which functions like a trip-wire, photographing the animal as it breaks the beam.

A passive infrared camera detects temperature changes in the sensor's field of view; temperature changes trigger the camera to take photographs. In order for passive infrared cameras to be effective for ectothermic species such as amphibians and reptiles, researchers need to make sure that detection areas have a uniform temperature gradient to allow sensors to differentiate between animals and the background (Welbourne 2013). Animals can be directed into the camera's field of view by drift fences (Swann and Perkins 2014, Hobbs and Brehme 2017, Martin et al. 2017, Richardson et al. 2017). Time-lapse cameras take many photographs and require researchers to spend significant amounts of time sorting through photographs that may or may not actually capture an animal; however, advancements in machine learning may help address this challenge. Infrared cameras take significantly fewer photographs but can potentially miss species' detections by triggering too quickly, too slowly, or not triggering at all. All cameras require maintenance, but, often, one visit every two months to replace batteries and memory cards may suffice.

div.head: BIRDS
div.p: Bird monitoring techniques vary widely based on the monitoring objectives, species or guild involved, and the dependent variable of interest. For abundance, density, and similar endpoints, point counts (fixed-or unlimited-radius), transects (line or strip), area searches, and spot-mapping are among the most commonly employed survey techniques. Many of these countbased survey techniques may be modified (e.g., using distance sampling) to allow estimation of detectability, which may be used statistically to increase confidence in measurements.

In addition, passive monitoring techniques, such as passive acoustic monitoring, various forms of telemetry, and additional remote sensing techniques offer increasingly sophisticated tools as technology advances. For demographic variables such as nesting productivity, recruitment, or survival, constant-effort mist-netting or nest monitoring techniques represent standard approaches. Species-(or guild-) specific survey techniques have been developed in special cases, typically based on one of the aforementioned survey concepts, to increase detectability based on unique life history or behavior attributes (e.g., for nocturnal or secretive species). Note that all monitoring techniques have limitations and inherent strengths and weaknesses and that any given technique should be selected within the framework of specific objectives, sampling design, funding availability, and other project-specific factors. Summarizing the details, pros and cons, and technical aspects of the many bird monitoring techniques available is beyond the scope of this document, but a rich literature is available for guidance (e.g., Gregory et al. 2004).

Birds represent the most widely studied animal group in North America; they are engaging, embraced by the public, widespread, and, generally, easy to detect, identify, and count (at least relative to other taxonomic groups). Because bird populations also respond to ecological and environmental changes, birds serve as ideal ecological indicators, and, as a result, a number of standardized, long-term bird monitoring programs exist. Some of these programs are continental in scale and have been in place for many years, while others are smaller in scale (e.g., state-or region-specific) or are specific to a particular species or guild.
Below is an overview of select monitoring programs for which LDWF is a partner or that are otherwise recognized as important in the conservation and management of Louisiana birds.

div.head: Colonial Waterbird Surveys
div.p: LDWF has used a number of methods to survey colonial waterbirds over the years but has typically relied on aerial surveys using list frame sampling. In this approach, observers survey known colonies and new colonies as they are discovered while flying between known colonies, estimating the number of nests (or pairs) for each species at each colony. These and R.G. Ford Consulting Company (Colibri) to conduct colonial waterbird surveys using aerial nest photography. These surveys provide high-resolution and georeferenced photographs of all nests in a colony, with incubating adults identified (manually marked, or "dotted," on the digital images by human experts) and enumerated by species, which provides a high level of accuracy and repeatability in both the number of nesting birds and the localities of their nests. Nest photographic surveys are conducted periodically both coast-wide, using a list of known and newly discovered colonies, as described previously, and at individual colonies for restoration project-specific performance monitoring. See: https://avianmonitoring.com.

div.head: Motus Wildlife Tracking System (Motus)
div.p: Motus is a collaborator-driven, automated radio telemetry network of passive-monitoring receiving stations that allows for tracking the movements of migratory birds carrying miniature radio tags ("nanotags"). Coordinated by Birds Canada, Motus processes, archives, and makes available detection data collected by the network's receiving stations. Because nanotags are digitally coded, many individual birds can be tracked simultaneously on the same radio frequency and thus be detected by receiving stations maintained by collaborators anywhere in the network. As a result, Motus is revolutionizing the tracking of small, flying animals, including insects, bats, and small-bodied migratory birds, allowing researchers to address key challenges in full annual cycle biology such as identification of important stopover sites, migration routes, post-breeding dispersal, and overwinter survival (Taylor et al. 2017). LDWF maintains a network of Motus stations across Louisiana. See: https://motus.org.

div.head: Global Positioning System (GPS)/Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) Telemetry
div.p: This technology may be utilized to study movement ecology of birds ranging in size from Blue-winged Teal (Spatula discors) to Greater White-fronted Geese (Anser albifrons). These lightweight (3-38 g), solar-powered devices collect highly accurate GPS locations (e.g., 3-5 m accuracy) at intervals as frequently as 15 minutes and transmit the data twice daily thru GSM/cellular networks. When not in service, data are stored on-board and later transmitted when birds reenter cellular service areas. These devices are also capable of collecting tri-axial accelerometer data, which can be used to determine a bird's behavior at the specific location (e.g., walking, flying [altitude and ground speed are also recorded], and sleeping). These data provide unprecedented insight into all life stages of ecology including nest initiation, incubation, brood rearing, molting, migration, winter and breeding site fidelity, use of habitats, survival, daily movements, energy landscapes, cross-seasonal effects, and others. These devices continue to miniaturize as technology improves, which provides exciting opportunities for smaller birds.

div.head: Autonomous Recording Units (ARU)
div.p: The conspicuous vocal behavior of many bird species maximizes their detectability, particularly during the breeding season, making them ideal for large-scale monitoring programs (e.g., BBS). Vocal behavior, however, often varies dramatically with season, time of day, weather conditions, and other factors, which affects birds' detectability and thus the most appropriate survey protocol. Further, species that are rare, occur at low density, are secretive in nature, or occur in remote areas or inaccessible habitats tend to be difficult to detect by traditional avian monitoring protocols and are, thus, typically under-represented in widely available monitoring data sets. Recent advances in battery life, digital storage capacity, and programmable scheduling of ARUs are revolutionizing the ability to detect those aforementioned species via passive acoustic monitoring. This approach involves deployment of ARUs to "listen" for target species over long time periods or during repeated survey periods, at any time of day or night, and then allows the biologist to download and analyze sound files at a later date.

eBird eBird is a community science platform and online database managed by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology that documents bird distribution, abundance, and trends. The platform's popularity with the birding public (>100 million bird sightings contributed annually) ensures a constant supply of data with the ability for users to track crowdsourced species' occurrences in near real time. Protocols that maximize data quality on the front end, combined with statistical tools to minimize bias (e.g., spatial, temporal, observer) on the back end, result in scientifically valuable data products representing heretofore unprecedented resources for monitoring, conservation, and management. eBird data, for example, are increasingly used as components of largescale monitoring efforts (e.g., USFWS 2020) and population status and trend analysis (e.g., Rosenberg et al. 2019). LDWF frequently uses eBird observation data and eBird data science products to inform monitoring priorities, conservation and management needs, and public outreach. See: https://ebird.org.

div.head: Other Surveys
div.p: In addition to the ongoing and routine survey efforts described above, LDWF and partners conduct additional types of monitoring on a less frequent or as-needed basis, including Bald Eagle nest productivity surveys, Swallow-tailed Kite roost surveys, International Piping Plover Census, and beach-nesting bird surveys, among others.

div.head: MAMMALS
div.p: Methods of detecting each of the mammal SGCN vary greatly because of the huge breadth of ecological niches that mammals occupy. Monitoring should be reliable, standardized, and easily repeatable so that results are comparable over time and across regions; unfortunately, for many mammals, established protocols are lacking. Working groups such as those for Eastern Spotted Skunk, weasels, and others are attempting to address some of these challenges. For many weasel species, targeted surveys are relatively new with most historical detections coming from trapping records or incidental sightings. Therefore, much of the current research is focused on testing methods to maximize detection. Once such methods are determined, they can be utilized to help address key data gaps.

Trapping is required for projects that mark animals, affix VHF or GPS collars, assess health or condition of the animal, or collect tissue samples. If trapping, researchers should check traps at an appropriate frequency to limit stress and reduce the risk of mortality. In addition, traps should be in locations protected from the sun, weather exposure, flooding, and potential predators, whenever possible (Silvy et al. 2020a). Researchers handling mammals should consider being up-to-date on rabies vaccinations.

Baits and lures have been used throughout history to increase mammal captures and can be paired with camera traps or more traditional, passive or active capture techniques. When used appropriately, baits can enhance trap success, but the efficacy of baiting is understudied. The type of bait needed to increase detections is often unknown, and the rate of decay of the bait can influence success.
The list of methods below is not meant to be comprehensive but to serve as a guide to methods that are currently used for monitoring mammal SGCN in Louisiana.

div.head: Mark-Recapture
div.p: Mark-recapture is a traditional method of gathering data on population dynamics, movement, behavior, and density. Surveyors can use a variety of methods to mark mammals, including ear tags, Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tags, collars, tissue removal, tattoos, branding, claw clipping, fur removal, and fur dye. Researchers must consider the length of time the mark will last and if the tag will cause discomfort or changes in behavior or survivorship (Silvy et al. 2020b). In addition, genetic data can be gathered from marking methods that utilize tissue removal.

div.head: Monitoring Devices
div.p: Wearable VHF or GPS remote monitoring devices, often affixed to collars, are also integral for monitoring movement and behavior of wildlife (Silvy and Catanach 2020). In addition to determining home range size and travel corridors, collars can provide data on mortality and survivorship. The main limitation of these collars was battery life and transmitter size. However, advances in cellular, battery, and GPS technologies have resulted in a longer battery life with transmitter options that have a wide array of applications for nearly every species of mammal. The main limitation now lies in equipment costs ranging from several hundreds of dollars to several thousands of dollars per device.

div.head: Traps
div.p: Cage traps, box traps, pitfall traps, foothold traps, and cable restraints are necessary tools for researchers conducting markrecapture studies or affixing VHF or GPS devices to individuals. Baited culvert traps, a cylindrical cage trap with a door that closes when triggered, can be used to capture and translocate Louisiana Black Bears (USFWS 1995). Small treadle traps are excellent for sampling small mammals like rodents; however, these small box traps often under-sample some small mammal species, specifically shrews and voles (Torre et al. 2010). For under-sampled species and semi-fossorial species, a pitfall trap, a simple container buried to its lip in the substrate, is effective (Umetsu et al. 2006). Foothold traps and cable restraints are useful for capturing larger mammals and come in a variety of sizes and modifications to best sample target species (Silvy et al. 2020a, Turnbull et al. 2011). Researchers interested in using foothold traps or cable restraints should attend a training workshop and consult additional literature for BMPs in an effort to reduce the chance of injury to animals (AFWA 2022).

Regardless of the technique used, surveyors should take care to reduce stress on captured animals by minimizing exposure to hazardous conditions and by checking traps frequently. When using pitfall traps, containers can become flooded with water and drown individuals; closing containers during periods of inundation or perforating the bottom to allow draining can help avoid this issue (Silvy et al. 2020a). Invasive fire ants will often prey upon small mammals caught in traps. Ant insecticide reduces mortality resulting from ant predation, and its use does not affect capture yield of small mammals; users should make sure to follow label instructions (Mitchell et al 1996). Surveyors should clean and decontaminate traps between uses to reduce presence of scent, ensure moving parts are clean and functioning properly, and minimize disease transfer (Silvy et al. 2020a).

div.head: Bat Capture Methods
div.p: Mist nets, harp traps, and hand nets can be used to capture bats in flight near roosts, flyways, or foraging grounds. Mist nets are fine nylon or polyester mesh netting extended between two poles. As bats fly, they are unable to detect the netting, subsequently flying into it and falling into a baggy portion below for collection. When selecting mist nets, researchers need to consider mist net height, mesh size, and denier/ply size. Ferreira and colleagues (2021) found that traditional mist nets (length: 12 m, height: 2.5 m, mesh: 16 mm, deniers/ply: 75/2) had a 1.5 times greater capture rate of bats than more modern, ultrathin mist nets (length: 12 m, height: 3.2 m, mesh: 20 mm, denier/ply: 45/1). Harp traps are A-framed stands with vertical strings and a collection area at the bottom. As bats turn vertically in flight to avoid the strings, they lose lift and fall into the collection area. These methods are particularly useful when researchers want to collect data on morphometric characteristics and genetics.

Harp traps can be more effective at capturing bats than mist nets but are smaller, which restricts their use to roost entrances and natural flyways (Ferreira et al. 2021). Researchers should check mist nets and harp traps at least once every 10 minutes but should remove individuals immediately when captured, if possible (USFWS 2024, Kurta and Kunz 1988). Users must exercise extra precautions while removing bats from nets as their narrow wing bones are easily broken (Kurta and Kunz 1988).

div.head: Disease Monitoring
div.p: Although many diseases pose threats to mammal SGCN, few have had as widespread an impact as White-nose Syndrome (WNS), the disease caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd). This fungus is a predominant threat to many bat species, and as such, monitoring for its presence is a priority;

div.head: Citizen Science
div.p: The wide use of hand held cameras, particularly cell phones, offers the opportunity for outreach through citizen science projects. Members of the public can report sightings on platforms such as iNaturalist (www.inaturalist.org). In addition, notices on social media platforms can alert members of the public of a researcher's interest in cryptic mammal sightings. For example, informational posters were created for Eastern Spotted Skunk and distributed through various media outlets in an effort to educate members of the public and to provide information on how to report sightings. Such reports from the public are an important part of monitoring marine mammals, as members of the public working or recreating along the coast may be more likely to spot these species.

div.head: Point-count Surveys
div.p: Point-count surveys, which involve researchers counting each individual animal in an area, are useful in monitoring easily detectible species. For example, surveyors can easily count muskrat colonies in coastal marsh which can provide an index of densities and distribution (Sadowski andBowman 2021, Mullin andHoggard 2000). Researchers can count individual bats in roosts or as they emerge (Anderson and LaCour 2022). Ideally, such data would be gathered consistently over long periods of time so that fluctuations can be discerned.

div.head: Environmental DNA
div.p: Organisms shed DNA into their environment and researchers can use assays to detect this eDNA in samples. A key limitation of eDNA studies is that they merely detect the presence of DNA and not the actual organism. However, this technique is particularly useful in informing researchers on where to target on the ground surveys to confirm the existence of the organisms. The two more commonly used methods are Quantitative PCR assays and metabarcoding. Quantitative PCR is best for targeting a single species, while metabarcoding is traditionally used for sampling a broad range of taxa groups (Wood et al. 2019). When using eDNA techniques, users should consider the various factors that can degrade eDNA or affect abundance in the environment such as ultraviolet radiation, temperature, and microbial activity, eDNA shed rate, and water chemistries (Eichmiller et al. 2016, Jo et al. 2020, Seymour et al. 2018).

div.head: PLANTS
div.p: Inventory and monitoring of rare plants are essential actions required for protecting and furthering our knowledge of plant SGCN. By consistently tracking population trends, distribution, and habitat conditions, we can identify threats, assess conservation status, determine priorities, and implement effective management strategies for conserving sensitive species. Systematically sampling a population for metrics such as frequency, density, and percent cover can provide insights into the viability of a particular species. Analyzing these data over time can allow us to identify threats and ameliorate their impacts on plant SGCN.

The inventory process often begins with review of herbarium specimens, biodiversity databases (e.g., NatureServe), and citizen science applications (e.g., iNaturalist). Detailed information such as exact location, population size, and habitat metrics can provide insight into the status and desired conditions for a particular species. Ideally, utilizing habitat data is most effective when research definitively links specific habitat conditions to target plant species. Since this information is limited for many rare plant species, hypothesized habitat associations derived from population data and known ecological relationships can often guide survey efforts for discovering new occurrences.
Chapter 9: Monitoring
An LDWF botanist conducts vegetation surveys.

div.head: NATURAL COMMUNITIES
div.p: Tracking and consistent monitoring of natural communities allows LDWF to determine the status, distribution, and overall ecological integrity of these communities and to identify changes in these attributes over time. These data are crucial for developing effective management strategies to conserve and restore these critical ecosystems.

Utilizing remote sensing technology can be an efficient and cost-effective way to conduct preliminary surveys and to further refine or constrain survey areas when resources are limited. Remotely sensed data are useful for locating and monitoring natural communities that have distinct associations with characteristic soil types, elevation and topography, specific landscape positions, or other natural patterns. Once a survey area has been constrained to a manageable size, field surveys can become more focused and frequently become more productive. Remote sensing methods commonly used include:

div.head: Light Detection And Ranging (LiDAR)
div.p: LiDAR sensors provide visualization of small elevation changes through the use of light in the form of a pulsed laser. This method is useful for differentiating areas that still retain natural surface topography (e.g., distinguishing Coastal Prairie remnants with pimple mounds and potholes from land-leveled agricultural lands and pastures). LiDAR data can provide important hydrologic information that can be used to identify existing, former, and restored hydrologically driven communities such as wetlands. These data can also be used to determine structure and species composition in several community types including forests with high canopy cover and marsh communities.

div.head: True Color Aerial Imagery
div.p: This method uses images captured via aerial photography to make preliminary observations of an area remotely and assess large-scale changes in structural features over time. For example, tracking changes to woody cover in prairie ecosystems can be used to evaluate whether a habitat is moving toward favorable or unfavorable conditions and if desired management goals are being achieved.

div.head: Infrared Imagery
div.p: This method uses instruments and cameras that detect and translate electromagnetic radiation beyond the visible light spectrum. Infrared imagery can allow for a better understanding of plant species, biomass, soil moisture, and water turbidity that true color aerial imagery may not be able to provide. For example, Field surveys that track and monitor species populations are essential to keep the status of plant SGCN up-to-date. These surveys can either be conducted as standardized routine assessments or incidental assessments. Common methods for tracking and monitoring rare plants are included below:

div.head: Meander Survey
div.p: This method is often used for detecting plants with known or hypothesized habitat associations. Surveys are conducted at sites with ideal habitat for a target species during the most optimal time of year for detection and typically focus on habitat features that are commonly associated with these species (e.g., surveying along a stream for obligate riparian species). Upon locating the species, data are collected on various metrics including number of individuals and their life stage, areal extent, plant and habitat conditions, associated species, soil, elevation, and other pertinent details. By employing this method, larger areas can be efficiently surveyed.

div.head: FIREMON Rare Species
div.p: In this method, developed as part of the Fire Effects Monitoring and Inventory System, individual plants are studied over time to quantify temporal changes in survivorship, growth, and reproduction for rare, perennial species (Lutes et al. 2006).

Plants are spatially located using distance relative to a physical baseline and marked with permanent tags. Over time, data are collected on the status, life stage, size, and reproductive effort for individual plants and can be tailored to the species of interest.

The response of rare plants cannot always be directly tied to management intervention. Along with habitat conditions, a matrix of factors must be considered including presence of invasive species, disease, herbivory/trampling, and changes to climatic conditions. In addition, certain species are more difficult to monitor such as plants with an annual life cycle, as their populations can fluctuate significantly from year to year, compared to more stable perennial species. Molecular methods such as utilizing eDNA for detecting and monitoring more cryptic species are in development and may prove useful (see Hartvig et al. 2021). Analyzing topographic maps, soils maps, and reviewing archived field data (e.g., historical land surveys, herbarium specimens, field notes) are also used to locate potential occurrences of target natural communities. Remote sensing may be followed up with ground-truthing to verify findings and collect more detailed data.

Natural community field monitoring may involve quantitative or qualitative assessments performed by a botanist or plant ecologist, who inspects a site prior to and during implementation of management activities. The biologist then determines if the natural community is responding to management interventions or if additional action is necessary. For example, a Flatwoods Pond may become overrun with invasive plant species. Through visual inspection, the extent of the infestation can be determined, and biologists can recommend adaptive management actions as needed.

More intensive monitoring for hypothesis-driven research can involve quantitative sampling. In order to obtain a comprehensive ecological assessment of a natural community, it is prudent to collect and test soil samples and, in some cases, to measure elevation and other abiotic factors such as slope percent and aspect. Because natural communities are typically defined by vegetation, evaluation of factors such as floristic quality, plant functional groups, species richness, and diversity is also essential to understanding community quality and condition. This can be achieved by conducting vegetation surveys recording metrics such as species frequency, percent cover, basal area, and density. Many vegetation sampling protocols are available, and potential modifications can be made based on the specific site and questions being addressed. Examples and brief descriptions of a few of these methods include:

div.head: Quadrat
div.p: Quadrat sampling is a highly variable method that should be customized appropriately to the plant community being sampled and the information that is being collected. A quadrat is a frame, varying in size and shape, placed on the area to be sampled. Within the quadrat, metrics of abundance including species frequency, percent cover, density, and basal area may be quantified and used to calculate species richness and diversity.
To adequately sample a community, quadrat samples must be performed repeatedly in areas chosen through random, systematic, or other standardized methods.
Chapter 9: Monitoring

div.head: Profile Board
div.p: Employing a profile board or other tool (e.g., Robel Pole, forage stick, density board, cover board) is a simple, efficient, and common technique used for quantifying vegetation vertical height and horizontal cover and structure. Through this method, horizontal cover is measured by placing a board (vertically, with measurement markings) a set distance or distances from the observer. Through ocular estimations, the observer determines the height of vegetation and the percent of the board obstructed by vegetation. Quantitative data gathered with this method can be used to better assess changes in vegetative structure and response to management action or environmental factors over extended periods of time. This method is often coupled with photo-point monitoring.

div.head: Photo-Point
div.p: Photo-point monitoring is also an effective and simple standardized method to capture changes in vegetative structure and landscape conditions over time. This method consists of taking baseline photographs of the location(s) of interest and returning at specified time intervals to take additional, follow-up photographs. These follow-up photographs must be taken from the same location(s) as the baseline photograph(s) and within the same field of view as the baseline photograph(s). With strict adherence to protocol and appropriate documentation, photopoint monitoring can be precisely replicated by different people many years apart, allowing for quantitative and qualitative assessments.

div.head: Bitterlich
div.p: This method uses a sighting device to measure basal area and canopy cover. From randomly located sampling points, the observer views shrubs or trees using a sighting device (e.g., densiometer) with a fixed viewing angle and a wedge prism to calculate basal area. Only shrubs and trees with diameters larger than the specified angle are to be included in the count. The Bitterlich method is a time-efficient way to quantify stand density and overstory structure. These gains, generated through active collaboration between engineers and ecologists (see detailed example below), have the capacity to inform future avian habitat restoration and enhancement, adaptive management, and performance monitoring. Further, when integrated within CPRA's ecological review process, these and future activities will provide realworld means by which CPRA and its partners can easily convey resource benefits realized to resource stakeholders with emphasis placed on the general public.

In 2004, the Coastwide Reference Monitoring System-Wetlands (CRMS) was implemented to improve the program's capability to evaluate the effectiveness of individual restoration projects as well as the combined effects of multiple projects by providing a network of reference sites to compare to project sites (Steyer et al. 2003). CRMS was also designed to determine the ecological condition of all Louisiana wetlands, not just those affected by projects. As a result, CRMS provides the user an opportunity to evaluate restoration efforts on the ecosystems as a whole. Thus, the effectiveness of landscape-scale restoration strategies can also be determined.

Detailed Example: Suitability of habitats for marsh-nesting birds can be influenced by elevation heterogeneity, land and water interspersion, hydrologic connectivity, vegetation characteristics, and proximity to human activity. The incorporation of these target habitat characteristics into existing project design, construction, maintenance, and related items in CPRA Marsh Creation Design Guidelines (CPRA 2017) has the potential to create high value habitat for wetland-dependent wildlife species including marsh-nesting birds.

Integration of the CRMS network plays a critical role in LDWF's and CPRA's capacity to understand how coastal processes influence biological outcomes. In one case, the Secretive Marsh Bird Habitat Relationships and Distributions in Selected Coastal Louisiana Marshes Project (2018-2025) designated all sampling stations be co-located to established CRMS stations throughout the project's geographic extent (Pontchartrain to Terrebonne coastal basins). In doing so, resource agencies are moving towards a more comprehensive (quantitative versus qualitative) means by which future coastal marsh projects can be designed, constructed, and adaptively managed to generate real-world benefits for marsh-nesting birds.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND COLLECTING PERMITS
div.p: LDWF issues Scientific Research and Collecting Permits to individuals conducting valid scientific studies on wildlife, including SGCN, in Louisiana. Each permit holder is required to submit an annual report detailing the outcome of field efforts and the numbers and types of organisms impacted. Those permitted to work with SGCN must also submit additional data such as precise location information (i.e. GPS coordinates). These reports are submitted to the Wildlife Diversity Program Data Manager and relevant taxa expert. In instances where a federally listed species is encountered, USFWS staff are also notified per reporting requirements of LDWF's Section 6 Cooperative Agreement. SGCN data from permit reports are entered into the Biotics 5 database, which can be used to inform S-ranks, SGCN status, species distribution, and more. LDWF also uses a variety of other methods to ensure the effectiveness of conservation actions and the efficacy of projects. h SWG interim annual and final reports are reviewed by LDWF taxa experts who provide feedback and request any needed edits or additional information. This level of review ensures that data are collected at appropriate times and locations, that conservation measures are taken to ensure incidental take is minimized or avoided, and that all actions are informed by the best available information. h Pilot studies are conducted by LDWF biologists to test new approaches or tools for species detections. These studies are a fraction of the cost and require less time than undertaking a full study. h Prioritization of monitoring projects is based off staff biologist's participation on regional, national, and international working groups; USFWS listing workplans; species petitioned for federal listing; funding opportunities; data gaps; and additional consultation with academic experts. h Collaboration with counterparts in other states allows LDWF biologists to receive information on successful, novel survey methods. Frecklebelly Madtom, for example, was a species that benefitted from a partnership between LDWF and the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks. This collaboration resulted in a listing not warranted determination by the USFWS after novel survey techniques were implemented by both states leading to successful survey efforts and increased detections of the species. h Reassessment of methods during an open grant allows staff to request changes if the original approach is not working (e.g., traps or lures are not catching the intended targets despite the species' likely presence). h Grants that support data analysis provide a mechanism to evaluate standardized monitoring protocols and determine if the protocol provides the necessary data needed to conserve species and ensure their persistence. h Data, particularly those from SWG-funded inventory projects, are used in the NatureServe ranking calculator to update S-ranks, which assist resource managers in designing and prioritizing projects for SGCN and their associated habitats.

div.head: ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT
div.p: If conservation actions are found to be inadequate, alternative strategies may be needed to achieve desired results under an adaptive management framework. Because the conservation of SGCN and their habitats is not a straightforward process, the SWAP is designed to be a living document. Conservation priorities are dynamic and have changed since the 2005 and 2015 versions were published, and it is expected that changes will occur before the 2035 SWAP. As such, LDWF understands the importance of adapting to changing conditions, priorities, and new information. Wind and solar energy, which were not mentioned with any urgency 10 years ago, are currently topics of immediate concern. In addition, climate change will act in combination with other threats and may prompt biologists to adapt near term and future conservation strategies to address SGCN and their habitats.
Adaptive management is a four-phase cycle, in which each phase leads into the next, and is a continual process (Stankey et al. 2005).
The four phases are as follows, adapted from Stankey and colleagues (2005):

h Phase 1 -planning (either at the project or the WAP level) h Phase 2 -on-the ground conservation action h Phase 3 -the results of the conservation actions are monitored h Phase 4 -the results are evaluated, leading back to Phase 1 This is a continually evolving process, with lessons learned from each project and action feeding back into the loop, improving the outcomes of future conservation actions.

LDWF can also address changing conditions through the use of emerging issues letters. These letters provide USFWS a mechanism to fund SWG projects for high priority conservation issues, new threats (e.g., new disease outbreaks), and species that are outside the scope of the current SWAP. This allows LDWF the flexibility to decide which methods are best for each situation to better fulfill the needs of the SWAP. To that end, it will be important to periodically evaluate the effectiveness of monitoring and determine if the monitoring protocols in place adequately document the impacts, trends, and status of SGCN and their habitats.
Chapter 10: Louisiana:

div.head: A Regional Perspective
div.p: In 2018, the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA) adopted a resolution that recognized "the importance of collaborating at landscape scales to help fish and wildlife agencies meet their statutory and regulatory responsibilities to conserve fish and wildlife and their habitats." In response to the resolution, AFWA established a President's Task Force on Shared Science & Landscape Conservation Priorities in 2020, which recommended that State Wildlife Action Plans (SWAPs) serve as frameworks for regional coordination and collaboration.

Within this SWAP, Louisiana has identified Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and outlined strategies, including conservation actions, to promote species recovery and prevent federal listings under the Endangered Species Act. However, to sustain the species that are the responsibility of the state, Louisiana must consider its role and the influences of the larger Southeast landscape.

This chapter serves to examine regional, landscape-scale considerations and a means for the state to find potential collaborations across the Southeast to best support Louisiana SGCN and Regional Species of Greatest Conservation Need (RSGCN). In addition, some of the threats that impact SGCN (e.g., climate change), as well as the residents and local economies of the state, are at a regional level. Addressing these threats effectively requires aligning conservation strategies across state boundaries. By using consistent regional information shared by other states to inform their SWAPs, Louisiana may be able to better address its contributions to regional conservation priorities, identify potential landscape level threats, and help connect the lands and waters of the Southeast.

div.head: LOUISIANA'S CONSERVATION PORTFOLIO: CONNECTING THE REGION'S LANDS AND WATERS
div.p: Louisiana supports a diversity of habitats, culturally and historically significant landscapes, and ecosystems that provide benefits to the state as well as the broader Southeast region. It plays an integral role in connecting the lands and waters of the Southeast region as well as hosting some regionally important ecosystems like Salt Marsh and Longleaf Pine savanna and woodland. Many regional and local partners are working with the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) to help conserve iconic and significant landscapes in the state. According to the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US, v4.0; USGS 2024), approximately 4.29 million acres (13%) in Louisiana are considered protected (Figure 10.1). This includes landscapes like the Kisatchie National Forest, national wildlife refuges, and state conservation areas, refuges, and wildlife management areas.

In addition to contributing to the conservation landscape of the Southeast, Louisiana lands and waters also benefit the state's economy. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) provides Outdoor Recreation Satellite Accounts for each state. In 2022, the BEA estimated that the outdoor recreation economy in Louisiana generated $7.9 billion in value for Gross Domestic Product and another $2.7 billion in related wages and salaries.
In addition to recreational value, natural landscapes support working lands such as agriculture and timber.

div.head: LOUISIANA AND THE SOUTHEAST CONSERVATION ADAPTATION STRATEGY (SECAS)
div.p: The Southeast Conservation Adaptation Strategy (SECAS) is a regional conservation initiative that spans the southeastern United States and the Caribbean. SECAS brings together diverse partners around an ambitious goal: a 10% or greater improvement in the health, function, and connectivity of southeastern ecosystems by 2060. The Southeast Conservation Blueprint (v2024; Blueprint) is the primary product of SECAS and is a living, spatial plan that identifies priority areas where conservation action would make an impact, based on a suite of natural and cultural resource indicators, towards creating a connected network of lands and waters across the Southeast. Over 1,700 people from more than 500 organizations have been actively involved in developing this Blueprint.

The Blueprint recognizes almost 22 million acres, or roughly 66% of the state, as a priority for connecting the region's lands and waters (Table 10.1, Figure 10.2). About 10 million acres (31%) are rated as high or highest priority, meaning that these are areas where conservation action would make the biggest impact based on a suite of natural and cultural resource indicators. An additional 10.2 million acres (30%) is rated as medium priority. These are areas where conservation action would make an above-average impact based on a suite of natural and cultural resource indicators. There are also 1.5 million acres (5%) that are considered priority connections, or areas that can help facilitate the flow of species and ecological processes within the state while also considering connectivity with the broader region.

The Blueprint also includes a connectivity analysis that identifies corridors that link coastal and inland areas and span climate gradients. Based on a least-cost path analysis, hubs provide anchors to link corridors across the shortest distance possible, while also routing through Blueprint priority areas. Inland hubs are large patches (approximately 5,000 acres) of the highest priority Blueprint areas and protected lands, while inland corridors connect those hubs within broad areas of established conservation interest.
