This type of survey is most useful in clear, shallow creeks (<1 meter in depth). Monitoring agencies have utilized this tool to survey for Louisiana Pearlshell since the 1980s. This labor-intensive technique involves the surveyor traversing the length of the clear, headwater streams where this mussel occurs, scanning the entire creek bottom through a transparent-bottomed bucket, and counting the individual Louisiana Pearlshells observed. Due to observed statistical limitations and the substantial time commitment required, monitoring agencies developed a statistically rigorous protocol in 2014. This protocol focuses solely on delineating and counting mussels in the dense aggregations formed by this species, thereby eliminating the need to travel the entire length of the creek. For more detailed information, see Quantitative Ecological Services, Inc. (2014).

Although, hydrological droughts have become less frequent in eastern regions of the country since the 19th century, higher increases in evapotranspiration (the processes by which water is transferred to the atmosphere from Earth's surface) have generally made the Southeast more drought-prone than the Northeast(Hoffman et al. 2023). However, future changes in the annual number of consecutive extreme dry days in Louisiana are fortunately not projected to increase substantially -by 2-4% by 2025-2049 and by 1-6% by 2050-2074 depending on ecoregions and emission scenario(Alder 2024).

All marine turtles occurring in Louisiana are federally and state listed: three of the five are endangered (Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle, Hawksbill Sea Turtle, and Leatherback Sea Turtle); and the Loggerhead Sea Turtle and Green Sea Turtle are threatened. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recovery plans have been developed for each species. Other federally and state listed species include the Dusky Gopher Frog, Gopher Tortoise, Ringed Map Turtle, Eastern Pinesnake, and Louisiana Pinesnake. In August 2024, the Pearl River Map Turtle became the species most recently added to the federally threatened list.

Threats to Louisiana birds include those widely recognized
as significant at the continental scale, with habitat loss and
degradation being the greatest of these threats. Migratory
species may be threatened by habitat loss within either or
both their breeding and nonbreeding ranges, including loss of
migratory stopover sites between breeding and nonbreeding
sites. Primary drivers of habitat loss and degradation (including
fragmentation) include industrial, commercial, and residential
development; conversion of natural areas to agriculture;
intensification of agricultural practices; and changing forest
conditions (e.g., due to fire suppression). Coastal disturbance
and land loss represent particularly important threats in
Louisiana, given the regional, and in some cases continental or
global, importance of the state's coastal habitats as breeding
sites for many state and regional bird SGCN. Indeed, among
Louisiana's most imperiled bird habitats are Barrier Islands and
coastal forests (e.g., Coastal Live Oak-Hackberry Forest, Barrier
Island Live Oak Forest, etc.), all of which are threatened primarily
by natural system modification, sea level rise, subsidence,
tropical cyclones, and development. The high mobility of birds
may mitigate impacts to some species, but the risk to coastal
obligates is exacerbated by effects of climate change.
In addition to loss of habitat or habitat function, birds are
threatened by direct anthropogenic mortality in the form
of predation by outdoor cats (Felis catus), collisions with
lines, wind turbines) and vehicles, ingestion of plastics,
electrocutions from power lines, fisheries' bycatch (e.g.,
entanglement in fishing gear), and other factors. Predation
by cats (including outdoor, owned cats) is the most significant
source of anthropogenic mortality, likely exceeding 2 billion
(and up to 4 billion) bird deaths per year in the United States

note.p: Salt Dome Hardwood Forest is only known from five salt domes having surface expression, which are located in Iberia and St. Mary parishes. The "Five Islands" are situated in a line extending northwest to southeast. Currently, Cote Blanche Island and Weeks Island support high quality forest. Belle Isle is much smaller with less topographic variation. Habitat on Belle Isle is intact but is not comparable to forest on the other islands. Only a small tract of forest remains on Jefferson Island. Avery Island has lost much of its forest habitat and has issues with invasive species. Remaining forest on Avery Island is in need of survey and evaluation.FOREST SYSTEMSSalt Dome Hardwood Forest, Cote Blanche Island, St. Mary Parish EXTENT OF SALT DOME HARDWOOD FORESTThreats At present, invasive plants and animals pose the most serious threat to this habitat. Disturbance from mineral extraction and other aspects of human intrusion are also of concern. Research Needs and Conservation Actions 1. Continue field inventory work for this habitat, especially on Avery Island. 2. Establish conservation servitudes protecting Salt Dome Hardwood Forest. 3. Support aggressive control of invasive species in this habitat, including problematic plants and Feral Hogs. LIVE OAK NATURAL LEVEE FOREST Rarity Rank: G3G4/S1 Synonyms: Natural Levee Forest, Frontland Forest This community occurs principally in southeastern Louisiana on natural levees or frontlands and on islands within marshes and swamps. It is similar in some respects to Coastal Live Oak-Hackberry Forest in that both develop on natural ridges in the coastal zone and overstory dominants are comparable. Palmetto (Sabal minor) is usually the most conspicuous midstory and understory shrub, often attaining heights of over 13 feet, but a number of other shrubs may be present. The herbaceous layer is often poorly developed. Vines are usually prominent, and epiphytes are significant community members. Several introduced species have become serious invaders of this habitat, including privets (Ligustrum spp.), Japanese Climbing Fern (Lygodium japonicum), Chinese Tallow Tree, Chinaberry (Melia azedarach), and Japanese Honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica). Extent and Status Louisiana's Live Oak Natural Levee Forest occurs in the Deltaic Plain of the southeastern parishes from Orleans and St. Bernard parishes westward to St. Mary Parish. Since this forest type is found only on natural levees, which are higher and drier than the surrounding swamps and marshes, it was among the first habitats to be cleared for agriculture and residential development. The original extent of this natural community in Louisiana is SALT DOME HARDWOOD FOREST: OBLIGATE OR NEAR-OBLIGATE SGCN Live Oak Natural Levee ForestEXTENT OF LIVE OAK NATURAL LEVEE FORESTunknown; however, very little remains. The majority of Live Oak Natural Levee Forest is in private ownership. A portion of the extant acreage is protected within Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve and Bayou Sauvage NWR. There are also a few remnant strips of this habitat on Pointe-aux-Chenes and Salvador WMAs. Numerous spoil banks occur within the Live Oak Natural Levee Forest range, and some of these have recruited Live Oak and are supporting habitat loosely referable to this type.ThreatsThe majority of remnant Live Oak Natural Levee Forests are altered and fragmented, and destruction and habitat disturbance continues from residential development, road construction, and utility installation. Invasive plants and animals also threaten this habitat. Subsidence of natural levees results in wetter site conditions which alters forest species composition. Subsidence of surrounding wetlands exposes Live Oak Natural Levee Forests to greater storm impacts. 6. Research Needs and Conservation Actions 1.HARDWOOD SLOPE FORESTRarity Rank: G2G3/S3 Synonyms: Mixed Pine Hardwood, Beech-Magnolia Forest, Mixed Hardwood Forest, Mixed Mesic Hardwood Forest Hardwood Slope Forest occurs on slopes (often steep) rising out of stream floodplains. Fire may have occurred very rarely in Hardwood Slope Forest but is not a process required to maintain this community. In Hardwood Slope Forest, American Beech (Fagus grandifolia) and Southern Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora) are typically conspicuous. However, in north Louisiana, Southern Magnolia may be infrequent or absent. Loblolly Pine may be present sporadically in the overstory, and Spruce Pine (Pinus glabra) is an occasional associate in the Florida Parishes.

figure.figDesc: Pondcypress Flooded WoodlandPondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest is strongly associated with blackwater streams and floodplains. It occupies the backwater portions of larger swamplands in places well removed from active stream channels. This habitat can also occupy isolated depressions in East Gulf Coastal Plain flatwoods embedded within a matrix of Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna. This swamp type may grade into Baldcypress-Tupelo-Swamp Forest which is more influenced by river flooding. Pondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest is acidic and nutrient poor. Floristic diversity is significantly higher than that of Baldcypress-Tupelo Swamp Forest. Fire may play a role in the stand density and species distribution of Pondcypress-Swamp Tupelo Forest, which can have a fairly open to dense canopy.

Residential development is also a serious threat as such development is occurring at rapid rates, replacing bogs or is occurring in close proximity to bogs, impeding proper management. Invasive species, especially Feral Hogs, pose serious threats to the remaining bogs in this region. Continue to encourage landowners to implement BMPs and adopt Sustainable Forestry Initiative standards in the management of this habitat type. 3. Provide cost-share funds for landowners to reduce or eliminate costs associated with conducting prescribed burns on their property.Eastern Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna are herb-dominated wetlands that are naturally sparsely stocked with Longleaf Pine. This community is most often dominated by numerous grasses and sedges in the understory and is noted for very high plant diversity, including insectivorous plants, showy orchids, lilies, and many other types of wildflowers. Pine savannas historically dominated the Gulf Coastal Plain flatwoods regions of southeast and southwest Louisiana(Smith 1996).

figure.figDesc: Historically, the eastern Florida Parishes of Louisiana were dominated by extensive stands of Longleaf Pine. Now only 1% to 5% of the original estimated 1 million to 2 million acres of Eastern Upland Longleaf Pine Savanna and Woodland remains(Smith 1993(Smith , 1999)). Habitat conversion, development, and fire exclusion are factors in this habitat loss. Today, there are a few thousand acres in small blocks scattered across this area. LDWF owns and manages Sandy Hollow WMA which is the largest tract of Eastern Upland Longleaf Pine Savanna and Woodland remaining in Louisiana. Louisiana State University's (LSU) Lee Memorial Forest located in Washington Parish also contains high-quality Eastern Upland Longleaf Pine Savanna and Woodland. There are several tracts of restorable habitat on private lands in the eastern Florida Parishes, some of which are enrolled in the NRCS Longleaf Pine Initiative, which provides funding for habitat restoration; and some properties have and may continue to receive assistance with prescribed fire through LDWF programs.

note.p: Rarity Rank: G1G2/S1 Synonyms: Sandhill Pine Forest This community type occurs in the hilly uplands of the central and eastern Florida Parishes of Louisiana. It occurs on acidic sandy loams, loamy sands, and acidic clays associated with Pleistocene terraces. This community is characteristically dissected by small to large creek bottoms. Longleaf Pine is the dominant overstory species, and, where fire has frequently occurred, it is often the only canopy species. Where fire is less frequent or suppressed, a number of overstory associates may occur, and a dense midstory and understory brush layer develop. The herbaceous flora may be exceedingly diverse if fire has frequently occurred. Grasses, composites, legumes, and mints are predominant in the ground cover. This community is home to the Gopher Tortoise, a federally threatened species, which depends on the sandy soils and open herbaceous understory for survival.EXTENT OF EASTERN LONGLEAF PINE FLATWOODS SAVANNAEASTERN UPLAND LONGLEAF PINE SAVANNA AND WOODLAND: OBLIGATE OR NEAR-OBLIGATE SGCN FIGURE 5.20 123 Chapter 5: Natural Communities Eastern Upland Longleaf Pine Savanna and Woodland, Sandy Hollow WMA, Tangipahoa Parish Extent and Status

figure.figDesc: Sparta Sand Ponds may be ancient inter-dune depressions that formed in dry shifting sands during historical dry climate intervals. Known examples are mostly wooded, but it is possible this is an artifact of fire exclusion. Black-fruited Spikesedge is a sand pond specialist, and its presence at one Louisiana Sparta Sand Pond is strong evidence that it is a natural feature. Louisiana muck bogs are hypothesized to be younger than some of the muck bogs in the Post Oak Savanna of Texas. However, the formation of West Gulf Coastal Plain Muck Bog seems similar in Louisiana as in Texas. Surrounding, deep sandy soils efficiently capture and transmit precipitation as groundwater, which converges on stream valleys. Small streams become impeded by Beaver (Castor canadensis), and constant saturation from seepage leads to peat accumulation.

note.p: Rarity Rank: GNR/S1 Synonyms: none Sparta Sand Ponds are extremely rare in Louisiana, with only a few known records on the Sparta Formation in Bienville Parish. and Status Sparta Sand Pond is common on sandy formations in Texas but very rare in Louisiana, where it is restricted to the Sparta Formation. All known occurrences are on industrial forest lands and likely occupy less than 100 acres.Sandstone Glade, Kisatchie National Forest, Natchitoches Parish EXTENT OF SANDSTONE GLADE/BARREN organic matter (e.g., peat). In some examples, the vegetation appears to form a mat that floats above or rests on top of a layer of organic slurry. The vegetation mat is not thick or well developed and cannot support the weight of a person, unlike coastal Freshwater Floating Marsh. The vegetation mat apparently floats during summer months and is submerged during winter and spring.Some West Gulf Coastal Plain Muck Bogs inTexas are very old, on the order of thousands of years (MacRoberts and MacRoberts 1998) and have several plant species not present in the Louisiana examples, notably Yellow Trumpet Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia alata) and Smooth Sawgrass (Cladium mariscoides). The substrate of West Gulf Coastal Plain Muck Bog in Texas is acidic, with a pH of 4.3 to 4.8 (MacRoberts and MacRoberts 1998), and Louisiana West Gulf Coastal Plain Muck Bog is almost certainly acidic as well. Summer fires sweeping off the adjacent Longleaf Pine uplands may have historically controlled woody plant growth and prevented conversion to a wooded habitat.

note.p: ThreatsSparta Sand Ponds are apparently naturally rare in Louisiana. Main threats come from adjacent land uses and include fire exclusion and woody encroachment on pond margins by planted or volunteering pines. This encroachment may have been prevented by frequent fires burning into the edges of Sparta Sand Ponds from adjacent Western Upland Longleaf Pine Savanna and Woodland.Research Needs and Conservation Actions1. figure.figDesc: Western Hillside Seepage Bog is underlain by an impervious clay or sandstone layer that, when conditions are right, causes groundwater to constantly seep to the soil surface. The herbaceous ground cover is dense, continuous, and floristically rich. It is dominated by sedges, grasses and grass-like plants, and many kinds of unusual forbs, including Yellow Trumpet Pitcher Plant and a variety of orchid species. Many species are restricted to this habitat and the closely allied Western Longleaf Pine Flatwoods Savanna. Patches of shrubs are often present within bogs and can become more prevalent, possibly degrading the habitat, if fire is excluded from the system. Western Hillside Seepage Bog is embedded in what is now, or historically was, Western Upland Longleaf Pine Savanna and Woodland, which is a fire-driven system. This bog type, therefore, evolved with frequent growing-season fire events. Among other things, frequent fire deters invasion by shrubs and trees and stimulates growth, flowering, and seed production by indigenous bog herbs

Sandhill Pine Forest, Clayhill Pine ForestThis habitat occurs in the hilly uplands in western and central Louisiana. It occurs on acidic sandy loams to acidic clays associated with Pleistocene or Tertiary formations. Soil moisture regimes range from dry-mesic to xeric. The community is characteristically dissected by small to large creek bottoms. Longleaf Pine is the dominant overstory species, and in locations where fire has frequently occurred, it is often the only canopy species. Where fire is less frequent or suppressed, a number of overstory species may occur. The herbaceous flora may be exceedingly diverse if fire has frequently occurred. Grasses, composites, and legumes are predominant in the ground layer.

55 plant species in Intermediate Marsh versus only 17 species in Salt Marsh. Intermediate Marsh is often dominated by Marshhay Cord Grass, bulltongues (Sagittaria spp.) and bullsedges (Schoenoplectus spp.). Two other major autotrophic groups in Intermediate Marsh are epiphytic and benthic algae. Intermediate Marsh occupies the smallest acreage of any of the four marsh types. This marsh type is important to many bird species including large numbers of wintering waterfowl. Intermediate Marsh is also critical nursery habitat for larval marine organisms. Gradual changes in salinity conditions can cause this habitat to shift towards Brackish Marsh.Hartley et al. 2000). In the Chenier Plain of southwestern Louisiana, Rockefeller Wildlife Refuge and Sabine NWR contain Intermediate Marsh. In the Deltaic Plain, Intermediate Marsh can be found on Pointe-aux-Chenes, Pass-a-Loutre, Pearl River, Biloxi, and Manchac WMAs as well as Bayou Sauvage and Big Branch Marsh NWRs, and Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve. In addition, limited nutrient availability and substrate instability also affect coastal dune vegetation. The vegetative cover ranges from sparse to fairly dense and is dominated by salt spray tolerant plants. Dune swales may be extensive and are considered as inclusions in this natural community. Dunes and ridges may be shifted or eroded by storm floods, destroying vegetation. Hypothetically, if dunes remain stable, allowing natural succession to progress, then Coastal Dune Shrub Thicket is formed. This community occurs on established sand dunes and beach ridges on Barrier Islands and the mainland coast. Coastal Dune Shrub Thicket is of very limited extent in Louisiana due to relatively poor development of coastal dunes. The sites are typically xeric and moderately exposed to salt spray. This community normally appears as a relatively dense stand of shrubs, often covered with a dense growth of lichens and various vine species. This habitat type may be destroyed by sand dune migration or erosion and may be replaced by Coastal Dune Grassland. Threats Both Coastal Dune Grassland and Coastal Dune Shrub Thicket habitats are threatened by several sources of disturbance and may face increased tropical cyclone frequency and intensity associated with climate change. Inadequate sand supply is a possible long term problem, especially for Coastal Dune Grassland. Sand supply is limited by the relatively sedimentimpoverished Mississippi River and impediments to longshore deposition of sediments.

note.p: Raccoon Island, Terrebonne Parish EXTENT OF BARRIER ISLAND NON-FORESTED GRASSLANDS AND OPEN TERRAIN Coastal Dune Grassland and Coastal Dune Shrub Thicket are distinct communities but combined here due to close spatial proximity and successional relationship. Coastal Dune Grassland occurs on beach dunes and relatively elevated backshore areas (ridges) above intertidal beaches. The dunes of Louisiana's Barrier Islands and mainland beaches are poorly developed because of the high frequency of overwash associated with tropical cyclones and storms and because of a limited amount of eolian sand. The sites are normally xeric because they are elevated above the highest flood mark (except during tropical cyclones) and substrates are sandy and excessively well-drained. These sites are exposed to moderate to high amounts of salt spray. and Status Coastal Dune Grassland and Coastal Dune Shrub Thicket are each estimated to have occupied less than 2,000 acres in presettlement times with 50% to 75% thought to remain today (Smith 1993). The only example of well-developed Coastal Dune Grassland in Louisiana occurs in Cameron Parish on the Chenier Plain from Johnson Bayou westward nearly to Sabine Pass. The entire extent of this habitat occurs on private property. Grand Isle supports Coastal Dune Shrub Thicket, specifically on the east and west ends of the island. A considerable portion of this habitat is captured by Grand Isle State Park. note.p: already greatly removed much of this landscape, and smaller prairies under 40 acres would likely have not been captured(MacRoberts and MacRoberts 1997). Only about 1% of the original extent is thought to be intact(MacRoberts and MacRoberts 1997). Currently, remnants of Calcareous Prairies occur on each geologic formation in the state. There are 15 known Morse Clay Prairies in Bienville, Bossier, and Caddo parishes. Two of these prairies are captured by Bodcau WMA (owned by USACE and leased by LDWF), and Barksdale AFB. Most of the prairie acreage on Bodcau WMA was, at one time, plowed and planted in food plots. Current management involves fire and brush control, which is expected to improve the quality of these prairies over time. On Barksdale AFB, most of the prairies are of high quality (McInnis 1997). The Barksdale prairies are intrinsically important, but they also present a standard by which the quality of other prairies may be evaluated. The Morse Clay Prairie in Bienville Parish is on private land and is being improved through stewardship by the landowner. Fleming Calcareous Prairies are scattered in Vernon, Rapides, and Natchitoches parishes. Several occurrences are on Fort Polk and KNF. Calcareous Prairies found on the Jackson Formation are concentrated near Copenhagen in Caldwell Parish. Many of these are captured by TNC's Copenhagen Hills Preserve. There is a high concentration of Cook Mountain Calcareous Prairies on the Winn Ranger District of KNF (e.g., Keiffer Prairies). The USFS has been working to remove invading woody vegetation and expand these prairies to their former extent. figure.figDesc: ThreatsRemaining occurrences of this very rare habitat are threatened by inadequate fire, incompatible grazing management, improper mitigation banking practices, and disturbance from human activities as well as invasive species. Lack of fire is particularly acute in railroad prairie remnants, which are being severely encroached upon by brush. Invasive species such as Chinese Tallow Tree and Feral Hogs threaten prairie remnants. Feral Hogs are particularly destructive in wetter prairies. More than half of the Coastal Prairie remnants, including the six largest Coastal Prairie remnants, and over 75% of the remaining Coastal Prairie acreage in Louisiana are restricted to Cameron and Calcasieu parishes(Early 2025).A rising threat to Coastal Prairie in Louisiana comes from unsound mitigation practices and permitting. The largest known, contemporary, single loss of Coastal Prairie acreage (approximately 31 acres) resulted from an improperly permitted mitigation bank, which allowed the conversion of a wetland Coastal Prairie remnant to a forested mitigation bank(Early 2025). In recent years, approximately 5,770 acres on Coastal Prairie-classified soils have been converted to "Bottomland Hardwood Forest" mitigation types, while only 0.11 acres of this area was actually classified as potential Bottomland Hardwood Forest soil(Early 2025). In addition, three coastal prairie remnants have been completely surrounded by several "Bottomland Hardwood Forest" mitigation banks, further fragmenting and isolating these Coastal Prairie remnants from other grassland types and potential reconnections or expansions via restoration efforts(Early 2025).

Prairie Pothole, an ephemeral pond type, occurs on the
Coastal Prairie landscape in southwestern Louisiana. Prairie
Potholes occupy swales and depressions remaining from
ancient Pleistocene eolian deflations or undeveloped stream
channels. These features are small (often < 1 to 2 acres) and
circular, elliptical, or sinuous when occupying relict drainage
channels winding through a prairie. Prairie Potholes may be
well-defined and distinct from the surrounding prairie. Pothole
depth determines vegetation composition, but detailed studies
of how vegetation relates to elevation, soils, and hydrology
are lacking. Some Prairie Potholes support Freshwater Marsh
vegetation, with Maidencane being the dominant species,
while other potholes are rich in sedges and rushes. Although
the hydro-geomorphology of Prairie Potholes and Flatwoods
Ponds is the same, these systems differ drastically in species
richness, diversity, and composition for unknown reasons.

note.p: PONDSRarity Rank: S5 Synonyms: none Ponds are very frequent on the Louisiana landscape and are often artificially created by impounding streams or excavating earth. The typical recreational or farm pond is relatively "sterile," as it is surrounded by anthropogenic habitats such as lawn or pasture. Beaver ponds are small, natural ponds that can support open swamp vegetation and recruit freshwater SAV. Such ponds can provide excellent habitat for both fish and wildlife, including Research Needs and Conservation Actions 1. Provide education on the existence and ecological importance of natural Ponds to landowners and the general public. Water turbidity, temperature, salinity, substrate, wave action, nutrient loads, and light penetration are key factors in determining the composition of the flora and fauna of SAV beds. River Delta Freshwater Submerged Aquatic Vegetation beds can consist of both submerged species and floating-leaved species. As sediments accumulate, this SAV type gives way to the Vegetated Pioneer Emerging Delta habitat. Salinities for this community typically range from 0 to 5 ppt.

Chapter 5: Natural Communities h Sandy Bottom Rarity Rank: SNA Synonyms: None Sandy Bottom is an estuarine and seawater bottom dominated by coarse sediments, often low in organic matter. This habitat is usually maintained by high energy influences (e.g., waves and currents) that remove or prevent the deposition of finer sediment fractions. As such, there is a continuum of sediment types ranging from nearly pure sand to silt or clay bottoms with a relatively small fraction of sand. High energy sand bottom is limited to the foreshore environments of barrier islands and, to a lesser extent, beaches of the Chenier Plain. High energy beaches are nursery areas for a unique suite of marine organisms, including the Florida Pompano, Gulf Kingfish (Menticirrhus littoralis), and Broad Flounder (Paralichthys squamilentus), and are often found in association with the Marine Submerged Aquatic Vegetation natural community type at the Chandeleur Islands. Other types of sandy bottoms may be found in submerged sandbars, remnants of former barrier islands, and offshore shoals. h Soft Mud Bottom Soft Mud Bottom habitat of coastal open lakes, bayous, and bays tends to have greater densities of large vertebrate and invertebrate predatory species than do the more cryptic habitats of the Soft Mud Bottom of small ponds, marsh creeks, or other similar habitats. As a result, Soft Mud Bottom usually provides suitable nursery grounds for postlarval or young juveniles. Predation within this cryptic habitat occurs more from terrestrial sources (e.g., wading birds, shorebirds, and mammals) as compared to Soft Mud Bottom in openwater habitats. The loss of this cryptic habitat is a major issue associated with the ongoing changes to the geomorphology in the coastal zone. As water bodies expand and merge into larger areas, there is a reduction in suitable nursery habitat, which could lead to a decrease in abundance and biodiversity.

figure.figDesc: The source of the river is in the Ouachita Mountains of west-central Arkansas near the Oklahoma border. The river flows south through northeast Louisiana and joins the Tensas River north of the town of Jonesville to form the Black River, which empties into the Red River. The total length of the river is 542 miles. In Louisiana, the Ouachita Basin covers 10,000 square miles of drainage area(LDEQ 1993) which mostly consists of rich alluvial plains cultivated in soybeans, cotton, and corn. The northwest corner of the basin is cultivated in Loblolly Pine plantations. Bayou Bartholomew and Bayou D'Arbonne are the major tributaries of the Ouachita River with Bayou Bartholomew being home to one of the most diverse assemblages of freshwater mussels and fishes in the United States.There are two sets of locks and dams on the Ouachita River in Louisiana. The Jonesville and Columbia locks and dams were constructed by the USACE and opened to navigation in 1972. Each structure impounds a slack-water pool approximately 100 miles long. The Catahoula Diversion Channel and Control Structure and the Little River Closure Dam are located in the Jonesville Lock and Dam pool southwest of Jonesville. The diversion channel diverts flows from Catahoula Lake into Black

figure.figDesc: Pearl River Map Turtle (Graptemys pearlensis) from the Pearl Basin Many rivers drain the Florida Parishes, introducing fresh water into Lakes Maurepas, Pontchartrain, and Borgne. The largest of these, the Pearl and Amite rivers, have headwaters in Mississippi. The rivers of this basin have eroded and incised the uplands to form distinct river valleys. Lakes Maurepas, Pontchartrain, and Borgne form a shallow brackish receiving basin for freshwater from the Amite, Tickfaw, Blind, Tangipahoa, Tchefuncte, and Pearl rivers as well as Bayou Lacombe and Bayou Bonfouca. Freshwater is also introduced through regional drainage and diversion canals, whereas salt water enters these lakes from the Gulf of America via the Mississippi Sound, Mississippi River Gulf Outlet (MRGO), Chef Menteur Pass, and Rigolets Pass. The Mississippi River Deltaic Plain lies to the south of these lakes. The extreme eastern edge of the basin is bordered by thin ribbons of sand and marsh known as the Chandeleur Islands. These islands are the headland remnants of the St. Bernard Delta of the Mississippi River but have undergone extensive erosion through the years, most recently due to strong hurricanes such as Katrina, Gustav, Isaac, and Ida. These islands are of critical importance to a number of SGCN, including sea turtles and many species of shorebirds and colonial nesting waterbirds.

For Crustaceans and Non-crustacean Arthropods, the data gaps and research needs are so extensive that a table would not have been informative; instead, the needs are listed within the General and Species-specific Research Actions and Needs section. figure.figDesc: Using nested containers allows the collector to more easily remove the inner container, in which specimens are trapped, while leaving the outer container in the substrate for easier redeployment of the trap. Usually each trap is covered with a roof to prevent filling from rain and disturbance by curious animals. Pitfall traps may be deployed dry or partly filled with alcohol or other killing/preserving agents; trap-checking intervals can vary among types. These traps are effective for capturing ground-dwelling arthropods in many different habitats, but, typically, require a settling in period to avoid disturbance effects from trap installation(Montogomery et al. 2021).Hohbein and Conway (2018) provide a thorough review of pitfall trap-related studies, and Brown and Matthews

Common practice includes utilizing multiple active sampling techniques within a single survey effort to increase detection rates. It is important to record abiotic factors (e.g., temperature, time, relative humidity) during survey efforts to evaluate how these parameters influence species' presence and aid in comparisons among survey results.

figure.figDesc: Mark-recapture surveys involve uniquely marking captured individuals with the intent to recapture those marked individuals at a later time. Biologists can gather information on species' life history data such as growth rates, maturity rates, and age from recaptured individuals. This method, which may be paired with other survey techniques, can provide relative population abundance and population density as well as estimates of population size and structure(Winne 2013). Commonly used marking methods include but are not limited to, scute drilling and notching, paint marking, scale clipping and cauterizing, Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tags, and Visible Implant Elastomer (VIE) tags.

Coordinated marsh bird monitoring has developed since 2010, both within Louisiana, spurred by response to and assessment of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, and continentally with the publication of a standardized marsh bird monitoring protocol(Conway 2011). The Conway protocol consists of three surveys per season, encompassing the breeding phenology of all focal species, conducted at a number of permanent survey points located at least 400 m apart. Individual surveys are essentially point counts that consist of alternating periods of silence and periods of focal species call-broadcast (to elicit vocal response), and utilize distance sampling to estimate detection rates. North American marsh bird monitoring data are housed on the Avian Knowledge Network. Initiated in 1989 and coordinated by the Institute for Bird Populations (IBP), the MAPS program represents the standard for the collection of breeding bird demographic data utilizing LDWF Waterfowl Surveys LDWF conducts several different aerial surveys to develop population indices for monitoring relative changes in the abundance and distribution of different guilds and species of waterfowl. Annual surveys of the coastal zone between the Gulf of America and U.S. Highway 90 are conducted from September through January along north-south transects that are one-quarter mile in width and range from eight to 48 miles in length. These transects are spaced at 7.5-mile intervals in southwestern Louisiana and at 15-mile intervals in southeastern Louisiana, resulting in 3% and 1.5% sampling rates in the two areas, respectively. Observers conduct these transect surveys using a fixed-wing aircraft flying at an altitude of 125 feet, at approximately 100 mph, estimating counts of waterfowl by species and habitat type. Separate aerial, transect surveys are also conducted to estimate the number of scaup (Lesser Scaup and Greater Scaup, combined) on Lakes Pontchartrain and Borgne in December and January each year and to estimate the number of breeding Mottled Ducks in the West Gulf Coast population in April. The Mottled Duck survey, which occurs simultaneously with a comparable survey in Texas, consists of 42 north-south transect lines surveyed using a low-flying, zigzagging helicopter; randomly selected five-mile segments are re-surveyed to generate a visibility correction factor.

note.p: North American Marsh Bird MonitoringSeveral species of marsh birds tend to be secretive in behavior, typically remaining hidden in dense vegetation, and are frequently only detectable by their vocalizations. Like nightjars, marsh birds are a group of conservation interest that traditional LDWF Waterfowl Surveys: Aerial Waterfowl Rest Area Program survey.survey constant-effort mist netting. Data on demographic vital rates, including productivity, recruitment, and survival, are critical for understanding population biology of bird species and necessary for determining causes of population declines. MAPS data also link species' demographic data with breeding habitat, which is valuable in understanding bird response to habitat management, and thus of particular interest for land managers. The MoSI program, initiated in 2002, collects data similar to MAPS, but on the nonbreeding grounds, to fill data gaps on the full annual cycle of migratory birds. As with all monitoring methods, it is important to recognize certain biases associated with constant-effort mist netting when using and interpreting MAPS and MoSI data (e.g., variation in capture rates related to net height and species-specific ecology and behavior). See: https://birdpop.org/pages/maps.php and https://birdpop.org/ pages/mosi.php.

figure.figDesc: dogs have assisted with wildlife research and management for centuries, there is renewed interest in the use of detection dogs, especially for cryptic mammals. When a variety of scent samples are available, trainers can teach dogs to locate signs of scent in the wild. When dogs detect scat, researchers can analyze it for genetics, physiological characteristics, diet, and parasites. Some southeastern states have used this methodology in an effort to locate Long-tailed Weasels and other mustelids(Jachowski et al. 2024, Hassler et al. 2024). Limitations to this technique include length of time to train, lifespan of the dog, personality of the dog, ability to secure an appropriate number of scent samples for training, lack of standardized protocols, and lack of understanding regarding degradation of scent in the wild(Jachowski et al. 2024). Despite the difficulties of training detection dogs, this technique can be a more cost effective means of detecting species than many common practices such as camera traps and hair snares(Long et al. 2018).

surveyors can collect through hair snare stations which can include Motion activated, time-lapse, and video camera traps have barbed wire, brushes, or sticky paper. This technique allows become a common method for sampling a wide array of mammals, replacing other more time intensive methods such researchers to gather data on species distribution, occupancy, and
as track plates or traditional trapping. Researchers can use
camera traps to estimate density, relative abundance, species
diversity, and/or activity patterns (Parker et al. 2020). If species
have unique pelage patterns or visible tags, researchers may be
able to identify individual animals on camera. When deployed
in a grid pattern, researchers can model other parameters such
as occupancy. However, cameras can generate a large volume
of data, that then needs to be processed. Artificial intelligence
programs can help filter through the data, but more testing
is needed to ensure small animals or partial captures are not
missed. Martin and colleagues (2017) employed camera traps
augmented with drift fences to direct animals towards cameras.
LDWF applied a modified version of this technique at Coastal
Prairie sites in southwest Louisiana with great success, detecting
numerous shrews and rodents including the Northern Pygmy
Mouse and the Eastern Harvest Mouse (Manuel and Battaglia
2024). Currently, the Weasel Working Group is investigating
this method for Long-tailed Weasels throughout their range

note.p: Ultrasonic Recording DevicesSimilar to camera trapping, ultrasonic recording devices are another non-invasive way to detect highly vocal mammals such as bats or whales. Most mammals have an acute sense of hearing and use sounds for echolocation or to communicate. Distinguishing vocalizations between similar species can be problematic; nonetheless, this method can be useful for detecting certain species(Szewczak et al. 2020).Anderson and LaCour (2022) used this approach to determine species composition in bat communities across 18 parishes in Louisiana. Similar to camera traps, ultrasonic devices can generate a large volume of data. Researchers can use artificial intelligence programs to filter data but should take care to avoid misidentifications and missed detections.densities. O'Connell (2013) employed this technique and paired it with genetic markers to determine abundance, survivorship, and growth rates in Louisiana Black Bear.

figure.figDesc: Gauging the effectiveness of conservation actions outlined in the SWAP is critically important to ensure that conservation goals are met. LDWF monitors the effectiveness of State Wildlife Grants projects through the use of the USFWS Office of Conservation Investment Tracking and Reporting Actions for the Conservation of Species (TRACS) reporting module. TRACS provides a standardized grant reporting tool that allows users to create, manage, review, and approve grant proposals and performance reports. This enables the USFWS and state agencies to highlight program accountability and adherence to federal reporting requirements, demonstrate sound grant management, and provide transparency on the use of grant funds. TRACS also documents grant performance and standardizes reporting of accomplishments through numerical metrics identified by objectives that are specific, measureable, achievable, relevant, and time bound (SMART). SMART objectives provide an easy way to demonstrate achievement of goals outlined in the project. A list of past and current SWG projects can be found on the LDWF website (www.wlf.louisiana.gov/page/completed-and-ongoing-louisiana-swg-projects).

Identifying adaptation strategies to address impacts and vulnerability is a step towards climate resiliency. Climate adaptation and mitigation come in various forms, and multiple frameworks have been built to support planning and implementation of climate adaptation. Most climate adaptation frameworks include: 1. Recognizing limitations to adaptation such as the degree of natural resource management, availability of funding, or staffing capacity; and 2. Deciding which type(s) of adaptation approach(es) meet specific conservation goals. Two well-known examples of frameworks include the Resist-Accept-Direct (RAD) Framework developed by the U.S. National Park Service and the Climate Adaptation in Practice: Resistance, Resilience and Transition (RRT) Framework developed by Colorado State University. There are also multiple sources for adaptation and mitigation strategies. The Adaptation Workbook (Swanston et al. 2016), a compilation of resources developed by the Northern Institute of Applied Climate Science and its partners, provides an excellent overview of strategies.

Critically Imperiled -at very high risk of extirpation³ in Louisiana due to very restricted range, very few populations or occurrences [5 or fewer known populations], very steep declines, severe threats, or other factors S2: Imperiled -at high risk of extirpation in Louisiana due to restricted range, few populations or occurrences [6 to 20 extant populations], steep declines, severe threats, or other factors S3: Vulnerable -at moderate risk of extirpation in Louisiana due to a fairly restricted range, relatively few populations or occurrences [21 to 100 extant populations], recent and widespread declines, threats, or other factors S4:Apparently Secure -at a fairly low risk of extirpation in Louisiana due to an extensive range and/or many populations or occurrences [100 to 1000 known extant populations], but with possible cause for some concern as a result of local recent declines, threats, or other factors S5: Secure -at very low or no risk of extirpation in Louisiana due to a very extensive range, abundant populations or occurrences [1000+ extant populations], with little to no concern from declines or threats S#S#: Range Rank -range used to indicate uncertainty about the exact status of a taxon or community type (e.g., S1S2) SU: Unrankable -Species may be imperiled, but lack of information or substantially conflicting information about status or trends makes ranking impossible.State Rank Qualifiers: B, N, and M -If a species' occurrence or abundance in Louisiana is seasonal or otherwise temporally dependent, State Ranks may contain qualifiers to designate separate ranks; this is most commonly found in birds or other migratory elements. Resident populations of species that are not augmented by migrant populations and migrant species in which abundance remains the same for both breeding and nonbreeding will not have qualifiers; instead, those species receive a single rank applicable the entire year (e.g., Northern Bobwhite, a resident species not augmented by migrants, is ranked S3 in Louisiana). S#B: Breeding -Numerical rank refers to the breeding population of the species; if not followed by "S#N," then the species is only found in Louisiana during its breeding season (e.g., Louisiana Waterthrush breeds in Louisiana but is absent from the state in nonbreeding season; its State Rank is S3B). S#N: Non-breeding -Numerical rank refers to the nonbreeding population of the species; if not preceded by "S#B," then the species is only found in Louisiana during its nonbreeding season. S#B, S#N: Breeding, Non-breeding -Numerical ranks refer to breeding and non-breeding populations, respectively (e.g., Grasshopper Sparrow is a critically imperiled breeding species, but the species occurs in greater abundance in non-breeding season; its State Rank is S1B, S3N). S#M: Migrant -migrant species occurring regularly on migration at particular staging areas or concentration spots where the species might warrant conservation attention; rank refers to the aggregating transient population of the species in Louisiana.Endangered -at risk of extinction; take or harassment of this species is a violation of State and federal laws. Threatened -at risk of becoming endangered; take or harassment of this species is a violation of State and federal laws. Prohibited -possession of this species is prohibited; no legal harvest or legal possession is allowed without valid Scientific Research and Collecting Permit issued by Department. Restricted -harvest restrictions regarding the take and possession of this species exist; see current seasons and regulations at www.wlf.louisiana.gov. Delisted -no longer listed as State threatened or endangered Field blank (i.e. null) -usually indicates that the taxon does not have any state status; note that this does not preclude protection under other possible applicable federal protections (e.g., Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, etc.) or municipal or other local protections (e.g., bird sanctuary designations).

div.head: Acknowledgments
div.p: The 2025 Louisiana State Wildlife Action Plan was truly a team effort. LDWF staff from the Wildlife Diversity Program, Office of Wildlife, and the Office of Fisheries (Inland and Marine sections) invested more than 7,000 hours in the revision of this document. Ensuring the best available information was utilized, taxa team members spent numerous hours writing their respective chapters, recalculating conservation ranks, and identifying research and conservation actions. div.head: CHANDELEURS
div.p: The Chandeleurs COA was delineated in 2015 to capture priority areas for protection and restoration actions of seagrass and barrier island ecosystems (Table 7.12). This COA was included in the 2025 set without further analysis. However, the 2023 Blueprint Report (see supplemental materials) identified only 18% of seagrass and barrier island ecosystems in this part of the state that scored in fair to good or better coastal condition. Further, the assessment found 2,211 acres with seagrasses present and 97% of the acreage ranked above the 70th percentile for sea turtle habitat. The area also showed about 15% being above the 70th percentile for marine mammals. However, NOAA sea level rise inundation data indicates nearly all the island acres evaluated would be affected by a 2' sea level rise by 2060.

div.head: DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE PRIORITIES AND LOUISIANA
div.p: The Department of Defense (DoD) manages nearly 29 million acres within the United States. While one of the primary functions of these lands and waters are to support vital military readiness testing, training, and operations, they also encompass some of the most important and biodiverse lands under federal control. DoD managed lands provide habitat for nearly 500 federally listed plant and animal species and for over 550 additional at-risk species. Sixty federally listed species and 74 at-risk-species occur only on DoD lands. Protecting species and managing natural resources helps DoD sustain the use of their lands for realistic and mission-essential testing, training, and operations. Given the frequent alignment between military and conservation goals, working with the DoD bases offers opportunities to promote conservation actions and collaborate with the DoD to support both regional and state SGCN.
